AC Arthritis

Shoulder & Elbow · 1 / 60

1Basics

Epidemiology

Frequencymost common cause of AC joint pain

Demographics↑ with age; can start by 2nd decade

Classic patientweight-lifters + overhead throwing athletes (constant heavy overhead activity)

Risk factorstrauma · post-traumatic (clavicle fracture, AC instability) · distal clavicle osteolysis · inflammatory (RA) · post-infectious (septic arthritis)

Pathophysiology

Mechanismlarge axial loads through a small contact area → repetitive microtrauma → OA (same mechanism as distal clavicle osteolysis)

Aggravatorsarticular disc degeneration + oblique joint surface orientation → ↑ contact forces

Anatomy – AC joint & ligaments

AC jointdiarthrodial; scapula ↔ clavicle; fibrocartilaginous intra-articular disc (analogous to knee meniscus); small surface, high axial + rotational loads

Ligament Stability provided Injury →
AC ligaments Anterior–posterior (horizontal) AP instability
Posterior + superior AC ligaments Most important AC stabilisers Posterior instability of distal clavicle
Anterior + superior AC ligaments Anterior Anterior instability (one OB explanation) · no instability (another OB explanation) — read the options
CC ligaments (conoid + trapezoid) Superior–inferior (vertical) Superior instability

Not AC stabiliserscoracohumeral ligament (rotator interval) · coracoacromial ligament (anterior acromion; released in subacromial decompression) · deltotrapezial fascia (only elevated in open DCE)

Rare instabilitiesinferior (CC ligaments resist superior displacement) · rotational (rotation is normal baseline load)

3Presentation

Symptomsactivity-related superior shoulder pain; overhead activity, pressing (bench press, push-up), lying on affected side

Palpationdirect AC joint tenderness; prominent distal clavicle (osteophytes)

Provocativecross-body adduction test (most classic) · O'Brien active compression (90° forward flexion) → AC pain

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Modality Finding
X-ray – Zanca view (15° cephalic tilt; 10–15° in TO/OB) Best view; osteophytes, joint space narrowing, distal clavicle osteolysis
X-ray caveat Changes often present without symptoms (poor clinical correlation)
MRI ↑ signal + oedema in AC joint; shows associated cuff / LHB pathology

Diagnostic injection

AC joint injection (corticosteroid / local anaesthetic, e.g. bupivacaine)diagnostic + therapeutic; relief confirms AC source

Accuracyjoint hard to access, often missed → ultrasound ↑ accuracy; most get no long-term relief

5Management

Symptomatic AC arthritis
  • First line→activity modification (avoid pressing) + PT (shoulder girdle) + NSAIDs
  • Persistent→corticosteroid injection (US-guided)
  • Failed nonop, severe symptoms→distal clavicle excision (Mumford)
    • Arthroscopic→resect 0.5–1 cm, evaluate + treat GH pathology
    • Open→meticulous deltotrapezial fascia repair

Distal clavicle excision – preserving posterosuperior capsule

Mumford proceduredistal clavicle resection, arthroscopic (burr) or open; indication = severe symptoms, failed nonop

Resection amount Source
0.5–1.0 cm (lateral clavicle) Orthobullets, OB
4–8 mm may suffice arthroscopically (preserves superior AC ligaments → less bone than open) OB (Nuber)
>1–1.5 cm = aggressive → instability Orthobullets, OB

Structure to preserveposterosuperior joint capsule / posterior + superior AC ligaments → prevents AP (posterior) instability

Over-resectionAC or CC ligament damage → instability; even correct length + posterosuperior damage → AP instability

Under-resectionpersistent pain

Arthroscopic vs open distal clavicle excision

Outcomessimilar; choice = surgeon preference

Only proven arthroscopic advantageevaluation of the glenohumeral joint + treat associated pathology (rotator cuff, LHB, labrum / SLAP)

Missed pathology with open15 missed SLAP lesions in failed open DCE (Berg) → do diagnostic arthroscopy even with open DCE

Not proven arthroscopic advantageslower complication rate · lower infection rate · ↓ surgical time · preservation of CC or inferior AC ligaments

Other arthroscopic pluses (OB)direct view of clavicle end, less soft-tissue violation, shorter rehab, quicker return

Open DCErequires meticulous deltotrapezial fascia repair

6Complications

Complication Cause
AP instability Over-resection >1–1.5 cm · sacrificing posterior + superior AC ligaments
Superior–inferior instability Iatrogenic; resection compromising CC ligaments
Persistent pain Incomplete resection – most commonly posterior-superior distal clavicle
Heterotopic ossification
Stiffness, infection Causes of failed DCE (OB)
Deltoid dehiscence Inadequate deltotrapezial fascia repair after open DCE

Failed DCE managementconservative, revision, or ligament reconstruction

X vs Y

AC ligaments CC ligaments
Components Superior, posterior, anterior, inferior Conoid + trapezoid
Plane Anterior–posterior Superior–inferior
Injured by Aggressive DCE / debridement Over-aggressive resection (iatrogenic)
Instability Posterior (post + sup injured) Superior
Arthroscopic DCE Open DCE
GH evaluation Yes No (add scope)
Key closure step — Deltotrapezial fascia repair
Specific risk Under-resection (visualisation) Deltoid dehiscence, missed SLAP

How it's asked

"Weightlifter, superior shoulder pain with bench press — best X-ray view?"Zanca (15° cephalic tilt)

"Weightlifter, persistent popping after arthroscopic DCE, posterosuperior ligaments damaged — instability direction?"posterior
✗ Wrong options: anterior · inferior · rotational · superior = CC ligaments

"Structure most important to preserve during arthroscopic DCE?"posterosuperior joint capsule
✗ Wrong options: coracohumeral · coracoacromial · anterosuperior capsule · deltotrapezial insertion

"Only documented benefit of arthroscopic over open DCE?"ability to evaluate the glenohumeral joint
✗ Wrong options: lower complications · ↓ surgical time · CC / inferior AC ligament preservation

"Persistent pain after DCE — commonest cause?"incomplete resection of posterior-superior distal clavicle

"Deltoid weakness after open DCE?"inadequate deltotrapezial fascia repair

"How much clavicle to resect arthroscopically?"0.5–1 cm (4–8 mm may suffice; >1–1.5 cm → instability)

Acromioclavicular Joint

Shoulder & Elbow · 2 / 60

1Basics

Osteology & articular disc

Joint typediarthrodial; capsule + intra-articular synovium + articular cartilage interface

Intra-articular discfibrocartilaginous; usually meniscoid-like · complete disc very rare (TO); variable size/shape

Cartilage (TO)hyaline → fibrocartilage: acromial side by age 17 · clavicular side by age 24

Motion

Claviclerotates 40–50° posteriorly with shoulder elevation

Through AC jointonly 8° of rotation; remainder = scapular rotation + SC joint motion

Joint itselfgliding motions only; most motion from the bones, not through the joint

Stability – AC vs CC ligaments

Restraint Direction Key facts
AC ligaments / capsule (superior, inferior, anterior, posterior) Horizontal (AP) Superior strongest, then posterior; constrain posterior clavicular rotation; small-displacement vertical stability (TO)
Trapezoid (CC; anterolateral) Horizontal + vertical loads Inserts 3 cm from clavicle end; >3× thicker at clavicular end (TO); origin posterior half of coracoid dorsum (TO)
Conoid (CC; posteromedial) Vertical Inserts 4.5 cm from clavicle end, posterior border; more important CC ligament; clavicular insertion ~2× wider/thicker than coracoid → inverted cone (TO); origin more posterior on coracoid base (TO)
Deltotrapezial fascia, capsule, deltoid, trapezius Additional Secondary stabilisers

Normal CC distance11–13 mm (superior coracoid → inferior clavicle)

Biomechanics of the AC ligaments (TO)

AP vs vertical (TO)AC capsule + ligaments give 3× more control in AP than vertical direction

Thickness (TO)1–5 mm; inner osseous insertion 3–4 mm from joint line, peripheral fibres farther

Superior ligamentmost robust; principal horizontal stabiliser; ~50% of AP strength (OB); thickest posteriorly

Posterior ligamentadds ~25% of AP strength (OB)

Two-bundle model (TO)superoposterior bundle resists posterior clavicular translation · thin anteroinferior bundle limits anterior displacement

5Management

Distal clavicle excision – posterosuperior AC ligaments

Mumford procedure(arthroscopic) distal clavicle resection for AC arthrosis; resection length debated

Must preservesuperior + posterior AC ligaments / capsule → prevents post-op AP (posterior) instability

Over-resection signpopping + pain + mild posterior instability, no deformity on X-ray (e.g. 8 mm excised in weightlifter) → posterior + superior AC ligaments compromised

✗ Wrong option: anterior + superior ACopposite answer; these resist anterior translation

✗ Conoid / trapezoidvertical restraints; injured in grade III or higher separations → superior clavicular migration

✗ Wrong option: coracohumeral ligamentnot an AC stabiliser

AC separation – reduction & stabilisation

AC separation Feature Treatment
Type III — Controversial
Type V Clavicle elevated 100–300% + extensive soft-tissue stripping Surgical AC reduction + stabilisation

✗ Type V distractorssling · NSAIDs + rapid return · arthroscopic partial claviculectomy · acromionectomy

X vs Y

AC ligaments CC ligaments (conoid + trapezoid)
Plane Horizontal / AP Vertical
Strongest component Superior (then posterior) Conoid (more important)
Threatened by Distal clavicle excision (too much) Grade ≥III AC separation
Failure → Posterior instability, popping Superior clavicle migration
Trapezoid Conoid
Position Anterolateral Posteromedial
Distance from clavicle end 3 cm 4.5 cm
Shape (TO) >3× thicker at clavicular end Inverted cone
Role Horizontal + vertical Vertical (primary)

How it's asked

"Structure responsible for AP stability of AC joint?"posterosuperior part of capsule (TO)
✗ Wrong options: anteroinferior capsule · trapezoid · conoid

"Arthroscopic distal clavicle excision — preserve what to prevent AP instability?"superior + posterior AC capsule
✗ Wrong options: trapezoid · conoid · coracohumeral

"Popping + posterior clavicle instability after Mumford — what was compromised?"posterior + superior AC ligaments
✗ Wrong options: anterior + superior

"Quarterback, clavicle tenting under skin (type V) — management?"AC reduction + stabilisation
✗ Wrong options: sling · NSAIDs · claviculectomy · acromionectomy

"Primary vertical stabiliser of AC joint?"conoid ligament

"Strongest AC ligament?"superior (~50% AP strength), then posterior (~25%)

Acromioclavicular Joint Injury

Shoulder & Elbow · 3 / 60

1Basics

Epidemiology

Frequency9% of shoulder girdle injuries · 40–50% of shoulder injuries in sports (OB)

Demographics♂ > ♀, athletes, young

AKA"shoulder separation" = disruption of AC ± CC ligaments

Anatomy

AC jointdiarthrodial; medial acromion + lateral clavicle; oblique surface

Intra-articular discfibrocartilaginous (≈ knee meniscus); involutes, gone by age 40

Motionmainly gliding; clavicle rotates 40–50° posteriorly with elevation but only ~8° through AC joint (synchronous scapuloclavicular motion)

Dynamic stabilisersanterior deltoid + trapezius (deltotrapezial fascia)

AC vs CC ligament function (horizontal vs vertical stability)

Ligament Controls Key fact
AC ligaments (sup, inf, ant, post) Horizontal = anterior–posterior stability Posterior + superior (posterosuperior) most important → preserve in distal clavicle resection
Conoid (CC) Vertical = superior–inferior Most important for vertical stability; conoid tubercle, posteromedial; inserts 4.5 cm medial to lateral clavicle edge
Trapezoid (CC) Vertical Trapezoid tubercle, anterolateral; inserts 3 cm medial to lateral edge
Coracoacromial (CA) — Spared in AC injuries

✗ Ligament traps✗ Wrong options: anterosuperior AC = vertical · conoid = horizontal · inferior AC = no significant horizontal role · trapezoid "most posteromedial" (that is conoid) · anterior + inferior AC most important · trapezoid at 4.5 cm

Normal CC distance11–13 mm (top of coracoid → undersurface of clavicle)

2Mechanism

Mechanismdirect blow to the shoulder (fall onto adducted shoulder); bike falls, contact sport

3Presentation

Symptomspain over AC joint ± referred to trapezius; visible step-off

ExamAC/lateral clavicle tenderness; abnormal contour vs other side

Stability testinghorizontal (AP) = AC ligaments → cross-body adduction; vertical (sup–inf) = CC ligaments

Horizontal instability (ISAKOS IIIB)may need more aggressive treatment

Type IV clueskin tenting + posterior fullness

Type V cluesevere shoulder droop, not corrected by shrug

Type VI cluerare, associated injuries, paraesthesias

Provocative tests

Test Technique Positive =
O'Brien (active compression) Resisted flexion at 90° flexion, 10° adduction, full IR Superficial pain → AC joint · deep pain → SLAP
Cross-body adduction Arm adducted across chest AC joint pain
✗ Wrong option: Jobe / empty can Resisted abduction 90° scapular plane, pronated Supraspinatus tear
✗ Wrong option: apprehension Supine abduction + ER Anterior instability
✗ Wrong option: belly press Palm on abdomen, resisted IR Subscapularis tear
✗ Wrong option: Neer Passive forward elevation in IR Subacromial impingement

Persistent AC pain after nonop type III (6 wk)O'Brien / cross-body adduction → if pain + instability → AC + CC reconstruction

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

View Technique Use
Bilateral AP AC joints 1/3 penetration of standard shoulder AP Compare CC distance with contralateral (III vs V)
Axillary lateral — Required to diagnose type IV (posterior)
Zanca 10–15° cephalad tilt, 50% penetrance Most accurate view of AC joint
Cross-body adduction (Basmania) Scapular Y with cross-body adduction stress Horizontal stress view
Alexander Scapular Y centred on AC joint, 15° cranial tilt Posterior displacement (also superior)
Weighted stress views — Rarely used; II vs III
CT — Degree/direction of displacement; often unnecessary
✗ Wrong option: Serendipity 40° cephalic tilt SC joint
✗ Wrong option: Stryker notch · West Point · supraspinatus outlet · Velpeau — Not for AC joint

PenetrationAC joint needs 1/3–1/2 of glenohumeral exposure → standard AP over-penetrates (dark) AC joint

Zanca tilt10–15° (Orthobullets, OB) · 15° (one OB explanation)

Rockwood classification & ligament injury pattern

Type AC lig CC lig Exam Radiograph Reducible Treatment
I Sprain Normal Tender, no instability Normal Yes Sling
II Torn Sprain Horizontal instability AC disrupted; CC ↑ < 25% Yes Sling
III Torn Torn — CC ↑ 25–100% Yes Controversial
IIIA (ISAKOS) Torn Torn Vertical instability, no horizontal CC ↑ 25–100% Yes —
IIIB (ISAKOS) Torn Torn Vertical + horizontal instability CC ↑ 25–100% Yes May need more aggressive
IV Torn Torn Skin tenting, posterior fullness Clavicle posterior through trapezius on axillary No Surgery
V Torn Torn Severe droop, not improved by shrug CC ↑ > 100% No Surgery
VI Torn Torn Rare; associated injuries; paraesthesias Inferior — subacromial or subcoracoid, tethered by conjoint tendon No Surgery

Type III CC threshold25–100% (Orthobullets, OB) · 20–100% (one OB explanation) — read the options

Type I trapwritten in one OB explanation as "AC sprain + CC sprain, no instability" (Orthobullets: CC normal)

Types III–VIboth AC + CC torn; IV–VI = irreducible

Type V irreducibleclavicle buttonholed through deltotrapezial fascia (most common culprit)

✗ Interposed-structure trapsconjoint tendon (coracoid tip) · CC ligaments (ruptured, not incarcerated) · CA ligament

Type IV and trapeziusclavicle pierces trapezial fascia → muscle innervated by CN XI (spinal accessory)

✗ Nerve trapsaxillary (deltoid, teres minor) · CN VII (face, platysma) · pectoral nerves · suprascapular (SS, IS)

ISAKOS consensusRockwood misses nuances → added biomechanical stability (IIIA vs IIIB)

Differential (mimics)

Mimic Distinguishing feature
Base of coracoid fracture Superiorly displaced clavicle but normal CC distance (CC ligs intact)
Distal clavicle fracture Neer 2A Ligaments stay on distal fragment; medial fragment displaces
Distal clavicle fracture IIB (OB) Fracture between conoid + trapezoid → only conoid disrupted; distal fragment CC distance intact
Paediatric distal / medial clavicle physeal injury Physis

AC separation vs IIB clavicle fractureAC separation = conoid + trapezoid both injured (CC ↑ 25–100%)

5Management

AC joint injury (Rockwood)
  • Type I–II→sling, ice, early ROM + PT
  • Type III, most patients→nonop (good if displacement < 2 cm)
    • laborer / elite athlete / cosmetic concern / failed nonop→surgery
  • Type IV, V, VI (acute)→ORIF / CC reconstruction

Low-grade injuries – sling & early motion

Nonop regimenbrief sling (2–4 wk for I–III, OB), ice, activity modification, early ROM, PT; ± steroid injection

Timeline (nonop)functional motion by 6 wk · normal activity at 12 wk

20% ↑ CC distance= type II → sling + early PT
✗ Wrong options: CC reconstruction · AC capsule repair · retrograde pinning · distal clavicle excision

58-yo accountant, non-dominant, II vs III, no AP translationsling + early ROM
✗ Wrong options: Weaver-Dunn · CC recon

Nonop complicationsAC arthritis, chronic subluxation/instability

Operative criteria

Indication Detail
Acute type IV, V, VI Recent studies: no functional difference op vs nonop even for high grade (IV–V may be treated nonop, OB)
Acute type III Laborers, elite athletes, cosmetic concerns
Chronic type III Failed nonop
Contraindications Poor rehab compliance; skin problems over approach

Timingacute stabilisation usually within first 2 wk (OB) · surgery after 6 wk failed nonop = same outcome as immediate (Orthobullets)

Old teachingacute → ORIF, chronic → CC reconstruction (no longer supported)

Type III injuries – operative vs nonoperative

Outcome Operative Nonoperative
Complications Higher (hardware commonest) Lower
Return to work/sport Slower Faster
Early function (6 wk, 3 mo) Worse Better
Function / PROs / QoL at 1 yr Equal Equal
Return to athletics at 1 yr Equal Equal
Cosmesis Better (only consistent benefit) Poorer
Radiographic alignment Better (hook plate, COTS RCT) Worse
Disability at 2 yr Both improve significantly Both improve significantly
ROM / strength / endurance No difference No difference
Secondary surgery Higher (hardware removal) Lower
Cost Higher Lower

Early-score wordingnonop "higher DASH at 6 wk & 3 mo" (Orthobullets; ↑ DASH = worse) · nonop better early scores/function at 6 wk (OB) — read the options

Spencer systematic reviewsurgery not better, higher complication rate, longer recovery

Canadian (COTS) RCThook plate: better radiographic alignment, not clinically superior; nonop better early scores

Surgical techniques

Technique Pros Cons / complications
CC screw (Bosworth) — clavicle → coracoid, sup → inf Rigid Out of favour; screw too long → critical structures; routine removal 8–12 wk (breakage from clavicle–scapula motion); failure at coracoid thread purchase
CC suture fixation — around/through clavicle + around coracoid base (or anchors) No hardware failure/migration Weaker than screw; careful passage under coracoid (NV structures); suture erosion → distal clavicle fracture
AC pin (Phemister) — wire across AC joint Percutaneous High pin migration (catastrophic); rarely done
Hook plate Rigid 2nd surgery for removal; acromial erosion, hook pullout
Modified Weaver-Dunn — distal clavicle excision + CA ligament transfer to clavicle — CA ligament only 20% as strong as CC; failure without internal fixation
Free tendon graft CC reconstruction — figure-of-8 around coracoid, clavicle tunnels Closest to native CC strength Graft morbidity; needs internal fixation backup
Cortical flip button (Dog Bone) ± arthroscopy — —

Graftsautograft palmaris longus, semitendinosus · allograft tibialis anterior

Post-op rehabsling 6 wk, no ROM · full activity at 6 months

AC joint cyst (Geyser sign) (TO)

Entity (TO)synovial cyst of AC joint; uncommon; elderly; chronic shoulder pain, ↓ ROM, large lump, cosmetic concern

Type (TO) Cause Treatment (TO)
Type 1 AC joint chronic arthropathy Excision + lateral clavicle resection
Type 2 (most common) Chronic rotator cuff tear Mild/moderate pain + reparable cuff → distal clavicle resection + cuff repair · severe pain + irreparable cuff (elderly) → shoulder arthroplasty (RSA > hemi)

Mechanism (TO)chronic cuff tear → superior humeral head migration → erodes inferior AC capsule → fluid escapes into AC joint + subcutaneous tissue

Geyser sign (TO)fluid jet through AC joint on MRI / arthrogram / USG; MRI reliably shows cyst type

(✗ Wrong options: Distractors (TO) — AC exostosis) · SLAP type 4 · biceps sheath GCT

6Complications

Complication Fact
Residual AC pain 30–50%
AC arthritis More common after surgery than nonop (nonop: no articular contact → no arthritic symptoms; surgery: cartilage injury + incongruity)
Hardware failure CC screw breakage/pullout at coracoid
Pin migration AC pinning (Phemister)
Coracoid fracture Coracoid tunnel drilling
Distal clavicle fracture Suture erosion
Acromial erosion Hook plate
Neurological injury Musculocutaneous nerve closest to coracoid (✗ Wrong options: axillary (runs at inferior subscapularis, distant))

Surgical complications (Weaver-Dunn AP translation, AC arthritis)

Failed modified Weaver-Dunnpersistent symptoms from anterior–posterior (horizontal) translation
✗ Wrong options: sup–inf translation · inadequate resection · over-reduction · SC instability

Preventionanatomic repair/reconstruction preserving distal clavicle → less horizontal instability

CC screw statement traps✗ Wrong options: "more migration than AC pinning" · "fails at clavicle" (coracoid) · "avoid removal" (remove at 8–12 wk) · "axillary nerve"

Type III Type V
CC distance ↑ 25–100% > 100%
Reducible Yes No (deltotrapezial fascia)
Shrug Corrects Does not correct droop
Treatment Controversial / mostly nonop Surgery
Type IV Type VI
Direction Posterior (through trapezius) Inferior (subacromial/subcoracoid)
View Axillary lateral (Alexander) AP
Clue Posterior fullness, skin tenting Rare, paraesthesias, associated injuries
Zanca Serendipity
Joint AC SC
Tilt 10–15° cephalad 40° cephalic

Adhesive Capsulitis (Frozen Shoulder)

Shoulder & Elbow · 4 / 60

1Basics

Epidemiology

Prevalence (TO)2–5% of population · incidence in diabetics 10–36%

Demographics♀ > ♂, 40–60 y; nondominant arm most often; minorities > Caucasians
✗ Wrong options: Caucasian ↑ risk

Bilateralage <50 and diabetes → ↑ risk of bilateral disease; sequential, not simultaneous

Risk factors & associations (diabetes, thyroid disease)

Risk factors (TO)female, age >40, preceding trauma, HLA-B27 positivity, prolonged immobilisation of GH joint

Associations (TO)diabetes, thyroid disease, cerebrovascular disease, coronary artery disease, autoimmune disease, Dupuytren's

Other associationsatherosclerotic disease, cervical disc disease, history of MI, Crohn's, breast cancer treatment / axillary dissection, previous surgery

Diabetes (both types)most common association; stiffness may be first manifestation of DM → work up · often bilateral · worse outcomes regardless of treatment (nonop + surgical)

Insulin-dependent (TO)more severe limitation + more resistant to nonop than non-insulin diabetics

Risk ↑ within diabeticsolder age (>50) · duration of DM · autonomic neuropathy · history of MI

Not risk factors in diabeticstype of diabetes (↑ in both type I and II) · diabetic regimen (insulin vs non-insulin) · glycaemic control

Thyroidautoimmune aetiology; hypothyroidism (↑ TSH) classic

✗ Distractorsmenopause (no association) · steroid use (steroids treat it) · epilepsy · renal disease · prior dislocations

Genes & lab markers

Test Finding in AC ✗ Distractor meaning
TSH ↑ (hypothyroidism) ↑ free T4 = hyperthyroidism (wrong option)
HbA1c (hemoglobin A1C) ↑ (diabetes) —
HLA-B27 (TO) Positivity = risk factor —
Uric acid Normal ↑ = gout
ESR / CRP Normal ↑ = infection / inflammatory arthropathy
RF / anti-CCP Normal ↑ = RA
ANA Normal + = lupus

Workupmetabolic panel + endocrine labs (TSH, HbA1c) before choosing treatment

Pathophysiology – fibroblastic proliferation & reduced capsular volume

Formsprimary/idiopathic (most) · post-traumatic (proximal humerus fracture, immobilisation) · post-surgical (RCR, axillary dissection)

Pathoanatomyinflammation (subsynovial layer, TO) → fibroblastic proliferation of capsule → thickening, fibrosis, adherence of capsule to itself + humerus → mechanical block · ↓ intracapsular volume

Cell typefibroblasts / myofibroblasts
✗ Wrong options: adipocytes · granulocytes · lymphocytes · monocytes

Collagenabundant type III collagen

Essential lesioncoracohumeral ligament (CHL) + rotator interval capsule

Why ER lost first (TO)changes start in subsynovial layer of capsule in rotator interval

✗ Wrong options (other processes)isolated posterior capsular tightness = GIRD · ↓ blood supply = AVN · degenerative tendon tear = cuff tear (active loss only)

Rotator interval anatomy

Boundary Structure
Superior Anterior edge of supraspinatus
Inferior Superior edge of subscapularis
Medial (base) Coracoid process
Lateral (apex) Transverse humeral ligament
Contents LHB tendon, SGHL, CHL, RI capsule

✗ RI trapsLHB = content · AIGHL + axillary pouch lie inferior to RI · MGHL is not the inferior border (subscapularis is)
✗ Wrong options: superior border

RI clinicalclosed for instability · contracted in AC → released

Capsuloligamentous restraints

Structure Restraint Release effect
RI (SGHL + CHL + capsule) Inferior translation + ER in adduction ↑ ER at side + inferior translation
SGHL Inferior translation at 0° abduction —
MGHL Anterior (± posterior) translation at ~45° abduction + ER ↑ anterior translation at 45°
AB-IGHL Anterior + inferior translation at 90° abduction + max ER ↑ anteroinferior translation at 90°
Posterior capsule IR + cross-body adduction ↑ IR + cross-body adduction

Normal rolecheck reins at extremes of motion; IGHL complex = anterior band + axillary fold + posterior band

Clinical diagnosis – loss of active and passive motion

Symptomsinsidious diffuse pain preceding loss of motion · night pain / difficulty sleeping · ADL difficulty (reaching overhead)

Examsymmetric loss of both active AND passive ROM · tethered endpoint · pain throughout arc or at terminal motion (stage-dependent)

First movement lost (TO)external rotation
✗ Wrong options: IR · flexion · abduction

Most common + most sensitivepassive ER deficit vs contralateral shoulder

Provocative testsimpingement, biceps, SLAP often positive (false); cuff testing limited by stiffness

✗ Wrong option: exam pattern Diagnosis

Stage Features Duration

Total durationself-limited; average 3–6 mo, up to 18 mo – 2 y (OB) — read the options

5Management

Adhesive capsulitis
  • Early (freezing)→reassurance + gentle stretching ± IA steroid + NSAIDs
    (treat diabetes / thyroid)
  • Failed nonop (3–6 mo)→MUA and/or arthroscopic capsular release
    • diabetic / post cuff or labral repair→release (MUA 50% fail)
  • Residual IR / cross-body loss→add posterior capsular release

Nonoperative management – stretching, injection & natural history

First-linePT + NSAIDs ± IA steroid injection ± heat/cryotherapy; often effective, majority succeed

PT programgentle, pain-free stretching + moist heat; supervised; 3–6 mo; stress motion, not strengthening

Home exercise programas helpful as organised therapy

IA steroid↓ inflammation → allows stretching; earlier return of ROM, no long-term difference (OB, TO) · stage II → IA steroid + stretching

PT detail (TO)stretching then strengthening = mainstay regardless of stage; avoid abduction initially (impingement)

(✗ Wrong options: Wrong early — sling (↑ contracture, prolonged recovery)) · immediate aggressive therapy (counterproductive unless pain controlled) · PRP (no evidence) · MUA / arthroscopy before conservative trial · cuff strengthening

Distension arthrographyrarely performed

Natural historyself-limited; most resolve without surgery

Most common outcome after nonop stretchingdecreased range of motion vs contralateral shoulder
✗ Wrong options: limiting pain · recurrence (low) · surgery (rare, >90% satisfied)

Stretching exercise mechanics

ER wand exercise (arm adducted, elbow flexed)stretches anterior-superior capsule, SGHL, CHL, IGHL · LEAST stretch on posterior capsule

Most commonly contractedanterior-superior capsule (RI) → limits ER in adduction

Operative criteria

Factor Threshold / rule
Failed therapy before release 3 mo (Orthobullets) · 3–6 mo (OB) · ≥6 mo (OB) · 4–6 mo compliant therapy (TO) — read the options
Indication Progressive loss of motion despite prolonged PT
MUA contraindication Diabetics (50% failure) · after RCR or labral repair · freezing phase (controversial)
Arthroscopy (TO) Reserve for recalcitrant cases (✗ Wrong options: RCT superiority over MUA)

Manipulation under anaesthesia

Techniquedocument ROM first · full muscle paralysis · indwelling regional catheter · steady force · early PT

FEAR sequence (TO)Flexion, Extension, Abduction, adduction, external + internal Rotation

Post-MUA (TO)20 ml 0.5% bupivacaine + corticosteroid IA

Results (TO)up to 94% subjective relief, sustained long term

Arthroscopic capsular release – structures & outcomes

Portalsslightly higher than normal (contracted capsule)

Rotator interval releasefrom anterior biceps to superior subscapularis → CHL visualised + released → restores ER at side

ReleasedSGHL, MGHL, IGHL, CHL (circumferential) · not coracoacromial ligament (= landmark for complete RI release)

Posterior capsular release↑ IR + cross-body adduction

Subacromialbursectomy + adhesion release; no acromioplasty

SequenceMUA before or after release; TO: release before manipulation allows inspection + precise capsulotomy; anterior release always ± posterior (posterior: early benefit, similar outcome)

Advantage over openspares subscapularis; releases intra-articular + subacromial adhesions

Not donecompletion + repair of small partial tear (that is for >6 mm or 50%) · capsular plication (instability) · distal clavicle resection (AC arthritis)

Outcomegains in ROM + function maintained at long-term follow-up

Infection, instability, impingement Less common

Avascular Necrosis of the Shoulder

Shoulder & Elbow · 5 / 60

1Basics

Pathogenesis & diagnosis (corticosteroid risk)

Pathogenesisinterrupted blood supply → cellular death of subchondral bone → resorption + remodelling → subchondral collapse → incongruity → arthritis

✗ Pathogenesis distractorscell-mediated synovial hypertrophy = RA · humoral response after infection, HLA-B27 = Reiter's · hyperuricaemic crystals = gout · bacterial PMN cartilage destruction = septic arthritis

Most common causecorticosteroids (asthma, Crohn's flares, SLE, leukaemia chemotherapy, graft-versus-host disease); also sickle cell, chronic alcohol

Young patientshigh-dose steroids in chemotherapy regimens → ↑ demand for arthroplasty in the young

vs hiphumeral head AVN less common than hip; same pathophysiology (genetic predisposition + risk factors such as steroids); treatment similar to hip, based on subchondral collapse

Workupproximal humerus AVN on X-ray → also get hip radiographs

ASEPTIC mnemonic Cause
A Alcohol, AIDS
S Steroids (most common), Sickle cell, SLE
E Erlenmeyer flask (Gaucher)
P Pancreatitis
T Trauma
I Idiopathic / Infection
C Caisson's (the bends)

Gaucher (wrong option)large bony infarcts + severe pain; less common cause than chronic steroids

Post-traumatic AVN

Proximal humerus injury AVN rate
4-part fracture-dislocation ~100%
Displaced 4-part ~45%
3-part ~14%
Valgus-impacted 4-part ~11%

Anatomy – humeral head blood supply

Anterior humeral circumflexascending branch runs lateral to LHB tendon in bicipital groove → arcuate artery = intraosseous continuation, penetrates head · 35%
✗ Wrong options: injure when plating

Posterior humeral circumflexmain supply per most current literature · 65%

3Presentation

Symptomsinsidious shoulder pain, often no inciting event · ↓ motion · crepitus · weakness

Examlimited ROM (pain throughout arc) · crepitus · cuff + deltoid weakness (cuff strength may be normal)

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

X-ray5 views; best seen on neutral rotation AP · normal at onset · osteolytic lesion first at superior-middle humeral head (most common initial site)

Stage signs (X-ray)"snowcap" sign = sclerosis, contour preserved (II) · crescent sign = subchondral fracture (III) · flattening/collapse, loss of sphericity (IV) · glenoid changes (V)

MRIpreferred modality · ~100% sensitive · early = ↓ subchondral signal on T1 and T2 (oedema) · variegated pattern · metaphyseal oedema common/normal

Cruess classification

Stage Radiographic findings Treatment
I Normal X-ray, MRI changes only Core decompression
II Sclerosis (wedged, mottled), osteopenia; snowcap Core decompression
III Crescent sign = subchondral fracture Resurfacing or hemiarthroplasty
IV Flattening and collapse (glenoid spared) Hemiarthroplasty (or resurfacing)
V Degenerative changes extend to glenoid TSA

Ficat-Arlethip staging adapted to the shoulder (used in core decompression series)

5Management

Humeral head AVN
  • First line→analgesia, activity modification (no overhead/manual labour), PT
  • Precollapse (Cruess I–II)→core decompression ± arthroscopy
  • Collapse, glenoid + cuff intact (III–IV)→hemiarthroplasty
    • focal III defect + enough epiphyseal bone→resurfacing
  • Glenoid involved (V)→TSA
  • Older, cuff pathology→reverse TSA

Operative criteria

Procedure Indication Not when
Core decompression (+ arthroscopy to confirm cartilage) Precollapse Cruess I–II Subchondral fracture/flattening (post-collapse = contraindicated)
Resurfacing hemiarthroplasty Stage III focal chondral defect + sufficient epiphyseal bone; least bone removal Large defect · global head involvement
Hemiarthroplasty III–IV: collapse, glenoid intact, cuff intact; young → preserves glenoid bone stock for later TSA Irreparable cuff tear · glenoid changes
TSA Stage V (glenoid involved) Young + intact glenoid (glenoid loosening)
Reverse TSA Older + cuff pathology Intact cuff, young

Treatment by stage – core decompression vs resurfacing/hemiarthroplasty

Core decompression↓ subchondral marrow pressure → neovascularisation → slows progression · ± bone graft into void · percutaneous small-diameter technique (Harreld: no arthroplasty at 32 mo, 95% improved)

Core decompression (LaPorte, ~10 y; Ficat stage) Success
I 94%
II 88%
III 70%
IV 14%

Stage I–II outcomegood/excellent 88–100% at 5–10 y → ~90% successful long term · better in non-steroid than steroid cases
✗ Wrong options: 50% satisfied · most need arthroplasty by 10 y · unpredictable · not indicated

Conflict on core decompressioneffective for I–II (Mont, LaPorte; LaPorte recommends I–III; Harreld tries it with arthroscopy in III) · role in precollapse "highly debated" and drilling did not alter progression (L'insalata) · Sarris: I–II conservative, surgery when persistently symptomatic + collapse — read the options

Arthroscopic debridement / releaseno sustained benefit; AVN keeps progressing; role unknown

Most reliable, durable treatment after collapseprosthetic arthroplasty → hemiarthroplasty
✗ Wrong options: arthroscopic debridement · arthrodesis · resection arthroplasty · cortisone injection

Arthrodesis indicationsbrachial plexus injury · infantile paralysis · deltoid + cuff insufficiency · chronic infection · failed revision arthroplasty · refractory instability · tumour resection bone loss

Stemless resurfacingpreserves metaphyseal bone · Levy & Copeland 285 cementless · Hawi (Eclipse) 9 y, no loosening

"Ream and run"HA + glenoid reaming → unnecessary with intact glenoid cartilage

Arthroplasty outcomesHA + TSA both safe/effective · 10-y survivorship HA 88.9%, TSA 80%; TSA better internal rotation (Wang) · RSA ≈ TSA when cuff compromised · AVN arthroplasty has ↑ complications vs other diagnoses (bone quality, comorbidity)

Prognosisrelated to stage; stage + lesion size predict progression

6Complications

Hemiarthroplastyglenoid cartilage wear over time → 45% unsatisfactory (Smith, steroid AVN); still used in young active III–IV

Glenoid component in youngloosening risk → avoid TSA/RTSA when glenoid spared

Onset Insidious, steroid user Severe acute pain Long-standing symptoms Severe pain
Imaging Subchondral ↓ T1/T2 signal, collapse, fragmentation Hypointense deposit in cuff soft tissue No subchondral collapse/fragmentation Large bony infarcts
Stage Core decompression Hemiarthroplasty TSA
Cruess I–II (precollapse) III–IV (collapse, glenoid spared) V (glenoid)
Cuff — Must be intact Intact
Key trap Not after collapse Not with irreparable cuff or glenoid cysts Not in young with intact glenoid

Biceps Subluxation

Shoulder & Elbow · 6 / 60

1Basics

Association with subscapularis tears

DefinitionLHBT subluxes/dislocates medially out of the bicipital groove → recognised cause of anterior shoulder pain

Most common associated pathologysubscapularis tear (even partial); biceps subluxation is almost always associated with a subscapularis tear

Most important medial restraintsubscapularis tendon = most important restraint to medial subluxation/dislocation of LHBT

Walch seriesdislocated LHBT associated with partial/complete subscapularis tear in 96%

Other causedisruption of the biceps sling (pulley)

Not the causesubacromial impingement does not cause LHBT instability · isolated degenerative tendinosis (instability is from the subscapularis tear) · SLAP

Biceps pulley stabilisers (coracohumeral & transverse humeral ligaments)

OriginLHBT arises from supraglenoid tubercle + superior labrum → intra-articular → bicipital groove

Functiondynamic stabiliser; shoulder flexion, abduction

Biceps sling / pulley (intra-articular) Rotator interval tissue?
Coracohumeral ligament (CHL) Yes
Superior glenohumeral ligament (SGHL) Yes
Subscapularis fibres Contributes to sling
Supraspinatus (anterior fibres) Contributes to sling

Transverse humeral ligament (THL)stabilises LHBT in the groove at the level of the greater + lesser tuberosities (distal to pulley); not rotator interval tissue

Bicipital groovelength 81–87 mm · width 7.7–11.6 mm · depth 3.7–6 mm · bottleneck ~2/3 down from top → THL may constrain groove → anterior pain; tenodesis below the groove may be preferred

✗ Distractor Why wrong
Coracoacromial ligament (CAL) Not rotator interval; no LHBT stability at tuberosities
IGHL Not rotator interval; not an LHBT stabiliser
AIGHL Not associated with biceps subluxation (injured in anterior dislocation)
Superior labrum / infraspinatus / posterior labrum Not associated with medial biceps subluxation

Imaging finding = injured structureMRI medial biceps subluxation → CHL disruption (sling)

Anterosuperior cuff tearsling disrupted → LHBT subluxes medially → signals subscapularis tear (often missed on MRI)

3Presentation

Symptomsanterior shoulder pain ± clicking

Yergason testanterior pain with resisted supination, arm at side, elbow flexed 90°

Speed testanterior pain with resisted forward flexion, shoulder 90° flexed, elbow extended, palm up

Palpable clickwith abduction + external rotation as tendon subluxes/dislocates out of groove

Always test subscapularis strengthlift-off (Gerber), belly press, push-off

Lift-off test (Gerber)back of hand held off mid-lumbar spine in IR; hand falls or patient extends elbow/shoulder to compensate → subscapularis tear

✗ Exam distractor Tests
Drop arm Supraspinatus
External rotation lag Infraspinatus
Hornblower's Teres minor
Kim test Posteroinferior labral tear

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

MRI↑ T2 signal + LHBT displaced out of bicipital groove (axial: on lesser tuberosity → fully medial); coincides with subscapularis tear

MRI limitationmisses subscapularis tears unless tear extends ≥½ cranio-caudal length → small tears missed → test lift-off

LHBT subluxation on MRI as predictor of full-thickness subscapularis tear (Shi)sensitivity 82% · specificity 80% · PPV 35% · NPV 97% → value lies in NPV (no subluxation → full-thickness subscapularis tear unlikely); correlates with tear severity

Ultrasounddynamic test of biceps instability

Arthroscopy↓ biceps–glenoid angle associated with subluxation (87° vs 90°; Koh) → statistically significant but not clinically relevant

5Management

Biceps subluxation
  • Initial→NSAIDs + PT + steroid injection
    (injection near, not into, the tendon)
  • Refractory→arthroscopic/open tenotomy or tenodesis
    • subscapularis tear→+ subscapularis repair

Nonoperative

First lineNSAIDs, PT strengthening, activity modification, steroid injection (adjacent to tendon, not into it)

Operative

Indicationrefractory symptoms

Optionsarthroscopic vs open biceps tenotomy vs tenodesis ± subscapularis repair; instability can be tested intra-op

Acute traumatic medial LHBT instability (Maier)open subscapularis repair + LHBT stabilisation = equal function to tenotomy/tenodesis, better cosmesis, less cramping

THL releaseroutine release at tenotomy/tenodesis may ↓ post-op anterior pain

Biceps tenotomy for irreparable cuff tear

Indicationlarge/massive irreparable cuff tear, pain main complaint, good active elevation (e.g. 120°), normal articular surfaces → biceps tenotomy

Alternative When
Latissimus dorsi transfer Severe ER deficit + deficient teres minor
Reverse TSA Cuff tear arthropathy + pseudoparalysis
✗ Wrong option: SLAP repair Contraindicated in this age group

Symptomsanterior shoulder pain ± radiating down biceps; mimics cuff/impingement pain

Groove tendernessover bicipital groove; worse with arm internally rotated 10°

Test Manoeuvre Positive
Speed Forward elevate against resistance, elbow extended + forearm supinated Pain in bicipital groove; also + in SLAP
Yergason Active supination against resistance, elbow 90°, forearm pronated Pain in bicipital groove
Popeye Distal bulge of biceps muscle Rupture

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

USthickened tendon within bicipital groove

MRIevaluates concurrent pathology (subscapularis, cuff) · thickening + tenosynovitis of proximal LHB · ↑ T2 signal around tendon · longitudinal split tears

Diagnostic US-guided injectiongroove steroid → temporary relief supports LHB as pain generator (e.g. 90% relief × 4 wk)

5Management

Biceps tendonitis
  • First line→NSAIDs + activity modification + PT + steroid injection
    (injection near, not into, tendon)
  • Refractory to nonop→arthroscopic / open tenotomy or tenodesis
    • faster, simpler, less rehab; ↑ Popeye→tenotomy
    • natural contour; drilling / retraction nerve risk→tenodesis (supra- or subpectoral)

Nonoperative

RegimenNSAIDs, PT strengthening, activity modification, steroid injection (in proximity, not into tendon)

Tenodesis vs tenotomy

Only proven differencePopeye (cosmetic) deformity ↑ with tenotomy

No differencestrength, pain (VAS), ASES / patient-reported outcomes, shoulder + elbow ROM, supination (level 1 evidence)

Crampingtenodesis possibly ↓ arm cramping (surgeon belief) · not shown in high-level studies — read the options

Tenotomy prosfaster, simpler, less rehab, faster return to activity

Tenodesis prosnatural muscle contour; but extra risks: nerve injury (bicortical drilling, musculocutaneous retraction)

Bite study (OB)tenotomy vs suprapectoral tenodesis with cuff repair: differences small; non-inferiority statistically inconclusive on Constant-Murley at 1 y

Tenodesis technique – suprapectoral vs subpectoral, arthroscopic vs open

Arthroscopic suprapectoral Open subpectoral
Fixation site Proximal in groove Distal groove, at pectoralis major insertion
Rationale — Removes tendon from groove (eliminates groove pain)
Residual / groove pain Similar Similar
Popeye, ROM, strength, PROMs, revision Similar (revision very low) Similar
Nerve injury Lower (unicortical drilling) ↑ transient neuropraxia · axillary n. (bicortical drilling) · medial NV structures (retraction)

Complicationsoverall complication rates similar (OB) · subpectoral ↑ transient neuropraxia (OB) — read the options

Groove painOrthobullets lists tenodesis → possible "groove pain"; recent prospective studies → no difference supra vs subpectoral

Postoperative function after tenodesis

Rehabfull active shoulder ROM; avoid active supination with elbow 90° + resisted elbow flexion until healed

Long-termno change in shoulder or elbow strength
✗ Wrong options: ↓ elbow flexion · ↓ supination · ↓ shoulder abduction/elevation

Brachial Neuritis (Parsonage-Turner Syndrome)

Shoulder & Elbow · 8 / 60

1Basics

Epidemiology

Incidence1.6–3/100,000/y (Orthobullets text) · 1–30/100,000/y (Orthobullets INA vs HNA table); underdiagnosed

Demographics♂ > ♀ (1.5:1 to 11.5:1) · middle age (4th decade), 20–60 y, mean 41 (range 3–81)

Sideunilateral · bilateral 10–30% (16% simultaneous)

Synonymsneuralgic amyotrophy (NA) · idiopathic neuralgic amyotrophy (INA) · Parsonage-Turner syndrome (PTS) · acute brachial neuritis/plexitis · idiopathic brachial plexus neuropathy

Nerves involved

Distributionany brachial plexus nerve/branch · outside plexus in 17% · usually upper plexus + >1 nerve

Most common nerveslong thoracic (→ medial scapular winging) · suprascapular · axillary · musculocutaneous · radial (Orthobullets, OB)

Otherscervical roots, AIN, PIN, LABC

Musclesdeltoid, supraspinatus, infraspinatus, serratus anterior, biceps

Pathophysiology

Aetiologyunknown; multifactorial → inflammatory response in brachial plexus

Autoimmune↑ blastogenic lymphocyte activity vs plexus tissue · ↑ complement-fixing antibodies to peripheral nerve myelin

Biomechanicalmobile upper trunk → wear of blood–nerve barrier → immune factors reach nerve (strenuous exercise, manual labour)

Operative findinghourglass-like constrictions of nerves, no external compression

Risk factors / antecedent events

Trigger Frequency Examples
Viral infection (most common) 25–55% EBV, VZV, Coxsackie B, parvovirus B19, CMV, mumps, smallpox, HIV; "flu-like illness", URTI
Bacterial infection — Leptospira, TB, Yersinia, Salmonella, Borrelia
Immunisation 15% Tetanus, hepatitis B; influenza vaccine (OB stem)
Perioperative / peripartum 14% Elective surgery
Strenuous exercise 8% Cross-training, heavy upper-body work
Drugs — Abacavir, streptokinase, heroin, infliximab, interferon
Iatrogenic — Interscalene block, surgery, LP, irradiation; burns

Viral illness figure25–55% (Orthobullets, OB) · 25–50% (one OB explanation) — read the options

Genes & lab markers

HNA geneautosomal dominant · SEPT9 (septin 9) on chromosome 17q24 (cytoskeletal protein in glial cells) · ~200 families worldwide

Routine labsCBC + ESR usually normal

Inconsistent labs↑ liver enzymes · + antiganglioside antibodies · + ANA

CSFusually normal; ± mildly ↑ protein, slight pleocytosis, oligoclonal bands

3Presentation

Diagnosis – acute pain followed by weakness

Phase Features Duration
I – Pain Sudden, severe, unrelenting shoulder pain (90%); radiates to proximal arm/neck; wakes from sleep; burning; often atraumatic Days–weeks (♂ 45 d vs ♀ 23 d)
II – Painless flaccid paralysis Weakness as pain subsides: within 24 h (33%) to 4 wk (80%); patchy paresis (muscles of same nerve unequally affected) —
III – Recovery Slow, steady motor return; length ∝ length of pain phase 6–18 months

Key exam patterninability to actively abduct with full passive motion · normal cervical spine exam (–ve Spurling)

Pain behaviournot worsened by motion or palpation · not relieved by subacromial lidocaine (neuropathic)

Motorsevere weakness of ER + abduction (SS, IS, deltoid) · hypotonia, areflexia (LMN) · atrophy, fasciculations · medial winging (serratus anterior)

Sensorychanges in 78%: paraesthesia/hypoaesthesia over deltoid, lateral arm, radial forearm; often unnoticed · sensation may be normal (OB stems)

Autonomic (15%)trophic skin, temperature dysregulation, ↑ sweating, altered nail/hair

Upper trunk patternpain → weakness + atrophy + scapular winging after viral illness = upper trunk neuralgic amyotrophy
✗ Wrong options: isolated LTN palsy (doesn't explain whole picture)

4Diagnosis & Classification

Diagnosisclinical; often a diagnosis of exclusion; tests rule out mimics; EMG confirms

Key radiology findings

X-ray shoulder / C-spinenormal; rule out calcific tendinitis (also severe incapacitating pain)

Chest X-raybaseline to exclude compressive Pancoast tumour (OB)

MRI timing Sequence Finding
Early T2 / STIR Diffuse ↑ signal (oedema) in muscles of plexus (SS, IS, deltoid, teres minor most common)
Late T1 Fatty infiltration + atrophy

MRI also excludescuff tear (intact cuff) · SSN notch/spinoglenoid cyst · brain MS plaques · cervical disc

EMG findings

EMGcompatible findings in 96%; confirms diagnosis + monitors recovery (serial)

Timing EMG
Early — 3–4 wk (Orthobullets) · first 3 wk (OB) Acute denervation: positive sharp waves + fibrillation potentials in both peripheral nerve AND nerve root distributions
Late — 3–4 months (Orthobullets) · as early as 6 wk (OB) Chronic denervation + early reinnervation: polyphasic MUPs (= resolving PTS)

Sensory NCSless useful than EMG · ↓ amplitude (axonal loss), preserved conduction velocity + distal latency · may be normal (doesn't exclude)

✗ EMG distractor Diagnosis
Normal EMG PTS shows denervation
Fibrillations from spinoglenoid notch compression SSN compression (cyst on MRI)
Sharp waves + fibs deltoid + biceps only C5 root compression
Polyphasic MUPs, early reinnervation Resolving PTS (not early)

Classification – INA vs HNA

Factor INA (idiopathic) HNA (hereditary)
Incidence 1–30/100,000/y Very rare (~200 families)
Gene — Septin 9 (chr 17q24), AD
Age at onset Middle age (20–60) Young (childhood/adolescence; mean 28)
Recurrence Rare (~1.5 episodes) Frequent (3.5 episodes)
Appearance Normal Dysmorphic: short stature, hypotelorism, cleft palate, facial asymmetry, skin folds
Nerves outside plexus Uncommon (17%) Common (56%): lower cranial nerves (VII, IX, X, XI, XII), lumbosacral plexus, phrenic, recurrent laryngeal
Severity / outcome Better More severe paresis, worse outcome

Differential diagnosis

Mimic Distinguishing feature
Cervical radiculopathy (C5/C6–7, disc) Single root dermatome/myotome; pain from neck; ↑ with movement; abnormal neck exam/Spurling (normal neck exam here makes it unlikely)
Rotator cuff tear / impingement Pain persists with weakness; impingement signs; relieved by subacromial lidocaine; MRI shows tear; does not explain winging
Calcific tendinitis Calcification on X-ray; no acute severe weakness
Adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder) Loss of passive + active motion
Entrapment neuropathy (SSN) Single nerve distribution on EMG (SS + IS only)
Poliomyelitis No (excluded by acute severe weakness pattern, OB)
ALS UMN + LMN signs, painless, no sensory loss, cranial nerve signs
Idiopathic hypertrophic brachial neuritis Painless; plexus hypertrophy on MRI; demyelinating NCS (slow velocity, prolonged latency)
Multiple sclerosis Brain MRI demyelination

Exclusion logic (OB)loss of active motion excludes radiculopathy + impingement · normal MRI excludes cuff tear · full passive motion excludes adhesive capsulitis · normal C-spine exam excludes disc disease

5Management

Brachial neuritis
  • Pain phase→NSAIDs, judicious opioids, immobilisation
    • severe pain→oral prednisone 1 mg/kg/d × 2 wk + 2-wk taper
  • Weakness phase→physical therapy (ROM + shoulder girdle strengthening)
    • follow monthly: exam + serial EMG
  • No clinical/EMG recovery by 6–9 mo (9–12 mo in summary)→exploration
    • hourglass constriction→neurolysis

Nonoperative

Mainstayobservation + pain control; self-limiting

Corticosteroidsearly, severe pain; 2 wk prednisone 1 mg/kg/d + 2 wk taper · faster pain resolution, no change in progression/prognosis · OB: may shorten symptoms/accelerate recovery

Physical therapyonce pain abated; ROM + strengthening; reduce traction on nerves · reverses atrophy · observation alone = observation + PT at 1 y

Operative criteria

Indication Threshold
Exploration / neurolysis / graft / transfer No regeneration on exam + EMG by 6–9 months (Orthobullets treatment) · 9–12 months (Orthobullets summary) — read the options
Procedure Note
Neurolysis Superior to neurorrhaphy + grafting; LTN microneurolysis, ulnar transposition, Guyon/radial tunnel/carpal tunnel release
Neurorrhaphy / grafting Excise diseased segment
Nerve transfer —
Split pectoralis major transfer Serratus anterior paralysis (winging)

✗ Wrong options: decompression / arthroscopic repairnot indicated (no compressive lesion, cuff intact)

Prognosis

Overallgood; gradual return of strength without long-term functional deficit; slow · residual weakness may last months–years

Time Recovery
1 month 66% some motor recovery
1 year 35% recovered (excellent 36%)
2 years Excellent 75%
3 years ~90% full strength, no pain (89%)
Up to 8 years Full strength in some

Poor prognosisfemale · lower trunk involvement (upper trunk = best) · persistent pain + no motor recovery by 3 months · hereditary cases

No effectage

Recurrencerare in idiopathic (common in HNA)

X vs Y

Prognosis statement (OB distractor) Disease
Gradual return of strength, no long-term deficit ✓ PTS
Decompression improves strength SSN notch cyst
Immunomodulators ↓ relapses Multiple sclerosis
Arthroscopic repair best for active patient Rotator cuff tear
Progressive weakness → respiratory failure ALS (pure motor; no ↓ sensory amplitudes)
Brachial neuritis Cervical radiculopathy Rotator cuff tear
Pain onset Acute severe → resolves before weakness Neck → arm Persists with weakness
Pain with motion No Yes Yes
Subacromial lidocaine No relief — Relief
Distribution Multiple roots + peripheral nerves, patchy One root Cuff only, no winging
EMG Root + peripheral nerve denervation Root Normal

✗ Wrong options: C6–7 radiculopathy · impingement · cuff tear · adhesive capsulitis

✗ Wrong options: calcific tendinitis · poliomyelitis · cervical disc disease · impingement

✗ Wrong options: isolated LTN palsy · ALS · frozen shoulder · cuff tear

"EMG showing polyphasic MUPs / early reinnervation?"resolving PTS (late)

"Cross-training athlete, viral illness, pain → weakness, ↓ sensory amplitudes, normal brain/C-spine MRI — prognosis?"gradual return of strength without long-term deficits
✗ Wrong options: decompression · immunomodulators · arthroscopic repair · respiratory failure

"Most common antecedent event?"viral illness (25–55%)

"Most commonly involved nerve / cause of winging?"long thoracic nerve

"Gene in hereditary neuralgic amyotrophy?"SEPT9, chromosome 17q24, AD

"Poor prognostic factors?"female, lower trunk, no recovery by 3 months, hereditary

Calcific Tendonitis

Shoulder & Elbow · 9 / 60

1Basics

Epidemiology

Definitioncalcification + tendon degeneration near rotator cuff insertion → pain + ↓ ROM; unknown etiology

Age30–60 y

Sex♀ > ♂

Locationsupraspinatus most common · supraspinatus and/or infraspinatus (OB)

Risk factorsendocrine: diabetes, hypothyroidism

Genes & lab markers

Crystalcalcium hydroxyapatite (Orthobullets, OB) · "calcium carbonate apatite" (one OB explanation) — read the options

Histologyhydroxyapatite deposits surrounded by fibroblasts, macrophages, giant cells, lymphocytes

Molecular pathwaysosteopontin · cathepsin K · transglutaminase 2

✗ Wrong option: calcium pyrophosphatepositively birefringent rhomboid/rod crystals → CPPD / pseudogout

✗ Wrong option: calcium oxalatekidney stones, urine; excess in ethylene glycol (antifreeze) poisoning → renal failure

Processactive, cell-mediated
✗ Wrong options: purely degenerative; Uhthoff & Loehr

Phases of disease (resorptive phase pain)

Stage (Uhthoff) Phase Pathology Pain
Precalcific — Fibrocartilaginous metaplasia; tenocytes → chondrocytes Pain-free
Calcific Formative Cell-mediated calcific deposits ±
Resting No inflammation / vascular infiltration ±
Resorptive Phagocytic resorption + vascular infiltration Most painful
Postcalcific — Calcium resorbed + tissue remodelling —

✗ Resorptive distractors"vascular infiltration, painless" (it is painful) · lowest inflammation (= resting) · cell-mediated deposits (= formative) · fibrocartilaginous metaplasia (= precalcific)

Fibrocartilaginous metaplasiaonly in calcific tendonitis among shoulder pathologies
✗ Wrong options: cuff arthropathy · biceps tenosynovitis · chronic cuff tear · neuropathic arthropathy

Surgery timingavoid surgery in resorptive phase (Uhthoff & Loehr) · surgery for refractory cases in formative phase

3Presentation

Historysimilar to subacromial impingement

Symptomsatraumatic pain (worst in resorptive phase) · catching, crepitus · mechanical block · pain with overhead activity / active elevation

Examsupraspinatus fossa atrophy · ↓ active ROM · scapular dyskinesia · ± ↓ cuff strength · positive impingement signs

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Modality Fact
Radiographs Gold standard / mainstay; monitor progression; location, density, extent, delineation
AP, supraspinatus outlet, axillary Supraspinatus calcification
Internal rotation view Infraspinatus + teres minor
External rotation view Subscapularis
Deposit site 1–1.5 cm from supraspinatus insertion (Orthobullets) · 1–2 cm, zone of ↓ vascularity, can be multifocal (OB) — read the options
CT Rarely required; 3D anatomy
MRI Low signal on all sequences (globular, T1 + STIR/T2 hypointense); limited diagnostic use; refractory pain → concomitant cuff tear
Ultrasound Deposits hyperechoic; quantify extent; guides needle lavage
MR arthrography alone Poor sensitivity + inter-rater agreement (Zubler)

✗ Wrong options (next tests after failed barbotage)bone scan · MR arthrogram · EMG (no added value)

Imaging ✗ distractorsno acromial spur (✗ Wrong options: impingement) · no tear (✗ Wrong options: partial/full-thickness tear) · adhesive capsulitis = clinical diagnosis, no consistent X-ray findings

Gartner & Heyer classification

Type Appearance Phase Image
I Well circumscribed, dense Formative
II Soft contour/dense or sharp/transparent —
III Translucent, cloudy, no clear circumscription Resorptive

Radiographic types (one OB explanation)Type I = fluffy, fleecy, poorly defined → acute pain, formative phase · Type II = discrete homogeneous, well defined → subacute/chronic — conflicts with Gartner (Orthobullets: type I well circumscribed) — read the options

Mole et al. classification

Type Appearance
A Dense, homogeneous, sharp contours
B Dense, segmented, sharp contours
C Heterogeneous, soft contours
D Dystrophic calcification at cuff insertion

5Management

Calcific tendonitis
  • All phases, first line→NSAIDs + PT (stretch/strengthen, moist heat) ± steroid injection
  • Refractory, formative/resting phase→adjunct ESWT
  • Persistent, resorptive phase→US-guided needle lavage / barbotage
  • Progressive, refractory, ↓ ADLs→arthroscopic / mini-open debridement of deposit
    • remaining cuff defect→± rotator cuff repair (controversial)

Treatment – conservative, barbotage & arthroscopic debridement

Nonop outcomesymptoms resolve 60–70% at 6 months; most improve spontaneously

Failure more likelybilateral or large deposits · deposit under anterior third of acromion · deposit medial to acromion

Steroid injectioncommon but controversial; variable relief

Formative phase, 4-month mild painmoist heat + stretching first
✗ Wrong options: aspiration (deposit granular → hard to aspirate) · ESWT (role poorly defined, OB) · low-dose radiation (malignant transformation risk) · arthroscopic debridement (only after failed nonop)

ESWTadjunct; refractory formative + resting phases; dose-dependent: high-energy > low-energy for outcome scores + resorption, but also > procedural pain + local reaction (ecchymosis)

Needle lavage2 needles (inflow saline ± anaesthetic + aspiration outflow); indicated for resorptive phase; better outcomes Gartner II/III vs I

Barbotageneedle breaks up deposit → corticosteroid injection

Operative criteria

Indication for surgical decompression of deposit
Progression of symptoms
Refractory to nonoperative treatment (incl. failed barbotage)
Interference with ADLs / work

Surgeryarthroscopic or mini-open removal (shaver or spinal needle) ± SAD ± RCR; paste-like ("toothpaste") calcium expressed from cuff

After failed barbotagearthroscopic debridement
✗ Wrong options: isolated RCR without debridement (won't resolve symptoms)

RCR after debridementcontroversial; depends on remaining tissue integrity + defect size · debridement without RCR safe: 3.7% cuff tears at 7 y (El Shewy)

Deposit with osseous involvementsame results as tendon-only (Seyahi)

Debridement ± subacromial decompression

SAD + debridement vs debridement alone Result
Time to pain-free activity ↑ (longer) with SAD (Marder)
Pain at midterm No difference
ROM No difference
Recurrence No difference
Cuff tears ↑ in operated shoulder vs contralateral regardless (Balke, 6 y)

Debridement + SAD91% good/satisfactory at 26 mo (Ark); SAD gives no apparent benefit

Return to worklonger with SAD and/or RCR

Listrecurrence · persistent pain · stiffness (operative risk) · iatrogenic cuff injury · ↑ cuff tears after surgery

Hydroxyapatite CPP Calcium oxalate

Shoulder & Elbow · 10 / 60

1Basics

Epidemiology

Frequencyrare; ~10% of all biceps ruptures

Demographicsdominant elbow (86%) of men (93%) in their 40s (30–50 y)

Risk factorsanabolic steroids · smoking (7.5× risk) · hypovascularity · intrinsic degeneration · mechanical impingement in space available for tendon

Patternscomplete avulsion · partial (on radial side of tuberosity footprint) · intersubstance muscle transection (rope wrapped round arm, tug-of-war)

Rare associationmedian nerve compression

Footprint anatomy

Insertionradial (bicipital) tuberosity; innervation musculocutaneous only
✗ Wrong options: dual musculocutaneous + radial

Short head Long head
Origin Coracoid Supraglenoid tubercle / superior labrum
Footprint Distal + anterior (thin sliver) Proximal + posterior (oval; apex of tuberosity)
Better at Elbow flexion Supination (furthest from axis of rotation)

Biceps functionprimary supinator; lesser elbow flexor · brachialis = primary elbow flexor (inserts coronoid + ulnar tuberosity, not radial tuberosity)

Annular ligamentanterior radial head, PRUJ stability; does not attach to radial tuberosity

Lacertus fibrosus (bicipital aponeurosis)from medial side of distal short head, distal to elbow crease → obliquely distal + medial across cubital fossa → protects brachial artery + median nerve → continuous with flexor-origin fascia; may be mistaken for intact tendon; intact lacertus → ↓ deficit in low-demand patient

Antecubital fossa

Medial → lateralmedian nerve (most medial) · brachial artery · biceps tendon · radial nerve (most lateral)

Borderspronator teres ulnarly · brachioradialis radially

Radial recurrent arterysuperficial to biceps tendon, crosses near tuberosity

Superficial radial nervelateral (radial) + superficial to biceps tendon; radial nerve bifurcates (PIN + SRN) at level of antecubital fossa / radiocapitellar joint

LABCNterminal sensory branch of musculocutaneous (lateral cord) → exits between biceps + brachialis lateral to musculotendinous junction → pierces fascia, lateral to biceps tendon, deep to cephalic vein → superficial along brachioradialis → volar-lateral forearm sensation

Nerve course (✗ Wrong options: distractors for LABCN) Nerve
Branches 5–8 cm distal to lateral epicondyle, between 2 heads of PT, along volar FDP → pronator quadratus AIN
From radial n. at radiocapitellar joint, through supinator (arcade of Frohse), around radial neck → dorsal wrist capsule PIN
Deep to brachioradialis, lateral to radial artery, pierces fascia 7–9 cm proximal to wrist → snuffbox, dorsoradial hand SRN
With brachial artery between PT + biceps tendon, between FDS + FDP, emerges between FDS + FPL → carpal tunnel Median

Radial nerve motor order (Abrams)BR → ECRL → supinator → ECRB → EDC → ECU → EDQ → APL → EPL → EPB → EIP last

2Mechanism

Mechanism – eccentric contraction

Eccentric contractionmuscle lengthens during contraction; flexed elbow forced into extension ("flexed elbow unacceptably challenged")

Contributorsvascular watershed · mechanical attrition (abrasion during pronosupination)

Partial tear mechanismpronation → sharp radial margin of tuberosity impinges tendon → released in supination; rupture through pre-existing degeneration on radial aspect

✗ Wrong option: contraction type Definition
Isometric Constant length
Isokinetic Constant speed
Isotonic Constant force
Concentric Muscle shortens (biceps curl)

3Presentation

Historypainful "pop" as elbow eccentrically loaded (catching falling object, lifting furniture/engine, deadlift, curls)

Hallmarkweakness + pain in supination > flexion

Inspection"reverse Popeye" (proximal retraction of muscle belly), contour change, antecubital / medial ecchymosis, palpable defect

Complete vs partialtendon absent in complete · palpable but painful in partial (otherwise similar picture)

Diagnosis – hook test, MRI, partial tears

Hook test (O'Driscoll) (TO)patient looks at palm, shoulder elevated, elbow 90°, forearm supinated → intact tendon = cord-like structure finger hooks around; torn → brachialis is flat → nothing to hook

Hook techniqueindex finger hooks lateral edge of tendon, lateral → medial; intact/partial → finger 1 cm beneath tendon

Accuracysensitivity + specificity 100% → most sensitive exam for complete rupture

False "normal" hookpartial tear · intact lacertus fibrosus (hooking medial → lateral catches lacertus) · underlying brachialis

Partial tearshook test normal but painful; hook test not useful for partial tears

Ruland biceps squeeze testelbow 60–80° flexion, forearm slightly pronated, squeeze biceps belly → no supination = positive (like Thompson); sensitivity 96%

Other exam (OB)biceps crease interval test, passive forearm pronation test

✗ Wrong option: milking manoeuvretests UCL, not biceps

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

X-rayusually normal; occasionally fleck/avulsion from radial tuberosity

MRIdistinguishes complete vs partial, muscle vs tendon, degree of retraction; FABS position (elbow flexion, shoulder abduction, forearm supination) ↑ sensitivity

1Basics

Epidemiology

Demographics20s, mostly ♂; weightlifters (bench press, push-ups), overhead athletes, wrestlers

ClavicleS-shaped; last bone to fuse (medial physis fuses early 20s)

AC ligaments (esp. posterosuperior capsule) Horizontal
CC ligaments Vertical

Pathoanatomyrepetitive stress + micro-fractures of distal clavicle → osteopenia + bone resorption

Loadbench press / manoeuvres with elbows posterior to torso → traction through AC joint

3Presentation

Paindistal clavicle / anterosuperior shoulder; insidious; ↑ with repetitive loading (bench press, push-ups); mimics AC arthritis

Exampoint tenderness at AC joint / distal clavicle · pain with cross-body adduction · pain without weakness on resisted forward flexion + adduction · full ROM

Distal clavicle osteolysis
  • First line→rest + NSAIDs + PT + modify lifting technique

  • Failed nonop→distal clavicle excision (open or arthroscopic)

Indicationpersistent symptoms after failed nonop (rest, PT, cortisone)

Mumford (arthroscopic)resect only 0.5–1 cm; too much → AC instability

Open vs arthroscopicsurgeon preference; arthroscopic comparable pain relief, ↓ morbidity, fewer restrictions, quicker return, better cosmesis, evaluates GH joint + treats concomitant pathology

Openmeticulous deltoid-trapezial fascia repair

1Basics

Types & epidemiology

3 typesosteoarthritis (primary) · post-traumatic · inflammatory

Primary OA Post-traumatic Inflammatory (RA)
Frequency Rare (symptomatic ~2%) 2nd most common Most common / most prevalent elbow arthritis (historically)
Patient Middle-aged ♂ laborer, ♂:♀ 4:1, 20–70 y (avg 50), dominant arm Younger than other types Older ♀; elbow involved in 20–50% of RA
Cause Strenuous manual labour Non-op radial head fracture, (fracture-)dislocation, traumatic instability RA, psoriatic, SLE, PVNS
Joint Radiocapitellar preferentially; ulnohumeral relatively spared Whole joint or focal ulnohumeral/radiocapitellar Global; symmetric narrowing
Hallmark Osteophytes, capsular contracture, loose bodies Incongruity → altered load; stiffness, instability, malunion/nonunion Synovitis, osteopenia, ligament attenuation, instability

Secondary OA causespost-traumatic · OCD · synovial osteochondromatosis · MUCL insufficiency / valgus extension overload

Genes & lab markers

RA pathologypannus → hyperplastic synovium → collagen + proteoglycan degradation → chronic synovitis, ligament attenuation, periarticular osteopenia, contracture

RA trapsynovial proliferation from pannus, not rheumatoid factor mutation

RA pathoanatomyfixed flexion contracture · instability · ulnar (or less often radial) neuropathy · erosions · cysts · deformity · progressive bone resorption

Stabilisers (relevance to surgery)

Primaryanterior band MCL (anterior oblique fibres most important; valgus + distraction) · LCL · olecranon–coronoid–trochlea congruity

Secondaryradial head (most important secondary; 30% valgus stability; 0–30° flexion + pronation) · capsule (distraction in full extension) · anconeus + lateral capsule (varus)

3Presentation

OA symptomspain at end range · loss of terminal extension · painful locking/catching (loose bodies) · night pain unusual
✗ Wrong options: mid-range

OA examforearm rotation preserved early · ulnar neuropathy in up to 50%

RAhand + wrist precede elbow · fixed flexion contracture · ligamentous incompetence · ± ulnar neuropathy · rheumatoid nodule · evaluate C-spine in all RA

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Modality Fact
X-ray AP + lateral; C-spine X-rays for RA before surgery
OA osteophytes Coronoid process + fossa · radial head + fossa · olecranon tip + posteromedial olecranon fossa
Joint space Narrowing; ulnohumeral relatively preserved in OA
Loose bodies Underestimated on plain X-ray
RA Periarticular erosions + cysts, osteopenia; osteophytes not prominent (✗ Wrong options: characteristic)
CT Surgical planning; better defines osteophytes + loose bodies

Larsen grading (RA)

Stage Radiographs
1 Soft tissues involved; near-normal radiographs
2 Periarticular erosions + mild cartilage loss; soft-tissue swelling, osteopenia
3 Marked joint space narrowing
4 Advanced erosions penetrating subchondral plate
5 Advanced damage, loss of articular contour

TEA thresholdLarsen 3–5 in patients >65 y

5Management

Elbow arthritis – failed NSAIDs, injection, splint, activity modification
  • Mild–moderate OA, arc >90°, painful end-range, mechanical symptoms→arthroscopic OCA
  • Severe contracture (e.g. 40–90°), prior ulnar transposition→open: O-K or column procedure
  • Young (<65), high demand, END-STAGE (OA/RA/PTA), stable→interposition arthroplasty
    • isolated radiocapitellar→anconeus interposition / radial head replacement
  • >65, low demand, severe (Larsen 3–5)→semiconstrained TEA

Primary OA – osteocapsular arthroplasty (arthroscopic vs open) & patient selection

NonopNSAIDs · cortisone injection · resting splints · activity modification → mild–moderate symptoms

OCAremoval of osteophytes (coronoid, olecranon, fossae) + loose bodies + capsular release

Best OCA candidate<65 y, active, arc >90°, mild–moderate OA, painless mid-arc + painful end-range

Arthroscopic debridement / release
Indications Mechanical symptoms (loose bodies) · capsular contracture · bony block to motion · >90° motion preferred
Contraindications (relative) Prior ulnar nerve transposition (nerve location unknown) · severe contracture / arthrofibrosis · prior extensive open procedures
Not a CI Prior olecranon osteotomy · ulnar nerve subluxation (✗ Wrong options: absolute CI; identify pre-op, esp. prior submuscular/intramuscular transposition)
Complications Neurologic (ulnar palsy commonest, radial 2nd — anterolateral portal) · synovial fistula · recurrent stiffness
Arthroscopic vs open OCA Arthroscopic
Post-op pain ↓
HO / ankylosis ↓ (✗ Wrong options: equal)
Access Easy anterior + posterior, better cartilage view
Reliability Pain relief more reliable (open → more predictable ROM gain)

O'Driscoll & Blonna 8 stepsposterior view → remove debris + fat pad → osteophytes → posterior capsule release → anterior view → strip anterior capsule → coronoid osteophytes/reshape → excise anterior capsule; 4.8% transient nerve injury (502 pts)

Elbow arthroscopy indicationsseptic I&D · synovectomy (inflammatory) · debridement + loose body removal (OA) · contracture release · OCD capitellum · lateral epicondylitis release

Advanced radiocapitellar OAconsider radial head replacement

Avoid radial head resection in laborer↑ load on arthritic ulnohumeral joint; doesn't fix ROM or end-range impingement

No PT / dynamic splintsno role initially in advanced painful arthritis with fixed contracture · no static splinting when arc functional + complaint is pain

Fusionsevere functional loss; rare (unmanageable sepsis, Charcot)

Outerbridge–Kashiwagi (ulnohumeral arthroplasty)open posterior approach; burr fenestration of olecranon fossa → release posterior impingement + anterior access; younger pts with ↓ ROM; decompress ulnar nerve if pre-op flexion contracture; failure = missed anterior / peripheral (medial + lateral olecranon) osteophytes

Column proceduremedial or lateral open capsular release + bony resection for extrinsic contracture; lateral most common (access to all 3 joints) via lateral supracondylar ridge · anterior arthrotomy ECRL/common extensor interval, stay anterior to LUCL · posterior: elevate triceps · go medial to gain flexion (excise posterior band MCL)

Open releaseelderly regain motion more reliably than <20 y (Strubel & Cohen)

Ulnar nerve – neuritis & decompression when gaining flexion

Riskseverely limited pre-op motion: flexion <100° · extensor lag / max extension >60° → post-op ulnar nerve dysfunction

Ruleany motion-restoring procedure (OCA, O-K, column, interposition) in such patients → concomitant ulnar nerve decompression ± transposition

Not radial neuritisradial tension ↓ with gained extension

Not column procedure add-onsrelease anterior band MUCL (primary valgus) · release LUCL (primary varus) · radial head resection (rotation full + painless) · TFL interposition (reserved <50 y)

Young post-traumatic arthritis – interposition arthroplasty

Indicationyoung, high-demand, END-STAGE OA / RA / post-traumatic who would otherwise get TEA if older; no lifting restrictions; needs preserved bone stock + inherent stability

Techniqueburr distal humerus + proximal ulna congruent → graft over distal humerus (Achilles allograft, autogenous TFL, dermal/fascial) → ligament repair → hinged distracting ex-fix (offloads graft, early ROM, protects repairs)

Advantagecan convert to TEA later (successful; Blaine)

Interposition contraindication Type
Elbow instability / chronic instability without bone stock for ligament reconstruction Absolute
Active infection Absolute
Elderly >60 y (TEA candidates) Relative
Bone loss: destructive JRA, distal humerus osteonecrosis → prosthetic replacement
Not CI Young age · post-traumatic · inflammatory · previous debridement

Anconeus interpositionarthritis isolated to radiocapitellar joint

Failed interposition (68 y, pain + instability)convert to TEA
✗ Wrong options: revision interposition · hemiarthroplasty (ulnar side arthritic) · arthrodesis

Rheumatoid elbow – TEA & synovectomy

Synovectomyopen or arthroscopic; young RA, joint space preserved; most improve

Radial head resection + synovectomyonly if synovitis encircles radial head/neck + painful crepitus on rotation + PIN signs (can't extend thumb)

Complication of radial head resectionrapid progression of ulnohumeral arthritis
✗ Wrong options: loss of pronation/supination · longitudinal instability with intact IOM · ulnar palsy (less likely)

End-stage RAsemiconstrained TEA (concomitant ligamentous instability)
✗ Wrong options: constrained (high early loosening) · arthroscopy (incomplete, unpredictable)

TEA outcome RA vs OAequal or better for RA
✗ Wrong options: poorer

Operative criteria – TEA

TEA
Indications >65 y, severe arthritis (Larsen 3–5) · complex distal humerus fracture, elderly, poor bone · distal humerus non/malunion, elderly low demand · post-traumatic arthritis (lower demand) · failed interposition
Contraindications Active <65 y · infection · Charcot joint
Restriction Lifelong 5–10 lb lifting limit
TEA design Feature
Unconstrained Needs competent collaterals, soft-tissue envelope, good bone
Semiconstrained "Sloppy hinge" → some varus-valgus + rotational laxity → ↓ bone-cement stress → ↓ loosening; best longevity + function
Constrained High early loosening

Elbow arthrodesis position (TO)

Arthrodesis Position
Unilateral (TO) 90° flexion + neutral to slight valgus (✗ Wrong options: varus · 110°)
Bilateral (TO) One 110° (feeding) · other 65° (perineal hygiene)

6Complications

Total elbow arthroplasty complications

Rateup to 43% (Orthobullets) · up to 25% (OB) — read the options

Bushing wearmost common mode of failure of semiconstrained TEA at midterm, esp. post-traumatic indication (younger, non-adherence to restrictions, unstable injury, deformity, contracture)
✗ Wrong options: gender · smoking · cement · age

Infection / wound risk factorsprior elbow surgery · prior infection (S. epidermidis) · psychiatric comorbidity · RA · wound drainage · reoperation · poor skin (long-term steroids); two-stage revision → poor survival

Aseptic looseninglinked implants · post-traumatic OA

Instabilityunlinked implants

Othersulnar neuritis (iatrogenic or after motion restored without decompression) · triceps avulsion/insufficiency · fracture · mechanical failure

X vs Y

Arthroscopic OCA Interposition arthroplasty TEA
Stage Mild–moderate End-stage End-stage
Age / demand Active, <65 Young, high demand >65, low demand
Motion Arc >90° Any; needs stability Any
Key CI Prior ulnar transposition, severe contracture Instability, infection Active <65, infection, Charcot
Restriction — None 5–10 lb lifetime
Elbow OA Elbow RA
X-ray Osteophytes, loose bodies, ulnohumeral spared Erosions, cysts, osteopenia, symmetric narrowing
Symptom End-range pain Diffuse pain, effusion
Instability No Ligament attenuation
End-stage op OCA / interposition / TEA Semiconstrained TEA; synovectomy early

✗ Wrong options: loose bodies · contracture · bony block · olecranon osteotomy

✗ Wrong options: RA destruction · end-stage · elderly pain throughout

✗ Wrong options: radial neuritis · implant wear

✗ Wrong options: destructive JRA · osteonecrosis · 70-y RA

✗ Wrong options: young age · PTA · inflammatory · prior debridement
