Elbow Arthroscopy: Indications & Approach

Shoulder & Elbow · 14 / 60

1Basics

Indications

Source Indications
Orthobullets Loose body removal, osteophyte debridement, synovectomy, capsular release (stiffness), OCD capitellum, lateral epicondylitis, septic arthritis debridement
TO Loose bodies · OCD capitellum · osteochondral lesions radial head · osteophytes humerus/olecranon · RA (partial synovectomy) · stiff elbow (debridement, lysis of adhesions) · tennis elbow release · evaluation of painful elbow · inflamed olecranon bursa · intra-articular fractures

Osteocapsular arthroplastyyoung patient with degenerative elbow where TEA inappropriate, or significant contracture

Advantagesbetter articular visualisation, ↓ post-op pain, faster recovery

Disadvantagestechnically demanding; high risk of NV injury (proximity to joint)

Contraindications (prior ulnar nerve transposition)

Source Contraindications
Orthobullets Prior trauma, surgical scarring, previous ulnar nerve transposition
TO Bony ankylosis · severe fibrous ankylosis (scope can't enter safely) · active infection · surgery altering anatomy e.g. anterior ulnar nerve transposition (relative)
OB Ulnar neuropathy with prior submuscular transposition = contraindication

Not contraindications (OB)Panner disease · loose body ulnohumeral joint · s/p radial head ORIF · elbow stiffness · osteoarthritis

Ulnar nerve subluxationnot an absolute contraindication; identify pre-op (esp. prior submuscular/intramuscular transposition)

Capsular anatomy & distension (TO)

Capsule (TO)attached to articular margins; fibres blend with annular ligament; anterior → above coronoid + radial fossae; posterior → above olecranon fossa

Tension (TO)taut anteriorly in extension, posteriorly in flexion

Maximum distension (TO)70–80° flexion; capacity 25–30 mL
✗ Wrong options: 90–120° · 10° · 120–150°

5Management

Positioning & joint distension (TO)

Positionssupine (suspended), prone, lateral decubitus

Most commonly used (TO)lateral, elbow hanging freely on support (flexed)

All positions = elbow flexed (TO)elbow extended, prone = not a position

Anaesthesiageneral (muscle relaxation, tolerates prone/lateral) · regional: no immediate post-op nerve check, poor tolerance of position

Portal technique

Distend firstfully distend joint through lateral soft spot → NV structures move away from trocar

Nick and spreadskin only with blade, hemostat spread to capsule, blunt trocar

Elbow positionanterior portals at 90° flexion · posterior portals in some extension

Kitstandard 30° scope · tourniquet · solid cannulas → maintain distension, ↓ extravasation
✗ Wrong options: trephinated

Landmarksolecranon, both epicondyles, radiocapitellar joint, ulnar nerve; mark before insufflation (distension distorts)

Orderdistend → viewing portal (medial or lateral) → working portal under direct vision + needle localisation

First portalanterolateral after distension (TO, OB) · establishing a medial portal first (before swelling) may be advantageous (Orthobullets) — read the options

Viewing vs working (TO)anterolateral = viewing; proximal anteromedial = most common working portal + most commonly used medial portal

Posteromedial portalavoided (lies over ulnar nerve)

Factors that ↓ NV injury (TO)

✓ Manoeuvre (TO) Protects
90° flexion + joint distension Radial nerve moves anteriorly
Pronation PIN
Keep lateral portal more proximal Radial nerve / PIN
Avoid deep knife; hemostat + blunt trocar Lateral + posterior antebrachial cutaneous
Draw landmarks, palpate ulnar nerve Ulnar
Low-flow infusion 40–45 mL/min or gravity (✗ Wrong options: pressurised) Compartment syndrome
Instrument tips always in view; no suction near nerves All

NOT a protective manoeuvre (TO)more distal lateral portal (risk ↑ with distal placement)

Portals & nerves at risk

Portal Location Use Nerves at risk
Proximal anterolateral 1–2 cm proximal, 1 cm anterior to lateral epicondyle Views anteromedial joint; safest anterolateral (TO) Radial (↓ risk more proximally)
Mid anterolateral (TO) Just proximal, ~1 cm anterior to radiocapitellar joint — —
Distal anterolateral 1–3 cm distal, 1 cm anterior to lateral epicondyle; anterior to radial head/neck 1st portal supine; radial head, medial elbow, coronoid, trochlea, brachialis insertion, coronoid fossa PIN + lateral antebrachial cutaneous; radial at maximum risk (TO) → rarely used
Direct lateral (soft spot) Triangle olecranon – radial head – lateral epicondyle Initial distension; posterior compartment (capitellum, radial head, radioulnar joint) Relatively safe; LABC
Anteromedial (direct medial) 2 cm anterior + 2 cm distal to medial epicondyle; through flexor-pronator Augments proximal AM; medial recess; place under direct vision MABC + median (+ basilic vein, TO)
Proximal anteromedial (superomedial) 2 cm proximal to medial epicondyle, anterior to IM septum Entire anterior compartment, radial head, capitellum, coronoid, trochlea; most common working portal (TO) MABC; ulnar (7 mm, posterior to septum) + median (OB, TO)
Straight posterior (transtriceps) 3 cm proximal to olecranon, midline through triceps Partial extension; olecranon osteophytes, posteromedial loose bodies Posterior antebrachial cutaneous; ulnar 15–25 mm away (OB)
Posterolateral 2–3 cm proximal to olecranon, just lateral to triceps (centre of anconeus triangle) 20–30° flexion (relax triceps); best posterior compartment, radiocapitellar (OCD capitellum), olecranon fossa PABC, medial brachial cutaneous, ulnar (Orthobullets) · PABC + lateral brachial cutaneous (TO)
✗ Wrong option: posteromedial Medial to triceps Not used Ulnar nerve — unacceptably high

Distal anterolateral location1–3 cm distal (Orthobullets) · 2–3 / 3 cm distal (TO) · 1–2 cm distal (OB)

Posterior compartment workhorsesstraight posterior + posterolateral, both 3 cm proximal to olecranon tip
✗ Wrong options: any posteromedial portal

Anterolateral (joint line) Radial 4.8 mm · PABC 12.6 mm

Anteromedial MABC 1 mm · median 7 mm (one OB) · MABC 8.9 · median 12.9 · ulnar 22.1 mm (another OB)

Posterolateral Radial 4.8 mm (3–8) (OB)

Radial nerve & anterior capsulectomy

Radial nerve courseon the anterior capsule at mid-capitellum (OB), runs longitudinally medial to capitellum → at risk in capsular excision; seen near probe when viewing radiocapitellar joint from anteromedial portal

Protective layerbrachialis (~4 mm) between capsule and radial nerve proximal to radial neck
✗ Wrong options: anconeus · brachioradialis · biceps · pronator teres

Danger zonedistal capsule over radial head/neck → transect capsule ≥2–3 cm proximal to radial head

Nerve injury

Ratenerve palsy 1–5%; neurologic = most common complication, mostly transient

Greatest riskrheumatoid arthritis, elbow contracture

Ranking Answer
Most common complication / nerve (TO, OB) Transient (sensory) ulnar nerve palsy
2nd Radial nerve palsy (Orthobullets, OB) · persistent wound drainage, then transient sensory radial palsy (TO)
Most common permanent nerve palsy (TO) PIN, then ulnar
Least involved nerve (TO) Median

Deficit Nerve Portal

HO / ankylosisless than open; minimise bleeding

Infectionsinus tract (posterolateral portal); ↑ risk with intra-articular steroid at time of arthroscopy; possibly ↑ with inflammatory arthritis

Infection prevention – avoid intra-articular steroid

✓ Prevent infectionavoid intra-op steroid injection

✗ Trapsavoid posterior midline portals · avoid scope in OA · absorbable subcuticular suture only (no difference) · restrict ROM 3–4 wk (↑ stiffness)

Safety Safer → more commonly used Riskier → rarely used
Anteromedial Proximal anteromedial
Location 2 cm anterior + 2 cm distal to ME 2 cm proximal to ME, anterior to septum

Elbow Physical Exam

Shoulder & Elbow · 15 / 60

1Basics

Exam sequence & normal values

Sequenceinspection → palpation → ROM → stability → motor → sensory → vascular → provocative tests

Parameter Normal Functional
Carrying angle (full extension) ~11° ♂ · ~13° ♀ (exam note) · ♂ 5–10° / ♀ 10–15° (anatomy note); ↑ in throwers —
Flexion–extension 0–140° 30–130°
Pronation 75° 50°
Supination 85° 50°

Pronation–supinationtest with shoulders fully adducted + elbow at 90°; compare both sides, active + passive

End pointsoft = effusion / capsular tightness · firm = mechanical block (loose body, fracture, osteophyte)

Throwersloss of full extension even without pathology

Motor – muscle & root

Movement Muscle Root
Elbow flexion, full supination Brachialis + biceps C5–C6
Elbow flexion, neutral (thumb to ceiling) Brachioradialis C6

3Presentation

Inspection

Effusionelbow held at 70–80° flexion (= max capsular distension) · fullness of soft spot (radial head + lateral epicondyle + olecranon)

Cubital tunnel1st dorsal interosseous / 1st web atrophy · ring/small clawing (more with Guyon's — unopposed FDP)

Distal biceps rupturemedial ecchymosis + swelling · proximal retraction of belly = reverse Popeye sign

Palpation – point of maximal tenderness

Condition Tender point
MCL injury MCL origin, just inferior to medial epicondyle; palpate at 50–70° flexion (flexor-pronator mass moves anterior)
Valgus extension overload Posteromedial olecranon
Lateral epicondylitis ECRB insertion, few mm distal to tip of lateral epicondyle
Radial tunnel syndrome 3–5 cm distal to lateral epicondyle (more distal than tennis elbow)
Medial epicondylitis 5–10 mm distal + anterior to medial epicondyle; swelling/warmth if inflamed

Radial headbest palpated while rotating forearm pronation → supination

Ulnar nerve subluxationover medial epicondyle, extension → flexion · hypermobility in 33% of adults
✗ Wrong options: necessarily CuTS

Snapping medial tricepssnaps over medial epicondyle on resisted extension from full flexion (differentiate from ulnar nerve)

4Diagnosis & Classification

Stability – MCL (valgus)

Valgus stress testflex 20–30° (unlocks olecranon) + externally rotate humerus + valgus → tests MCL

Test Technique Positive Accuracy
Milking maneuver Pull patient's thumb, forearm supinated, elbow 90°; supine or seated/standing Apprehension, instability or pain at MCL origin Sens 87.5%, NPV 100%
Moving valgus stress Same position + valgus while ranging full arc; shoulder fully ER Pain at MCL origin between 70° and 120° (early acceleration 70° · late cocking 120°) Sens 100%, spec 75%

Valgus extension overloadpain with forced elbow extension · valgus in terminal extension reproduces pain · varus loading ↓ pain

Stability – LCL / posterolateral rotatory instability

Test Technique Positive / accuracy
Lateral pivot-shift Supine, arm overhead, shoulder fully ER, forearm supinated + valgus, extension → flexion Pain/apprehension or clunk at 40° (radiocapitellar dislocated); 2nd clunk with ↑ flexion (triceps reduces radial head); more reliable under anaesthesia
PLR drawer Supine, elbow 40°, forearm supinated, AP force over lateral proximal forearm Apprehension or skin dimple (radial head posterior subluxation)
Chair push-up Push up from chair, forearm supinated Unable / apprehension; sens 87.5% (100% with prone push-up)
Prone push-up Push-up, forearm supinated Unable; sens 87.5% (100% with chair test)
Table-top relocation Press-up on table edge, elbow lateral, forearm supinated; 3 parts Pain in parts 1 + 3, relief with thumb on radial head (part 2) = PLRI

Table-top (wrong option)pain in all 3 parts = intra-articular radial head fracture

Provocative tests – nerve

Condition Test / sign Finding
Cubital tunnel Froment Thumb IP flexion by FPL (AIN) on key pinch → compensates adductor pollicis (ulnar)
Cubital tunnel Jeanne Thumb MCP hyperextension + adduction by EPL (radial) on key pinch
Cubital tunnel Wartenberg Persistent small finger abduction + extension; weak intrinsics + unopposed EDM
Cubital tunnel Masse Flat palmar arch, lost ulnar hand elevation (weak ODQ, ↓ small MCP flexion)
Cubital tunnel Tinel Over cubital tunnel, elbow extended
Cubital tunnel Elbow flexion test Symptoms with flexion >60 s
Radial tunnel Resisted long finger extension · resisted supination (elbow + wrist extended) · passive pronation + wrist flexion Pain at radial tunnel (weakness from pain); supinator stretch → 250 mmHg (normal 50)
PIN syndrome Resisted supination ↑ pain · normal tenodesis (vs extensor tendon rupture) Weak finger MCP extension; wrist extends in radial deviation (ECRL intact, ECU absent)
AIN syndrome OK sign (FDP index + FPL) Can't make OK; weak PQ = weak resisted pronation with elbow maximally flexed
AIN vs FPL rupture (RA) Tenodesis Intact tendons: passive wrist extension flexes thumb IP + index DIP

Cubital tunnel motorweak pinch (up to 70% lost; adductor pollicis)

Pronator syndrome – site-specific tests

Pronator syndromeTinel proximal anterior forearm, not at wrist · wrist-flexion provocation as in CTS

Resisted test Compression site
Elbow flexion + forearm supination Bicipital aponeurosis (lacertus)
Forearm pronation, elbow extended Two heads of pronator teres
FDS contraction to middle finger FDS fibrous arch

Sensory

Cutaneous nervesmedial, lateral, posterior antebrachial cutaneous · ulnar · median · superficial radial

Cubital tunnel↓ 2PD small + ulnar ring · ↓ dorsal ulnar hand = proximal to wrist (dorsal branch arises 5 cm proximal to wrist)

Pronator syndrome↓ sensation in palmar cutaneous branch territory (arises 4–5 cm proximal to carpal tunnel) · not in CTS

Provocative tests – tendon

Condition Test Key fact
Triceps rupture Modified Thompson squeeze Prone, forearm hanging; squeeze triceps → no elbow extension = complete tear (triceps + lateral expansion)
Distal biceps Hook test Elbow 90°, full supination, hook lateral edge; intact = finger 1 cm beneath tendon; sens + spec 100%
Distal biceps Ruland biceps squeeze Elbow 60–80°, slight pronation; squeeze belly → no supination = positive; sens 96%
Distal biceps Biceps crease interval (BCI) Crease → cusp distance >6 cm or 1.2× contralateral; sens 92%, spec 100%
Distal biceps Passive forearm pronation Belly moves proximal on supination, distal on pronation (intact)
Distal biceps Strength Loss of supination > flexion

Hook test false positivespartial tear · intact lacertus fibrosus · underlying brachialis

Biceps triadhook + passive pronation + BCI in sequence → 100% sens + 100% spec for complete rupture

Lateral epicondylitispain on resisted wrist extension (elbow extended, pronated) · Maudsley = resisted middle finger extension (ECRB) · maximal wrist flexion · passive wrist flexion in pronation

Chair testelbow extended, forearm pronated, shoulder flexed, lift chair → lateral elbow pain = lateral epicondylitis

Medial epicondylitispain on resisted pronation + wrist flexion · no instability/apprehension on valgus stress or milking (vs MCL)

5Management

Olecranon bursitis – aspiration & compression

Causerepeated minor trauma (leaning on elbow, desk work) > single injury → inflamed lining secretes fluid

Aseptic olecranon bursitis
  • First line→nonoperative (more effective + safer than surgery)
  • Aspiration chosen→posterolateral needle, aspirate alone
    • then→compressive wrap (bursal walls adhere)

Aspiration ✓alone (no steroid) + compressive dressing → walls adhere, prevents reaccumulation

Approachposterolateral
✗ Wrong options: posteromedial → ulnar nerve

Avoid steroid↑ septic bursitis (local immunosuppression); no outcome benefit · recurrence occurs with or without steroid
✗ Wrong options: "steroid ↑ recurrence"

LUCL rupturefrom repeated steroid injections for lateral epicondylitis, not bursa aspiration

Finding Septic Aseptic
Tenderness 88% 36%
Erythema/cellulitis 83% 27%
Warmth 84% 56%
Trauma / skin lesion 50% 25%
Fever 38% 0%

Septic vs asepticclinical + lab data overlap → hard to distinguish

X vs Y

Lateral epicondylitis Radial tunnel syndrome
Tender point Few mm distal to lateral epicondyle (ECRB) 3–5 cm distal
Provocation Maudsley, chair test, resisted wrist extension Resisted long finger extension, resisted supination
MCL injury Medial epicondylitis
Tender point Just inferior to medial epicondyle 5–10 mm distal + anterior
Milking / valgus stress Pain, apprehension, instability No instability or apprehension
Provocation Moving valgus stress 70–120° Resisted pronation + wrist flexion
Pronator syndrome Carpal tunnel syndrome
Tinel Proximal forearm Wrist
Palmar cutaneous branch sensation ↓ Spared
Cubital tunnel Guyon's canal
Clawing Less More (unopposed FDP)
Dorsal ulnar hand ↓ Spared

How it's asked

"Olecranon bursa aspiration — true statement?"compressive wrap after aspiration alone promotes bursal wall adherence
✗ Wrong options: steroid ↑ recurrence · posteromedial · similar infection risk with steroid · LUCL rupture

"Steroid injected into olecranon bursa — risk?"↑ septic bursitis

"Needle approach for olecranon bursa?"posterolateral (avoid ulnar nerve)

"Position to palpate MCL origin?"50–70° flexion, just inferior to medial epicondyle

"Elbow position to test valgus stability?"20–30° flexion (unlocks olecranon), humerus ER

"Moving valgus stress test positive arc?"70–120°

"Clunk at 40° on pivot-shift?"dislocated radiocapitellar joint (PLRI)

Elbow Stiffness and Contractures

Shoulder & Elbow · 16 / 60

1Basics

Functional range of motion

Motion Functional range
Flexion–extension 30°–130° = 100° arc (Orthobullets, OB) · 90° arc (one OB explanation) — read the options
Pronation–supination 50°–50°

Tolerance30° loss of extension well tolerated · flexion loss causes more dysfunction than extension loss

Causes

AetiologyOA, trauma (fractures), surgery, CP, TBI, burns, prolonged immobilisation, recurrent haemarthroses, congenital (arthrogryposis, congenital radial head dislocation)

Type Causes
Intrinsic (intra-articular) Joint incongruity, synovitis, loose bodies, intra-articular fracture, malunion, OCD, post-traumatic arthritis (coronoid + olecranon tip osteophytes, radiocapitellar narrowing)
Extrinsic (extra-articular) Burn eschar, HO, capsular adhesions/contracture, ligament contracture (posterior oblique MCL)
Mixed Late effect of intrinsic → extrinsic stiffness

Elbow ligaments

Ligament Key fact
Anterior bundle MUCL (anterior oblique) Isometric; primary valgus + distraction stabiliser; highest tensile strength; Tommy John reconstruction · do not release → valgus instability
Posterior bundle MUCL (posterior oblique) Dorsal to axis of rotation; lengthens 9 mm between 60° and 120° flexion · contracture → loss of flexion · release → ↑ flexion without valgus instability
Transverse band MUCL Release does not improve ROM
Radial collateral ligament Do not release
LUCL Do not release → PLRI (pivot shift)
Annular ligament —

Anterior capsule contractureloss of extension

Ulnar nerveclose to joint → at risk when contracted / during flexion gain

3Presentation

Painmid-arc pain → intra-articular pathology · pain at extremes → extrinsic contracture (bony impingement + soft-tissue stretch)

Function↓ motion limits ADLs

Examscars, skin quality, inflammation · flexion/extension + pronation/supination vs contralateral · median, radial, ulnar nerve function

Flexion <90–100°posterior band of MCL contracted → release (+ consider ulnar nerve decompression/transposition)

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

X-rayAP, lateral, oblique; serial X-rays if HO

CTloose bodies, nonunion, joint incongruity, abnormal bony anatomy; HO planning

MRIrarely indicated

HO maturitywell-corticated margins + no change on serial X-rays · labs not needed · matures 12–18 mo (OB) → no bone scan years after injury

5Management

Elbow stiffness
  • Most / contracture <40°→NSAIDs + supervised PT (active + passive ROM)
    • failed PT + flexion contracture >30° or flexion <130°→static progressive splint
  • Plateau 4–6 mo, extrinsic, congruent joint→capsular release ± posterior band MCL
  • Intrinsic arthritis→choose by extent + demand
    • confined to olecranon fossa→osteophyte excision + capsular release
    • diffuse, young high-demand→distraction interposition arthroplasty
    • diffuse, elderly low-demand→TEA

Static progressive splinting

Indicationsafter failed PT with flexion contracture >30° or flexion <130°

Best initial option (OB)supervised therapy + static progressive (turnbuckle) splinting over 6 mo (6–12 mo) → greatest ↑ DASH + functional ROM

Not indicatedmechanical block (esp. pronation/supination) · ankylosis (extensive HO) · functional arc already (e.g. 10–140°) · routinely after arthroscopic loose body removal

✗ Alternative Why wrong
Self-directed exercise Poor results
Supervised therapy alone First line, but response variable, often unsatisfactory
CPM Limited role in established contractures; no end-range gain
Closed manipulation (MUA) Worsens stiffness: tearing, haemarthrosis, more fibrosis

Operative criteria

Procedure Indication
Capsular release ± posterior band MCL Extrinsic contracture + normal joint congruency (most predictable) · arthritis (less predictable) · ankylosis → less predictable
Osteophyte excision (+ capsular release) Intrinsic contracture, arthritis confined to olecranon fossa; bony block to terminal motion → remove coronoid, coronoid fossa, olecranon, olecranon fossa
Distraction interposition arthroplasty Intrinsic, diffuse arthritis, young high-demand
TEA Intrinsic, diffuse arthritis, elderly low-demand · high failure in young · permanent 5-lb lifting limit
Musculocutaneous neurectomy Neurogenic contracture, flexion deformity <90°
Timing of release 4–6 mo post-injury/surgery once ROM plateaued despite splinting/therapy
HO excision At maturity

Contraindications to releaseCharcot elbow, neurologic elbow disorder · poor skin (relative → rotational flap)

Release – posterior bundle of MCL for flexion

Flexion gaincapsular release + posterior oblique band of MUCL
✗ Wrong options: anterior band · transverse · RCL · LUCL

Flexion <100° preopconsider ulnar nerve transposition/decompression (↓ nerve injury)

Arthroscopic vs open release (prior ulnar transposition, HO)

Arthroscopictechnically demanding · posterior: olecranon fossa/osteophyte debridement + posterior capsular release (no suction medially — ulnar nerve) · anterior: coronoid fossa debridement + anterior capsulotomy/capsulectomy

Nerves at risk with portalsradial (most) > ulnar > median (stiffness note) · overall most common = transient ulnar, most common permanent = PIN (TO, arthroscopy MCQs) — read the options

Relative contraindications to arthroscopic releaseprior ulnar nerve transposition (variable nerve position) · HO · obesity · severe loss of pronation–supination · muscular contracture (CP)

Not contraindicationsage >40, gender, osteophytes / arthritis (unpredictable outcome only), heavy labour

Open approach Key points
Lateral column (Morrey) Lateral or posterior skin incision · elevate ECRL + BR off anterior supracondylar ridge, triceps posteriorly · brachialis off anterior capsule · robust anterior access → capsular release + HO excision; coronoid + olecranon tip/fossa, radiocapitellar joint
Medial "over the top" (Hotchkiss) Extrinsic contracture, MCL calcification, baseline ulnar nerve symptoms · with ulnar nerve decompression/transposition · release posterior band MCL · work anterior to flexor-pronator mass
Combined medial + lateral Single posterior incision → both columns

Rehabilitation & outcomes

Post-opregional block, CPM through full ROM, compressive dressing, active + active-assist ROM, extension / dynamic / static progressive splinting as needed

Compliancecritical

Outcomevariable; retain ~two-thirds of motion gained at surgery

6Complications

Complication Detail
Heterotopic ossification Prophylaxis low-dose radiation or indomethacin · no radiation with acute fracture (nonunion risk)
Transient ulnar neuropraxia After release (nerve close to contracted joint)
Ulnar nerve damage Transpose if preop flexion <100°
Recurrent contracture —

X vs Y

Posterior band MUCL Anterior band MUCL
Length change +9 mm (60°→120°) Isometric
Contracture → Loss of flexion —
Release → ↑ flexion, stable Valgus instability
Other — Valgus restraint in throwing; Tommy John; strongest
Arthroscopic release Open release
Best for Osteophytes, capsular contracture, loose bodies Extensive HO, prior ulnar transposition, severe contracture
Risk Radial nerve (portals) > ulnar > median Ulnar neuropraxia / damage

How it's asked

"Static progressive turnbuckle splint most appropriate?"3 mo post distal humerus ORIF, arc 45–100°, plateaued
✗ Wrong options: radial head block to supination · 10–140° arc · ankylosis with HO · after arthroscopic loose body removal

"2.5 mo after fracture-dislocation fixation, arc 75°, DASH 45 — best initial?"supervised therapy + static progressive splinting
✗ Wrong options: self-directed · CPM · MUA

"True about posterior oblique MCL?"released to gain flexion in post-traumatic contracture
✗ Wrong options: strongest · Tommy John · valgus restraint = anterior bundle · pivot shift = LUCL

"Lacks 40° extension, flexion to 80° — release capsule plus?"posterior band MCL (B)
✗ Wrong options: anterior band → valgus instability · LUCL → PLRI

"Relative contraindication to arthroscopic release?"prior ulnar nerve transposition
✗ Wrong options: age, gender, osteophytes, labour

"Terrible triad 5 y ago, arc 60–95°, extensive HO — treatment?"open capsular release + HO excision via lateral column approach
✗ Wrong options: bone scan · arthroscopy · downsize radial head · interposition arthroplasty

"Nerve most at risk with elbow arthroscopy portals?"radial

"Functional elbow ROM?"30–130° (100° arc); pronation/supination 50–50°

Glenohumeral Arthritis (Shoulder Arthritis)

Shoulder & Elbow · 17 / 60

1Basics

Epidemiology

Incidence↑ with age; mostly >60 y · ♀ > ♂

Dislocation as risk56% of primary anterior dislocators have arthrosis at 25 y

Aetiology

Type Key point
Primary OA No known cause · irreversible cartilage loss + hypertrophic subchondral bone · flattened head, osteophytes, cysts, posterior subluxation + posterior glenoid wear
Post-traumatic Healed articular incongruity (humeral fractures, chronic dislocations)
Dislocation arthropathy ↑ with age >25 y at dislocation + posterior dislocation · not related to number of dislocations
Post-capsulorrhaphy Over-tightening (e.g. Putti-Platt) pushes head one way → eccentric wear; presents 5th decade
Cuff tear arthropathy Torn cuff → head migrates up → abrasion against acromion
RA Affects 90% of RA patients · central glenoid wear + medialisation · cuff tear 25–50%
CPPD / gout Pyrophosphate (pseudogout) / urate crystals
AVN Proximal humerus fracture: 35% 3-part, 90% 4-part (this topic's Orthobullets note) · chronic dislocation · cuff repair · steroid, EtOH, haemoglobinopathy, Gaucher
Chondrolysis After arthroscopy: radiofrequency, continuous intra-articular anaesthetic infusion, bioabsorbable anchors, contrast · fewer osteophytes than OA
Neuropathic Charcot

Cuff tears with OA5–10% (Orthobullets) · full-thickness supraspinatus <10% in primary OA (OB) · CTA excluded by definition
✗ Wrong options: 30–55% = asymptomatic >60 y population

Anatomy

Versionglenoid ~3° retroverted · humerus 20–30° retroverted

Stabilisersstatic: GH ligaments, labrum · dynamic: cuff, rotator interval, biceps

2Mechanism

Posterior wear + subluxationposterior capsule stretched · anterior capsule + subscapularis contract → loss of ER

Walch B vs CB: posterior subluxation causes posterior wear · C: glenoid retroversion causes wear → subluxation later

3Presentation

Symptomspain with motion, often none at rest · difficulty sleeping · loss of ER (anterior capsule contracture)

Exam↓ ER, FF, IR · crepitus · catching/squeaking · examine cuff carefully

Subscapularis tearweak belly-press + ↑ passive ER (90° at side)

Outcome scoresASES · Constant · Oxford

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Viewstrue AP (Grashey) + AP + axillary lateral (axillary/CT to judge posterior glenoid wear)

Cause X-ray hallmark
Primary OA JSN, sclerosis, cysts, inferior "goat's beard" osteophyte, posterior glenoid wear, fixed posterior subluxation
Dislocation arthropathy Large osteophytes, hardware
RA Osteopenia, marginal erosions, few osteophytes, central wear + medialisation, ↓ acromiohumeral distance
CPPD Chondrocalcinosis
Gout Usually unremarkable; erosions after repeat attacks
AVN Normal early → central head resorption → crescent sign → collapse
CTA Superior migration, ↓ acromiohumeral interval, acromial erosion, superior glenoid loss, "acetabularisation" of CA arch, osteopenia

CTglenoid morphology + templating · underestimates full-thickness RCT and fatty infiltration vs MRI

MRIcuff assessment · less accurate than CT for glenoid type · Goutallier IV fatty infiltration = irreparable cuff

Glenoid wear patterns (Walch, posterior wear, medialisation in RA)

Most common OA wearposterior (or central)
✗ Wrong options: anterior · superior · inferior

Inflammatory (RA/JRA) vs OAconcentric erosion + medialisation of joint line · severe erosion → glenoid resurfacing not always feasible → some favour HA
✗ Wrong options: inferior osteophyte · posterior subluxation · sclerotic glenoid · posterior wear = OA

Walch Description
A (59%) Concentric, head centred · A1 minor central erosion · A2 deep central erosion (rim line transects head)
B Biconcave, asymmetric wear, posterior subluxation · B0 pre-arthritic subluxation · B1 (17%) posterior JSN, osteophytes, sclerosis, no bone loss · B2 (15%) posterior rim erosion, retroversion <25° · B3 monoconcave, posterior wear, subluxation ≥70% or retroversion >15°
C (9%) Dysplastic, retroversion >25° · C1 >25° regardless of erosion · C2 biconcave + posterior bone loss + posterior translation · subtypes "Lazy J" + "Delta"
D Anteversion or anterior subluxation (<40%)

B2 trapbiconcave + posterior subluxation + 10° retroversion = B2 · same with 25° = C2 · deep concentric = A2 · monoconcave + 70% subluxation = B3 · anteversion = D

B2 outcomespoorer after arthroplasty · anatomic TSA → instability/early glenoid loosening if retroversion >27° or 80% posterior subluxation → reverse often better in older/severe deformity

5Management

Glenohumeral arthritis
  • First line→NSAIDs, PT (capsular stretching), activity modification
  • Second line→intra-articular corticosteroid (HA/PRP/stem cell: limited evidence)
  • Young, high demand→arthroscopic debridement / CAM (temporising)
  • Failed nonop, end stage→arthroplasty by cuff status
    • cuff intact (incl. partial tear)→anatomic TSA
    • cuff deficient / >80% subluxation / Walch D→RSA

Operative criteria

Procedure Indications Contraindications / cautions
Anatomic TSA Intact cuff (partial tear OK), glenoid wear, posterior subluxation, failed nonop Deficient deltoid or cuff · active infection · Charcot · young high-demand (glenoid loosening)
Hemiarthroplasty Young · RA with irreparable cuff / poor glenoid bone stock · AVN without glenoid involvement Early failure, poor pain/function in OA (not routine)
Ream-and-run Young, intact cuff, no inflammatory arthropathy —
RSA Irreparable/large cuff tear · CTA · OA/RA with major glenoid pathology · age · failed arthroplasty · complex fracture Higher complication rate than TSA
Arthroscopic debridement Mild–moderate OA without structural change · loose bodies · small AVN lesions · synovial chondromatosis Advanced degeneration
Arthrodesis Paralysis · recurrent infection · poor deltoid/soft tissue · brachial plexus palsy · failed repair of instability —

Anatomic TSA vs hemiarthroplasty – indications & cuff status

TSA vs HATSA: better pain relief + function · HA: ↑ revision rate
✗ Wrong options: better pain · ↑ blood loss · ↑ instability · ↑ infection

End-stage OA, cuff strongTSA = most predictable pain relief
✗ Wrong options: RSA unnecessary · arthroscopic osteophyte removal · interposition · HA

Partial articular cuff tear (35%)good candidate for anatomic TSA (± repair)

Not anatomic TSA candidates52 y powerlifter (glenoid loosening → HA) · prior aTSA with high-riding humerus (cuff tear → convert to RSA) · Walch B 85% subluxation (RSA if >80%) · elderly Walch D (RSA)

Tight anterior structuresER <40–45° under EUA → subscapularis lengthening + anterior capsule release

TSA outcomes10-y survival 92–95% · complications: glenoid/humeral loosening, infection, fracture, nerve injury, cuff tear · ↑ PJI if within 3 months of arthroscopy · vs RSA: ↑ IR + ↑ glenoid loosening

Reverse shoulder arthroplasty – cuff deficiency, post-instability arthropathy, RA

Irreparable cuff + OA (Goutallier IV)NOT appropriate = arthroscopic cuff repair · appropriate = NSAIDs/injection, PT, activity modification, then HA or RSA after failed nonop

Elderly, can't elevate arm (CTA), failed nonopRSA most reliable (Delta III: Constant +42, +65° elevation, 96% minimal/no pain) · HA = historical standard, non-uniform results

OA + complete subscapularis tearRSA
✗ Wrong options: anatomic TSA: subscap repair fails

Post-Bankart arthropathy + supraspinatus fatty atrophy + posterior subluxation/erosionRSA
✗ Wrong options: HA: glenoid pain persists · TSA: incompetent cuff · arthroscopic release

RA + cuff tearRSA good outcomes, even with reparable tear · options = TSA + cuff repair or RSA · TSA > HA in RA (pain, elevation, ROM) · etanercept/DMARDs/prednisone: no effect on RSA outcome · RSA complications in RA ≈ CTA (not more) · no interposition arthroplasty in elderly

RSA outcomes10-y survival ~90–95% · complications: scapular notching, infection, instability, nerve injury

Young patients – nonoperative care & arthroscopic debridement (CAM procedure)

Young OA first stepNSAIDs, cortisone injection, PT / ROM stretching before any surgery
✗ Wrong options: TSA · fusion · resurfacing · arthroscopy as first step

Arthroscopic debridementtemporising · improves pain + ROM · better with age <50, little JSN, concentric joint, added subacromial procedure · ~20% convert to arthroplasty within 1 y
✗ Wrong options: 45%

Arthroscopic debridement predictor Effect
Nonconcentric joint space / moderate–severe degeneration Poor
Posterior glenoid wear, ↑ retroversion Poor (↑ failure)
Bipolar (head + glenoid) OA Poor
Preoperative stiffness, loose bodies Good
Prior infection / instability without degeneration No effect

Techniquetreat both glenoid and humeral head aggressively
✗ Wrong options: ream glenoid + spare humerus

CAM procedureyoung patient · GH debridement, chondroplasty, synovectomy, loose body removal, humeral osteoplasty (goat's beard excision), capsular release, subacromial + subcoracoid decompression, axillary nerve decompression, biceps tenodesis

Inferior humeral osteophyteaxillary nerve entrapment → teres minor fatty infiltration
✗ Wrong options: infraspinatus/supraspinatus = suprascapular · subscapularis = upper + lower subscapular · teres major = lower subscapular ± thoracodorsal

6Complications

Procedure Typical complications
TSA Glenoid / humeral loosening, infection, fracture, nerve injury, cuff tear (most common group)
RSA Scapular notching, infection, instability, nerve; overall > TSA
HA Glenoid wear/pain, ↑ revision
Arthroscopy (pain pump, RF) Chondrolysis

X vs Y

Primary OA RA CTA
Glenoid wear Posterior Central, medialisation Superior
Osteophytes Large, inferior Few —
Head position Posterior subluxation Medialised Superior migration
Bone Sclerosis Osteopenia, erosions Osteopenia, acetabularisation
Cuff Tear 5–10% Tear 25–50% Torn by definition
Arthroplasty TSA TSA (+ repair) or RSA; HA if no glenoid RSA
TSA RSA
Design Concave glenoid + convex humerus Convex glenoid (ball) + concave humerus
Cuff Must be intact Deficient OK
10-y survival 92–95% ~90–95%
Distinct ↑ IR, ↑ glenoid loosening Scapular notching, ↑ complications

How it's asked

"72 y, OA X-ray, neutral ER — where is glenoid wear?"posterior

"Inflammatory vs osteoarthritis at arthroplasty — more likely?"medialisation of joint line

"Walch B2 description?"biconcave, posterior subluxation + erosion, 10° retroversion
✗ Wrong options: 25° = C2 · anteversion = D · deep central = A2 · monoconcave 70% = B3

"TSA vs HA for OA with intact cuff — HA gives?"↑ revision surgery

"Best candidate for anatomic TSA?"60 y with 35% partial articular cuff tear

"80 y, drop arm, Goutallier IV, GH arthritis — NOT appropriate?"arthroscopic cuff repair

"75F, can't elevate arm, cuff arthropathy, most reliable surgery?"RSA
✗ Wrong options: HA · resurfacing · debridement · fusion

"Old cuff repair, weak belly-press, ER 90°, end-stage OA?"RSA

"Post-Bankart arthropathy, supraspinatus fatty atrophy, posterior erosion?"RSA

✗ Wrong options: TSA · HA + interposition · resurfacing · debridement first

✗ Wrong options: 45% conversion at 1 y · >50 y better · bipolar no effect · spare humerus

Glenohumeral Internal Rotation Deficit (GIRD)

Shoulder & Elbow · 18 / 60

1Basics

Epidemiology

Whooverhead athletes, esp. baseball pitchers; also javelin

Definitionloss of glenohumeral IR of throwing shoulder vs contralateral · ↑ ER · ↓ total arc (symptomatic)

Coursedeficit worsens with ↑ repetitions over a season + a career; may be painless

Definition & thrower adaptations (IR loss, total arc, posterior capsule)

Characteristic motion change↓ IR in throwing arm · pitchers: ↓ IR + ↑ ER
✗ Wrong options: ER, abduction, adduction, forward elevation

Adaptation (dominant throwing shoulder) Direction
Humeral head retroversion ↑ (✗ Wrong options: anteversion)
Glenoid retroversion ↑ (✗ Wrong options: anteversion)
Posterior capsule / PIGHL Tight + thickened
Anterior capsule / AIGHL Lengthened, attenuated (✗ Wrong options: stretch it)
ER at 90° + scapular plane ↑
IR ↓

Retroversion mechanismhumerus retroverted in utero → de-rotates until maturity → throwing stress on physis halts de-rotation → ↑ retroversion → more ER, less IR · bony changes in those who began pitching before skeletal maturity

Crockett CTathletes: ↑ humeral head retroversion, ↑ glenoid retroversion, ↑ ER at 90° + scapular plane, ↓ IR · not in non-athletes

Why ER gainarc of acceleration ↑ → velocity ↑ · short IR arc + tight posterior capsule → deceleration harder → overuse injury

Posterior capsule thickeningfrom repetitive eccentric stress in follow-through

Total arc of motion concept

Situation Total arc (IR + ER)
Adaptive, asymptomatic thrower (ERG ≥ GIRD) Normal vs other side; normal kinematics
Thrower vs average population ↑ overall arc (ER gain > IR loss)
Pathological GIRD (GIRD > ERG) ↓ vs contralateral → deranged kinematics

Total arcshould be equal between shoulders · ~180° (total motion concept)

Source nuance"tight posterior capsule with normal total arc" (OB) · "↑ total arc vs average population" (OB) · "↓ total arc" in symptomatic GIRD (Orthobullets, OB) — read the stem: adaptation vs pathology

Injury risk ✓↓ ER vs non-dominant arm independently linked to injury (esp. with pre-existing IR deficit)
✗ Wrong options: ↑ ER (compensatory) · ↑ IR (uncommon) · ↑ horizontal adduction · ↓ flexion

Newer viewloss of total arc + failure to gain ER may matter more than IR loss alone

2Mechanism

Causerepetitive throwing; during late cocking + early acceleration

Capsular constraint mechanismtight capsule → humeral head translates OPPOSITE to tight region

Tight region Position Head translation
Posterior capsule Flexion Anterosuperior
Posteroinferior capsule (PIGHL) ABER / cocking Posterosuperior ✓

Posterosuperior shift↑ clearance for greater tuberosity but → internal impingement + peel-back of biceps anchor (biceps vector shifts posterior)

Throwing phaseswind-up → early cocking → late cocking (max ER) → acceleration → deceleration → follow-through · "5 distinct phases" (OB)

Pathologic cascade↓ velocity + command → posterior stiffness, slow to loosen up → posterior pain in late cocking / early acceleration (no mechanical symptoms) → "SLAP event" (posterosuperior labrum + biceps anchor fail in tension) → surgery after SLAP event; stretching works before it

Internal impingement & associated lesions (SLAP, articular-sided cuff tears)

Most closely linked pathologyinternal impingement
✗ Wrong options: subacromial · HAGL · Hill-Sachs · biceps tendinitis

Internal impingementin ABER (late cocking) greater tuberosity + posterosuperior glenoid pinch articular side of posterior supraspinatus + infraspinatus and posterosuperior labrum

Cuff tear in throwersarticular-sided partial, SS–IS junction (posterior SS + anterior IS) · (✗ Wrong options: bursal-sided · full-thickness (not described)) · general population = anterior supraspinatus

Tear mechanismcompressive (GT vs glenoid) + tensile (repetitive eccentric load, hyper-ER twisting)

Lesion most associatedSLAP tear (type II, posterior extension)
✗ Wrong options: Bankart · HAGL · anterior capsular contracture

SLAP riskthrowers with GIRD 25% more likely to have SLAP · peel-back in late cocking

Cause of internal impingementposterior capsular contracture (GIRD) or anterior capsular laxity

Chondral injuryposterosuperior
✗ Wrong options: anteroinferior = anterior instability

Associated conditionsGH instability · internal impingement · articular-sided partial cuff tears · SLAP · ipsilateral elbow pain (altered throwing)

SICK scapula

Letter Meaning
S Scapular malposition (hangs lower)
I Inferior medial border prominence
C Coracoid pain + malposition (pec minor contracture → tendinitis)
K DysKinesis of scapular movement

3Presentation

Symptomsvague / posterior shoulder pain · may be painless · ↓ velocity + command · "dead arm" · arm heavy in later innings · slow to loosen up

Examstabilise scapula for true GH rotation · ↓ IR + ↑ ER at 90° abduction · ↑ sulcus sign (stretched CHL + rotator interval)

Internal impingement examdeep posterior pain at 90° abduction + max ER; negative apprehension

Subacromial impingement (wrong option)anterolateral pain with IR in abduction

4Diagnosis & Classification

Diagnostic criteria

Criterion Value
Clinically relevant GIRD IR loss >25° vs contralateral (Orthobullets, OB) · 20–25° (OB, Little Leaguer's) — read the options
Range reported up to 50°
Pathological GIRD > ERG (↓ total arc)
No <15° loss

Key radiology findings

X-rayAP + lateral; usually normal

CT↑ glenoid retroversion

MRIABER view shows associated lesions (articular-sided cuff tear, labrum) · often normal · not needed initially for isolated posterior tightness

Little Leaguer's shoulder (proximal humeral epiphysiolysis)

X-raywidened proximal humeral physis + metaphyseal changes · 17% normal

Riskpitchers throwing breaking pitches, ignoring pitch counts/rest, year-round pitching

GIRD linkGIRD exam findings at diagnosis → increased likelihood of recurrence (3×), mean 6.2–7.6 months · pain after 2 months PT = independent predictor of recurrence

Treatmentstop throwing (~3 months no pitching) → PT (restore motion, kinetic chain) → return-to-throw · no breaking balls until skeletal maturity

5Management

GIRD in thrower
  • First line→rest from throwing + posterior capsular stretching
    (sleeper + cross-body + periscapular/pec minor + cuff)
  • Fails extensive PT→arthroscopic posteroinferior capsular release
    (some advocate anterior stabilisation)
  • After "SLAP event"→surgery (SLAP repair)

Treatment – posterior capsular stretching (sleeper/cross-body) & scapular work

Initial ✓PT directed at posteroinferior capsule stretching + periscapular strengthening, regardless of pathology · then cuff + scapular stabilisation

Regimenrest from throwing + PT 6 months (Orthobullets)

Emphasisesleeper + cross-body stretches + periscapular strengthening

1Basics

Scapulohumeral rhythm

GH : ST ratio (TO)2:1
✗ Wrong options: 1:2 · 2.5:1 · 3:1

180° abduction120° GH (⅔) + 60° scapulothoracic (⅓)

Abduction needs ERclears greater tuberosity from acromion → IR contracture → cannot abduct >120°

Osteology

Structure Key numbers
Humeral head Spheroidal in 90% · diameter 43 mm · inclination 130° to shaft · tuberosities = cuff attachments
Glenoid Pear-shaped · upward tilt 5° · covers only 25–30% of head (TO)
Coracoid "Lighthouse" of deltopectoral approach · coracobrachialis, pec minor, short head biceps
Acromion 3 ossification centres: pre- (tip), meso- (mid), meta-acromion (base)
Acromiohumeral interval 7–8 mm

Glenoid & humeral version

Glenoid Humeral head
Orthobullets 5° retroversion avg (scapular body axis); 7° retro → 10° ante ~20° retroversion (transepicondylar axis)
TO Near 0°, more often slight retroversion; <10° either way Retroverted 26° ± 11°

Humeral retroversion20° (Orthobullets) · 26° ± 11° (TO) — read the options

Humeral head blood supply

Main supplyposterior humeral circumflex artery (current literature) → injury most likely → AVN

Why PHCA?AHCA disrupted in ~80% of proximal humerus fractures yet AVN infrequent

Ascending branch of AHCAruns parallel to lateral aspect of LHB in bicipital groove → arcuate artery = intraosseous continuation into head; do not injure when plating

Deltoid branch thoracoacromial 1
Axillary 2
Anterior humeral circumflex 3

Labral anatomy & blood supply

Compositionfibrocartilage (TO)

Function50% of socket depth · cavity-compression · ↑ depth, ↑ articular surface area, centralises head, seal → intra-articular pressure (TO)

Embryology (TO)labrum forms ~8th week; LHB + capsule insertion defined by 9th week

Blood supplysuprascapular · circumflex scapular (TO) / anterior humeral circumflex (Orthobullets) · posterior humeral circumflex; from capsule + periosteal vessels, not underlying bone

Poorest blood supplyanterosuperior labrum (TO)
✗ Wrong options: posterosuperior

Biceps attachment (TO)to labrum, mainly posterior

Weak linksanterior labrum anchors IGHL → Bankart · superior labrum anchors biceps → SLAP

Static vs dynamic stabilisers

Static Dynamic
Glenohumeral ligaments Rotator cuff (main)
Glenoid labrum Rotator interval

Bony articulationinherently unstable

Glenohumeral ligaments – function by arm position (IGHL, MGHL, SGHL, CHL)

Arm position Anterior restraint Inferior restraint Posterior restraint
0° (side) + adduction SGHL / CHL
45° abduction + ER MGHL MGHL
90° abduction + ER Anterior band IGHL Anterior band IGHL Posterior band IGHL
90° flexion, adduction, IR Anterior band IGHL SGHL / CHL

Anterior static stability (TO)anterior band IGHL = main restraint (90° abduction + ER) · MGHL (45° abduction + ER) · SGHL (arm at side)

Hammock (TO)at 90° abduction IGHL = hammock: anteroinferior band = anterior support, posteroinferior band = posterior support

Abduction + ER main stabiliser (TO)IGHL

>45° abduction, anterior + posterior stress (TO)anterior inferior GHL
✗ Wrong options: SGHL · CHL · anterosuperior labrum

SGHLanterosuperior labrum → humerus · inferior translation at 0° abduction / adduction (neutral rotation) → greatest stress = inferiorly translated, arm adducted · restrains ER of adducted arm · prevents anteroinferior translation of LHB (biceps pulley)

MGHLanterior (and posterior) translation in midrange ~45° (45–60°) abduction + ER · from labrum, crosses subscapularis obliquely (~45°) → just medial to lesser tuberosity · do not confuse with subscapularis

Anterior band IGHLanterior/inferior translation at 90° abduction + maximal ER (late cocking) · anchors anterior labrum → Bankart weak link

Posterior band IGHLposterior subluxation at 90° flexion + IR (forward flexed, adducted) · restraint in posterior instability (Kim test) → must repair · tightness → internal impingement + ↑ shear on superior labrum (SLAP)

Superior band IGHLmost important static stabiliser (Orthobullets); 100% ↑ strain with SLAP lesion

CHLcoracoid → rotator cable · limits posterior translation in flexion, adduction, IR · limits inferior translation + ER in adduction

Primary restraint to inferior translationCHL (OB; Bigliani: inferior capsule + IGHL also contribute) · SGHL/CHL at 0° (Orthobullets, OB) — read the options

Ligament Origin → insertion (TO) Note
CHL Proximal ⅓ of horizontal coracoid → variable: superficial fibres greater tuberosity; only 15–50% to lesser tuberosity Blends with supraspinatus + subscapularis
SGHL (Flood ligament) Superior glenoid tubercle → fovea capitis just above lesser tuberosity Key stabiliser of LHB in groove
MGHL Just beneath/medial to SGHL → just medial to lesser tuberosity Blends with subscapularis
IGHL Anterior + posterior bands + axillary pouch (reinforced by fasciculus obliquus) → humeral neck like a collar under articular margin Hammock

Foramina (TO)Weitbrecht = between SGHL + MGHL · Rouvière = between MGHL + IGHL

Dynamic stabilisers – concavity compression & rotator cuff

Rotator cuffmain dynamic stabiliser; compresses humeral head into glenoid; works most in midrange, not extremes

Internal Impingement

Shoulder & Elbow · 20 / 60

1Basics

Epidemiology

Whomajor cause of shoulder pain in throwing + overhead athletes; very common in elite baseball pitchers · also swimming, volleyball, javelin

Definitionrepetitive contact of undersurface (articular side) of posterior rotator cuff + greater tuberosity against posterosuperior glenoid/labrum

Impinged structureposterior rotator cuff
✗ Wrong options: anterior cuff · GH ligaments · biceps

Contactmay be physiologic or pathologic in throwers

Anatomy – glenohumeral stability & cuff force couples

Restraint Structures
Static GH ligaments, labrum, articular congruity + version, negative intra-articular pressure
Dynamic Rotator cuff, biceps, periscapular muscles
Force couple plane Balance
Coronal Inferior cuff (IS, TM, subscapularis) vs superior moment of deltoid
Transverse Subscapularis (anterior) vs IS + TM (posterior)

Cuff roledynamic stability, centres head → stable fulcrum; goal of cuff repair = restore equilibrium

Ligament Role in internal impingement
Posterior band IGHL (PIGHL) + posterior capsule Tight + thickened ✓ (target of sleeper stretch)
Anterior band IGHL Lax (✗ Wrong options: tight)
Anterior axillary pouch, MGHL, SGHL Not implicated
Superior band IGHL Most strain in SLAP lesions

2Mechanism

Pathomechanics – late cocking, abduction–external rotation & posterosuperior contact

Positionabduction + maximal ER
✗ Wrong options: adduction/IR · abduction/IR · flexion/ER

Phaselate cocking (+ early acceleration); max ER
✗ Wrong options: wind-up · early cocking · deceleration · follow-through

Peel-backposterosuperior labrum peeled back by biceps → SLAP

Internal vs externalinternal = articular side · subacromial ("external") = bursal side

Posterior capsular contracture & GIRD – stretching

Most clearly associated causeposterior capsular contracture (✓ primary process)
✗ Wrong options: anterior capsular laxity (variable, less direct) · CA arch stenosis (subacromial) · Bennett lesion (no causal link)

Contracture effectblocks normal anteroinferior translation in late cocking → obligatory posterosuperior translation → posterosuperior labral + articular cuff pathology

Etiologytight posterior band IGHL + anterior micro-instability · multifactorial: altered biomechanics, subtle instability, posterior contracture, scapular dyskinesia

Primary etiologyposterior capsular contracture (OB, Orthobullets) · GH instability commonly primary (one OB explanation) — read the options

Anterior labrummay become thinned (obligate translation → anterior micro-instability)

Associated conditionsGIRD, SLAP tears, SICK scapula + dyskinesia, biceps tendinitis, anterior instability

3Presentation

Symptomsdiffuse posterior shoulder pain (posterior deltoid), deep-seated · worse with throwing, esp. late cocking + early acceleration · ↓ velocity

Inspectionproximal humeral retroversion · tender along infraspinatus

ROM↑ ER + ↓ IR · IR loss >20° at 90° (Orthobullets) · stabilise scapula · total arc preserved (Orthobullets, OB) · total arc ↓ (one OB stem) — read the stem

Strengthrotator cuff weakness often (may be 5/5)

Isolated finding↓ IR with no other positive provocative test
✗ Wrong options: sulcus sign · Speed's · ↓ ER · ↓ abduction

Test Technique Positive
Apprehension test (internal impingement) Max ER + abduction + extension Posterior pain, relieved in neutral
Whipple Forward flexion + adduction + scapular retraction, resist Pain → partial supraspinatus tear
Sulcus sign Downward pull, arm adducted Inferior instability (superior GH laxity)
Speed's 90° FF, supinated, resist downward Biceps tendinitis

4Diagnosis & Classification

Classificationnone formal

Key radiology findings

X-raycomplete shoulder series; usually normal · Bennett lesion on AP

Bennett lesionmineralisation / exostosis of posteroinferior glenoid = traction spur of posteroinferior capsule (PIGHL) · formed in deceleration + follow-through · baseball pitchers · 22% of MLB pitchers, none needed surgery
✗ Wrong options: football, swimmers, rowers

MRI / MRAPASTA (partial articular supraspinatus–infraspinatus tendon avulsion), fraying, tear · signal at greater tuberosity (posterolateral head edema, cysts) + posterosuperior labrum · ↑ anterior capsular volume · thickened PIGHL

ABER viewreproduces impingement position; dynamic humeral + glenoid sides

Lesion (spectrum) Detail

Posterior + superior labral lesion SLAP with posterior extension; posterosuperior fraying

Chondral injury Posterior glenoid
Greater tuberosity Cystic changes
Capsule Lax anterior, tight posterior

Not part of itsubscapularis tear · bursal-sided tear · Bankart · Hill-Sachs · tight anterior capsule · lax posterior capsule · full-thickness tear (needs significant trauma)

✗ Wrong options: SLAP alone · subacromial = Hawkins + · calcific tendinitis

Javelin thrower, failed PT, SLAP with posterior extensioninternal impingement
✗ Wrong options: EDS/MDI · traumatic anterior instability · osteonecrosis

Asymptomatic MRI findings in pitchers

Common asymptomatic findingspartial cuff tear · SLAP / posterior-superior labral tear · ↑ humeral retroversion · thick posterior capsule · posterolateral head cysts

Asymptomatic pitchercontinue pitching
✗ Wrong options: rest · posterior release · cuff repair · rotational osteotomy

GIRD definitionIR deficit 15° + total arc deficit ≥10° (OB) · >20° IR loss (Orthobullets) · >25° (Orthobullets GIRD note) — read the options

5Management

Internal impingement
  • First line→stop throwing + PT (posterior capsule stretching)
  • Failed extended PT + PASTA <50% / Bennett / peel-back→arthroscopic debridement
  • Failed PT + partial >50% / full-thickness / unstable labrum→repair (arthroscopic or mini-open)
  • Persistent posterior contracture / anterior instability→add posterior release or anterior plication

Nonoperative

Regimenbreak from throwing until pain-free → supervised return with proper mechanics · sleeper + cross-body stretches, cuff strength balancing, scapular stabilisation, kinetic chain · 6 months stretching

Stretch targetposteroinferior capsule · posterior band IGHL
✗ Wrong options: superior, anterior, anteroinferior, inferior

Prevention ✓posterior capsular stretching ↓ shoulder + elbow injury risk
✗ Wrong options: cuff strengthening · periscapular strengthening (less direct) · SLAP / partial cuff repair

Outcomecorrelates with compliance; surgery results unpredictable → only after extended failed PT

Operative criteria

Procedure Indication (after failed nonop)
Arthroscopic debridement (cuff ± labrum) Partial tear <50% · Bennett lesion · peel-back labral lesion
Cuff ± labral repair (arthroscopic / mini-open) Partial >50% or full-thickness · unstable labral tear
Posterior capsule release vs anterior stabilisation Persistent posterior contracture or anterior instability (adjunct)

Techniques

DebridementEUA + diagnostic arthroscopy (intra-articular + subacromial) · shaver · accelerated rehab, shorter immobilisation

Cuff repairarthroscopic addresses labrum too · bursectomy · no acromioplasty if no bursal pathology · footprint abrasion · portal of Wilmington · partial: in situ trans-tendinous (pulley; functionally shortens tendon) or complete the tear → single/double row

Posterior releasecautery / shaver · axillary nerve risk at inferior border of infraspinatus

Anterior stabilisationcapsular plication most common

6Complications

Progression to full-thickness tearsmall risk after debridement alone

Return to playdelayed / worse after cuff repair in throwers

Axillary nerve injuryposterior release, inferior border of infraspinatus

Lateral Epicondylitis (Tennis Elbow)

Shoulder & Elbow · 21 / 60

1Basics

Epidemiology

Frequencymost common cause of elbow pain · 1–3% of adults/y · dominant arm

Demographics45–64 y · ♂ = ♀ · up to 50% of tennis players · labourers with heavy tools, repetitive gripping/lifting

Risk factors (TO)smoking, obesity, repetitive wrist extension

Tennis risk factorspoor swing technique (backhand), heavy racket, incorrect grip size, high string tension

Associationradial tunnel syndrome coexists: 5% (Orthobullets, associated conditions) · up to 15% (Orthobullets, missed-diagnosis complication) — read the options

ECRB anatomy – origin, insertion & innervation

Most common tendon (TO)ECRB; ECRB > ECRL (TO); also ED, EDM, ECU, supinator can be involved
✗ Wrong options: ECRL · supinator · ED · ECU

Muscle Origin Insertion Key fact
ECRB (extensor carpi radialis brevis) Lateral epicondyle (anterior aspect); 13 × 7 mm diamond superior to centre of epicondyle Base of 3rd MC Deep branch radial n. (fibres of sixth + seventh cervical nerves, C6–C7); tendon just superficial to capsule; deep + posterior to ECRL
ECRL Lateral supracondylar ridge (just below BR) Dorsal base 2nd MC First fleshy fibres proximal to common extensor tendon
Anconeus Same attachment site as ECRB — —
ED, EDM, ECU Lateral epicondyle (common extensor origin) — —
✗ Distractor Belongs to
Largest cross-sectional area of elbow flexors Brachialis
Lateral border of cubital fossa; greatest mechanical advantage of elbow flexors Brachioradialis
Inserts on Lister's tubercle No muscle

PINenters supinator just distal to radial head → radial tunnel syndrome

LUCLlateral epicondyle → supinator crest of ulna

2Mechanism

Overloadeccentric overload at common extensor origin → microtear of ECRB origin (± ECRL, ECU)

Triggersrepetitive wrist extension + forearm pronation · tenodesis effect to optimise grip → ECRB overuse · backhand in tennis · hammering

Underuse (TO)stress shielding / pain-inhibited underuse of ECRB → weakening → TRUE cause
✗ Wrong options: "underuse cannot cause it"

Shear (TO)shearing forces → fibrocartilaginous ECRB enthesis → weaker bone junction
✗ Wrong options: tensile

Histology – angiofibroblastic tendinosis

Lesionangiofibroblastic hyperplasia / dysplasia / tendinosis = fibroblast hypertrophy (dense fibroblasts) + disorganised collagen + vascular hyperplasia

InflammationNO inflammatory cells → "tendinosis", tendonitis/epicondylitis = misnomers; failed reparative process (TO)
✗ Wrong options: macrophages · neutrophils

Also presentnormal tendon histology, hypercellularity (TO), nerve sensitisation

✗ Histology distractorsabundant inflammatory cells · neutrophils around microvessels · cellular atypia · chondroblastic proliferation · primarily calcium deposition · osteoblastic rimming · reactive hyperaemia · cystic degeneration

Nirschl (OB)1,213 patients, 88 operated; immature fibroblastic + vascular infiltration of ECRB origin; 97% improved after excision + repair

Stages of lateral epicondylitis (TO)

Stage Features
1 Acute inflammatory response; may resolve completely
2 Angiofibroblastic hyperplasia (fibroblasts, vascular hyperplasia, disorganised collagen), hypercellularity → tendinosis; most common stage at presentation
3 Structural failure → partial or complete rupture
4 Stage 2/3 + fibrosis, soft matrix calcification, hard osseous calcification

3Presentation

Symptomslateral elbow pain with resisted wrist extension, gripping; ↓ grip strength

Tendernesspoint tenderness at ECRB origin, few mm distal to tip of lateral epicondyle

Neuro examdifferentiates from entrapment syndromes

Provocative test Manoeuvre
Cozen (TO) Resisted wrist extension, elbow extended (± forearm pronated) → lateral pain
Maudsley Resisted extension of 3rd (long) finger → lateral epicondyle pain
Passive stretch Maximal wrist flexion / passive wrist flexion in pronation
✗ Wrong option: radial tunnel Resisted supination (arm + wrist extended); tenderness 3–4 cm distal + anterior to epicondyle

Rule outLUCL insufficiency (chair test, push-up test) · OCD / arthritis (↓ ROM) · posterolateral plica (pain/clicking on passive flexion in pronation + supination)

Differential of lateral elbow pain in athletes

Differentialposterolateral plica · PLRI · radial tunnel · occult fracture · cervical radiculopathy · capitellar OCD · triceps tendinitis · radiocapitellar OA · shingles

Tennis player, continuous elbow pain (TO)source gives no key; Orthobullets causes = incorrect grip size, poor (backhand) technique, heavy racket, high string tension

4Diagnosis & Classification

Diagnosisclinical (symptoms + exam)

Key radiology findings

X-ray (AP + lateral)usually normal; calcification near epicondyle (up to ½); rarely changes management

MRInot needed; ↑ signal at ECRB origin (up to 90%), thickening/thinning, oedema · does not correlate with severity → does not dictate management · use when diagnosis unclear / refractory

USthickened, hypoechoic ECRB; most useful tool in experienced hands (operator-dependent)

5Management

Lateral epicondylitis
  • First line→activity modification + eccentric PT / OT ± counterforce strap
    (NSAIDs, ice; injections second line)
  • Persistent→injection (PRP better at 12 mo than steroid)
  • Failed ≥12 mo nonop + clear diagnosis→ECRB release + debridement (open = arthroscopic)

Nonoperative treatment – eccentric therapy, steroid & PRP injections

Natural historyresolves with time; recovery 6–12 mo; no consistent difference between nonop treatment modalities and placebo / observation

Success80–90% at 1 y, only 2–4% need surgery (Orthobullets, OB) · up to 95% (Orthobullets prognosis, TO) · >95% (OB) — read the options

Eccentric exercisefirst line; eccentric > concentric (TO); ↓ pain (grip gain unclear); beneficial effect on tendon biology

Occupational therapy (OB)activity modification + eccentric strengthening + pain management = best initial

PT at 1 yPT > steroid injection; steroid (± PT) = worst outcomes

NSAIDsshort-term benefit only; not an inflammatory condition; ↑ GI side effects

Injection Evidence
Corticosteroid Short-term (2–6 wk) ↓ pain + ↑ grip vs placebo (TO); not beyond 6 wk · RCT vs placebo: equivalent pain, grip, PROMs · worst at 1 y · skin/muscle atrophy, tendon attenuation + rupture · second line / not recommended
PRP Orthobullets: better than steroid for long-term pain, healing, function · OB: ↓ pain + ↑ PROMs at 12 mo vs steroid, no ↑ strength/function, no faster return to work, not better at 6 wk (steroid better short term) · TO (Cochrane): no patient-important benefit vs placebo — read the options
PRP type Leukocyte-rich promising (✗ Wrong options: leukocyte-poor best); heterogeneous preparations
Others Botulinum toxin, autologous blood, hyaluronate, acupuncture, ionto/phonophoresis, nitroglycerin patch

Steroid mechanismanalgesic on neuropeptides (CGRP, substance P) ↑ in tendinopathy; suppresses fibroblast collagen + ECM production

ESWTno difference vs placebo at 6 mo; + stretching = stretching alone (TO)

Orthoses (TO)inelastic, nonarticular, proximal forearm strap → may ↓ pain + ↑ grip at 3 wk; bracing ≤6 wk may help ADLs · conflicting: not better than sham; may be inferior short term to steroid + topical NSAIDs

Tennis modificationsslower surface, more flexible racquet, lower string tension, larger grip

Operative criteria

Criterion Detail
Indication Failed prolonged nonop (12 mo) · clear diagnosis (isolated LE) · intra-articular pathology
Contraindication Inadequate nonop trial · noncompliance with nonop
Poor-outcome / surgery predictors Depression, anxiety, poor coping (greatest) · ipsilateral radial tunnel · prior injection · workers' compensation

ECRB release & debridement

Openincision over common extensor origin → lift ECRL off ECRB → Nirschl scratch test → excise degenerate tissue → decorticate epicondyle → watertight capsule repair → side-to-side closure → reattach (anchor / tunnel)
✗ Wrong options: synovial fistula

Arthroscopicvisualises + treats intra-articular pathology · resect lateral capsule anteriorly · release ECRB where muscle begins · decorticate · do not pass mid-radial head

Outcomeopen = arthroscopic (satisfaction, return to work, complications) · 90–100% improve, up to 40% persistent pain

6Complications

Iatrogenic LUCL injury after debridement

Causedebridement posterior to equator of radial head → LUCL injury → PLRI

Safe vs unsafe zonesanterior + superficial resection safe · too distal → PIN at risk

Presentationlateral pain, clicking/catching, can't push up from chair / do push-ups → chair push-up test +

PLRI mechanisminstability with elbow extension + supination + valgus

Chronic iatrogenic PLRI (3 mo)LUCL reconstruction with palmaris longus or gracilis allograft
✗ Wrong options: primary repair (chronic) · revision ECRB debridement · MCL procedures (milking manoeuvre/thrower)

Complication Detail
Persistent pain Up to 40%
LUCL injury → PLRI Beyond radial head equator
Missed radial tunnel Up to 15%
Radial nerve / PIN injury Distal dissection
HO ↓ with thorough irrigation after decortication
Stiffness Esp. with intra-articular procedure
Synovial fistula Capsule not repaired watertight
Infection, missed PLRI —

Lateral epicondylitis Radial tunnel syndrome PLRI
Tenderness ECRB origin, just distal to epicondyle 3–4 cm distal + anterior (supinator) Lateral
Painful test Resisted wrist extension (elbow extended), long-finger extension Resisted supination, resisted 3rd-finger extension Chair / push-up test, clicking
Structure ECRB PIN LUCL

Lateral Ulnar Collateral Ligament Injury (PLRI)

Shoulder & Elbow · 22 / 60

1Basics

Primary elbow stabilisers (coronoid)

Primary constraint (TO)release alone → laxity · secondary — release alone insufficient, ↑ laxity only after primary divided

Primary constraints (TO) Secondary constraints (TO)
Ulnohumeral articulation (coronoid) Radiohumeral articulation (radial head)
Anterior MCL (AMCL) Common flexor-pronator tendon
Lateral collateral ligament complex (LCLC) Common extensor tendon
Capsule

Coronoid (TO)main stabiliser of elbow; transection affects stability most · loss of ≥50% → instability
✗ Wrong options: anterior band MCL · LCL · radial head

Main osseous stability (TO)trochlea ↔ ulnar olecranon articulation; LCL + MCL blend into capsule

LUCL anatomy & failure site (humeral avulsion)

LCL complex (4)radial collateral (LRCL) · annular · accessory lateral collateral · lateral ulnar collateral (LUCL)

LUCLprimary stabiliser to varus + external rotation (supination) stress; most robust of LCL complex; prevents ER subluxation of ulna on humerus

Origin → insertionlateral epicondyle → tubercle of supinator crest (crista supinatoris) of ulna

Failure sitehumeral origin (lateral epicondyle), just anterior + distal to it; common extensor origin may also avulse; radioulnar articulation intact
✗ Wrong options: ulnar attachment

✗ Distractor (labelled diagrams) Role
Annular ligament Stabilises radial head in pronation/supination; does not need repair; not part of LUCL recon
Radial collateral / accessory collateral Less important for PLRI
Orbicular ligament Much less important laterally
Anterior band MCL Primary valgus restraint (medial)
Posterior band MCL Disrupted in VPMRI
Transverse ligament of Cooper Coronoid → olecranon; no stability role
Posterior capsule Contributes but does not cause PLRI
Anconeus Does not need repair
✗ Location distractor Site
Supinator crest LUCL insertion
Radial tuberosity Biceps insertion
Medial epicondyle MUCL origin
Sublime tubercle MUCL insertion

2Mechanism

DefinitionPLRI = posterolateral subluxation/dislocation of radiocapitellar + ulnohumeral joints; ulna supinates (ER) away from humerus, radial head subluxes posteriorly on capitellum in supination + extension

Traumatic (most common)elbow dislocation: FOOSH → supination + axial load + valgus (posterolateral) + extension → LCL complex fails first → anterior capsule / coronoid → semilunar notch externally rotates off trochlea

Iatrogeniclateral elbow surgery (lateral epicondylitis / ECRB debridement, arthroscopic or open) going posterior to equator of radial head → excessive resection → stay anterior to equator

Chronic attenuationcubitus varus malunion → lateral thrust + abnormal triceps vector stretch LUCL

Radial head fracturesusually valgus posterolateral rotatory load → concomitant LUCL injury common (avulsed from epicondyle)

O'Driscoll stages (circle of Horii)

Stage Disruption Result
1 LUCL ± partial/total LCL complex PLRI (pain with varus stress)
2 + anterior capsule Incomplete posterolateral dislocation
3a All soft tissue incl. posterior MCL, except anterior bundle Dislocates posteriorly pivoting on anterior bundle
3b Complete MCL Full dislocation

Sequencelateral → medial

3Presentation

Symptomspain (vague, poorly localised) · mechanical: clicking, catching, snapping, clunking, locking with extension · frank dislocation is not the most common presentation

Classicpushing off armrests to rise from chair (axial load + supination + valgus) · difficulty with triceps dips, push-ups

Historyprior elbow dislocation ("never felt right"), or prior tennis elbow surgery

Examoften benign; tenderness over LUCL, varus instability (no firm endpoint); full ROM

Diagnosis – lateral pivot-shift, chair push-up & clinical signs

Lateral pivot-shift (O'Driscoll)supine, arm overhead (shoulder fully ER), forearm supinated, valgus + axial load, elbow from full extension → flexion (to 40° — Orthobullets; to 90° — OB)

Pivot-shift findingssubluxed in extension → reduces with flexion (triceps tension) with clunk; max rotatory/posterior displacement ~40° flexion; skin dimple proximal to radial head · awake = apprehension, anaesthetised = clunk (more reliable) · analogous to ITB in ACL-deficient knee

Test Technique / positive
Posterolateral rotatory drawer Supine, overhead, supinated; finger under radial head → posterior force + ER → radial head subluxes behind capitellum
Apprehension Overhead, supinated, valgus while flexing
Chair rise (chair push-up) Pain/apprehension pushing up with forearms supinated (= positive pivot shift)
Table-top relocation
Floor / prone push-up Can't push up with forearm supinated
✗ Wrong option: valgus (MUCL) tests Technique
Valgus stress Valgus at 30° flexion, medial pain
Milking manoeuvre Elbow 90°, supinated, thumb pulled posteriorly
Moving valgus stress Ranged 70–120°, supinated, valgus
Symptom Pain late cocking / acceleration = valgus instability

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

X-ray (AP + lateral)rule out fractures, confirm concentric reduction; often normal / little value in PLRI; may show impaction defect of posterolateral capitellum

Fluoroscopy / stress viewsduring pivot-shift → radial head subluxation (radiocapitellar + ulnohumeral)

MRIidentifies acute LUCL avulsion; poor in recurrent/attenuated LUCL (oblique course); detects LUCL pathology in only 50%

Elbow instability types

Instability Cause / association
PLRI LUCL — after dislocation; lateral pivot shift
Posteromedial rotatory (VPMRI) Varus + anteromedial coronoid facet fracture
Valgus MUCL — throwers, overuse
Varus Rare; lateral gapping
Longitudinal forearm Essex-Lopresti
VPMRI VPLRI
Radial head No fracture Fracture
Coronoid >15%, anteromedial facet <15%, tip
MCL Posterior band ruptured; anterior band intact (on AM facet) Anterior band ruptured
LCL LCL complex (LUCL) avulsion LCL complex (LUCL) avulsion
Exam Valgus stress, moving valgus, milking Varus stress, chair rise, lateral pivot shift

5Management

LUCL injury / PLRI
  • Acute simple dislocation, stable after reduction → splint 5–7 d→early ROM
  • Unstable after reduction / entrapment / complex→ORIF + LUCL repair
  • Mild chronic, low-demand→brace + extensor strengthening, avoid varus
  • Chronic PLRI, failed nonop→LUCL reconstruction with graft

Acute dislocation – splinting position

Splintposterior splint 5–7 days · 90° flexion (Orthobullets) · within stable arc, no specific angle (OB) — read the options

Ligaments disrupted Forearm position
LCL disrupted, MCL intact (usual) Full pronation (tightens lateral structures)
LCL + MCL Neutral
Isolated MCL Supination — not in PLRI (LCL always torn)

Thenearly active ROM; full pronation/supination from 90° → full flexion; ↑ extension by 30°/week in full pronation; full supination in extension after 6 wk

✗ Wrong options: sling only, no immobilisation · splint at 45°/90° in supination

Operative criteria

Procedure Indication
Open reduction + fracture fixation + LUCL repair Osteochondral fragment / soft-tissue entrapment blocks concentric reduction · complex dislocation (fractures) · acute instability (e.g. unstable 0–60° after reduction)
LUCL reconstruction with graft Chronic PLRI (tissue attenuated, not amenable to repair)
Bracing, extensor strengthening, avoid gravity varus Mild chronic PLRI, low-demand
MCL reconstruction / hinged ex-fix Only if lateral restoration fails — rare

Chronic ✗ trapsdirect repair, isolated plication (less reliable) · thermal shrinkage (long-term effect unclear) · continued bracing after failed nonop · ECRB debridement · RCL reconstruction · MUCL (Tommy John, docking) reconstruction

Most common lateral ligament needing repair after posterolateral dislocationLUCL (reliably torn, off humerus)

Reconstruction & postoperative protocol (avoid varus, pronation, splinting position)

Approachposterior midline or Kocher

Graftpalmaris longus (most common), gracilis, triceps fascia; auto- or allograft

Configurationtunnel at supinator crest → "Y" tunnel in humerus, tied over lateral column; graft must cover > posterior 25% of radial head (sling) · + capsuloligamentous plication

Tensioningneutral rotation + 45° flexion (Orthobullets)

Fixationdocking (humeral Y tunnels) · interference screws both sides · overlay (sutures over bone)

Coronoidlarge fragment → screw from dorsal ulna (ACL-type guide) · small → excise + suture plication of anterior capsule to tip

Post-oplocked hinge brace; avoid varus and shoulder abduction (gravity varus) 6–12 wk; ROM with extension block → full extension + supination by 6–8 wk

Forearm in rehabfull pronation during ROM / extension exercises until 6 wk (least stress on lateral repair); forearm most stable in pronation

Post-op avoidvarus + supination
✗ Wrong options: valgus + pronation

Ligament compromised Extension exercises with forearm
LUCL (lateral) Pronation
MUCL (medial) Supination
Both Neutral

Radial head arthroplasty + lateral repairextension exercises in pronation
✗ Wrong options: avoid motion 6 wk → stiffness

InjuredLUCL
✗ Wrong options: annular · orbicular · LRCL · anterior MCL

1Basics

Medial epicondyle apophysitis – pathogenesis & diagnosis

Definitionspectrum of medial elbow injuries in adolescent pitchers: medial epicondyle stress fracture / apophysitis · UCL injury · flexor-pronator mass strain

Most common cause of medial elbow pain in adolescent pitcherLittle League elbow (medial apophysitis) (TO stem; answer not given by TO source — OB: apophysitis far commoner than other throwing elbow conditions)
✗ Wrong options: golfer's elbow · olecranon bursitis · capitellar OCD

Age ruleyounger / open physis → apophysitis or avulsion > UCL sprain; medial epicondyle apophysis fuses at 16–18 y

Pathogenesisrepetitive valgus loading → tension overload of medial structures; repetitive flexor-pronator contraction stresses chondro-osseous origin → apophysitis

1Basics

Definition

Little Leaguer's shoulder (LLS)proximal humeral epiphysiolysis = overuse Salter-Harris type I stress injury of proximal humeral physis

✗ Wrong option: SH IILLS does not produce a Salter-Harris II fracture

Epidemiology

Whoskeletally immature overhead athletes: youth baseball pitchers (dominant arm); occasionally tennis, football, racket sports

Sex♂ > ♀

Age11–16 y (Orthobullets, OB) · 11–14 y, peak proximal physeal growth (OB)

Throwing10% of paediatric shoulder pain is throwing-related

Physeal zone affected

Zonehypertrophic zone = weakest part of growth plate

✗ Zone distractorsmetaphysis (not a physeal zone) · provisional zone of calcification · proliferative · reserve

2Mechanism

Forcesrepetitive rotational (torsional) + distraction stresses (± shear) on unossified physeal cartilage; rotation > distraction in importance

Throwing phase Physeal stress
Late cocking (max ER, just before acceleration) Extreme rotatory torque ~400% greater than physis tolerates → commonest cause
Deceleration Forward arm motion vs cuff → excessive eccentric physeal stress
✗ Wrong option: early cocking Not the peak

Risk factors

Most importantnumber of pitches thrown + frequency of pitching (innings, throwing days, pitches/innings per week–month–year, multiple teams, year-round play)

Breaking pitchesimplicated (Orthobullets) · refuted / not worse than fastballs (OB) — read the options; "% curveballs = most important factor" is wrong

Mechanics / body sizepoor throwing kinematics part of accepted theory (OB) · no clear relationship with weight/height or mechanics (another OB)

3Presentation

History↓ pitch velocity, ↓ accuracy / control; recent ↑ pitching (camp → season, two "select" teams)

Paindiffuse arm/shoulder pain with throwing, anterolateral/lateral; worse in late cocking / deceleration; resolves with rest → may progress to ADL / rest pain

Exampoint tenderness lateral proximal humerus over physis · pain with rotation · GIRD (e.g. 30° IR difference) · ROM often full · no atrophy, no neuro deficit

Mainstaycessation of throwing / pitching until completely asymptomatic → PT → progressive throwing programme

Rest duration3 months (Orthobullets; "minimum 3 months", OB) · 2–3 months (OB) · 6–12 wk (OB) · 6–8 wk then progressive throwing (OB) · brief immobilisation + no pitching for remainder of season (OB) — read the options
