1Basics

Epidemiology

Incidencevery rare: ~0.5% of all shoulder dislocations (anterior + posterior far more common)

Definitioninferior GH dislocation; head trapped under coracoid + glenoid

Anatomy – static glenohumeral ligaments

Ligament Restraint
SGHL Inferior translation at 0° abduction (neutral rotation)
MGHL Anterior + posterior translation in mid-abduction (~45°) + ER
Anterior band IGHL Anterior/inferior translation at 90° abduction + max ER (late cocking)
Posterior band IGHL Posterior subluxation at 90° flexion + IR
Superior band IGHL "Most important static stabiliser" (Orthobullets)

2Mechanism

Energytypically high-energy

Mechanismhyperabduction → proximal humerus levered on acromion → tears inferior capsule/labrum → head disengages inferiorly

Soft tissuevariable tearing of static GH ligaments

3Presentation

Clinical presentation – arm locked in abduction

Hallmarkarm fixed in abduction, overhead (e.g. 140°); can't lower arm → inferior dislocation
✗ Wrong options: anterior · posterior · superior · lateral

Clinical diagnosispossible on exam alone (unique posture); X-rays still for concomitant injury

Associated injury Rate / note
Neurological Up to 60% — highest NV injury of all shoulder dislocations
Vascular Up to 39% (axillary artery)
Proximal humerus fracture Esp. greater tuberosity
Rotator cuff tear Extremely common (older + young)
Anterior capsule / labral tear Common

NV exampre- AND post-reduction: radial + brachial pulse, axillary nerve + distal neuro exam

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

X-raycomplete shoulder series → inferior dislocation, arm fully abducted

MRIafter relocation (soft-tissue injury common) → capsulolabral pathology, cuff tears extremely common · prompt in young to avoid missed cuff tear

5Management

Luxatio erecta
  • All→closed reduction + NV check before and after
    (traction–countertraction or two-step technique)
  • Inactive elderly, no acute cuff tear → sling briefly→ROM + cuff/periscapular PT
  • Active young→arthroscopic or open repair
    • acute cuff tear→prompt repair

Closed reduction techniques

Traction–countertractionas for anterior dislocation

Two-step techniquestand at head · push humerus laterally + pull medial epicondyle superiorly → head rotates inferior → anterior around glenoid (arm moves from abduction to adduction against chest) → then any anterior-dislocation reduction

Post-reductionbrief immobiliser → ROM (if cuff intact) → periscapular + cuff strengthening

Operative criteria

Option Indication
Closed reduction + immobilisation Inactive elderly; no acute traumatic cuff tear
Arthroscopic / open repair (repair vs reconstruction) Active younger patients
Prompt cuff repair Acute traumatic cuff tear (delay → retraction → irreparable)

Arthroscopy advantageaddresses capsulolabral damage + traumatic cuff tear together

6Complications

Complication Key fact
Axillary nerve palsy Most common nerve palsy; may resolve with reduction · persists → EMG at 6–12 wk (prognosis)
Brachial plexopathy High energy + head displacement; usually resolves after reduction + observation
Axillary artery thrombosis May occur late
Rotator cuff tear Common in old + young → prompt MRI in young

X vs Y

Luxatio erecta (inferior) Anterior / posterior dislocation
Frequency 0.5% Much more common
Arm fixed in abduction/flexion Yes (overhead) No
NV injury Highest (neuro ≤60%, vascular ≤39%) Lower
Reduction Two-step → convert to anterior Standard techniques

"Late vascular complication?"axillary artery thrombosis

"Two-step reduction converts inferior to?"anterior dislocation

Test Condition

Prolonged nonopappropriate: surgery less predictable than lateral epicondylitis

Modalitiescounterforce brace / kinesiology tape · therapeutic US beneficial · ESWT: no definitive recommendation, equivocal (Orthobullets, OB) · ESWT "~90% pain relief" (one OB explanation) — read the options

Next step after 2 mo brace + NSAIDs + PT + restcorticosteroid into CFT peritendinous area (short-term benefit)

Failed nonop in compliant patient Up to 6 mo (Orthobullets) · 4–6 mo · at least 6 mo (OB)

1Basics

Epidemiology

Definitionattenuation / rupture of elbow UCL → valgus instability in overhead throwers

UCL component Facts
Anterior oblique ligament (AOL) = anterior bundle Strongest, most important valgus stabiliser; origin anteroinferior medial epicondyle → sublime tubercle, 2.8 mm distal to ulnar articular margin; mean length 54 mm; primary 30–120°; greatest resistance at ~70°
Posterior oblique ligament (POL) = posterior bundle Greatest change in tension flexion → extension; tight in flexion; fan-like capsular thickening; inserts sigmoid notch; not subdivided into bands; secondary stabiliser at 30°
Transverse ligament No stability — originates + inserts on ulna (same bone)

Terminology trapAOL = "anterior bundle" = older "anterior band"

AOL band Strain / tautness Primary role
Anterior band Isometric through ROM (✗ Wrong options: isokinetic); taut 0–85°; tightens at end-range extension; most vulnerable in extension Most important valgus restraint; primary at 30°, 60°, 90°
Posterior band ↑ strain in flexion (✗ Wrong options: isometric); taut beyond 55°; vulnerable in flexion Primary at 120°

Posterior bundle rangeresists from 60° to full flexion (one OB) · beyond 90° (others)

Axis of rotation / isometric pointat UCL origin = anteroinferior medial epicondyle
✗ Wrong options: anterosuperior · posteroinferior · sublime tubercle = insertion

Flexion Main valgus restraint
0–20° (extension) Bony: olecranon in fossa + radiocapitellar articulation
~25° Olecranon unlocked → UCL takes over
30–120° AOL (anterior band)
>90° / max flexion POL

Radial headimportant secondary stabiliser in extension + flexion

Max valguslate cocking → early acceleration: forearm lags behind arm → valgus while elbow depends on anterior band; forces near tensile limit of UCL

Single best phaselate cocking (Orthobullets, several OB) · early acceleration (other OB: "highest in early acceleration") — choose late cocking/early acceleration if offered; else whichever of the two is listed

Forcesvalgus up to 64 N·m · 500 N compression at radiocapitellar joint · elbow 110° → 20° · 3000°/s

Phase Key activity / pathology
Wind-up Benign for elbow
Early cocking Peak deltoid; cuff active
Late cocking Max shoulder ER ("layback"), high torque → max elbow valgus; FDS + FCU protect
Early acceleration Peak triceps; valgus + rapid extension
Late acceleration Peak pec major, latissimus, serratus anterior
Ball release Not a phase; end of acceleration
Deceleration Eccentric contraction of all muscles, highest torque, "most harmful" → SLAP, biceps, brachialis, teres minor (✗ Wrong options: UCL)

Plain MRI 57% sensitive, 100% specific
MR arthrogram Diagnostic, more accurate: 92% sensitive, 100% specific (✗ Wrong options: "lacks specificity")
"Capsular T-sign" Contrast extravasates around distal (undersurface) tear at sublime tubercle
Dynamic US Laxity under valgus; operator dependent

MRI labels (water polo Q)1 = flexor-pronator origin · 2 = UCL · 3 = RCL

Differential diagnosis

Diagnosis Discriminator
MUCL injury Moving valgus +, milking +, loss of velocity
Medial epicondylitis / flexor-pronator strain Pain on resisted wrist flexion/pronation
Ulnar neuropathy (isolated) Doesn't explain valgus instability
Valgus extension overload Pain at terminal extension; posteromedial osteophyte
Little leaguer's elbow (medial epicondyle stress fracture) Skeletally immature

5Management

MUCL injury
  • Most patients / partial tear / non-thrower→rest 6 wk + PT + throwing program
    • fails & high-level thrower→reconstruction
  • High-level thrower, wants to continue (pro: often immediate)→reconstruction (docking, autograft)
  • Young athlete, avulsion tear, no intraligament calcification→repair ± suture augmentation

Non-thrower partial injury – nonoperative care

First linemost patients + partial tears: rest / activity avoidance 6 wk + NSAIDs → flexor-pronator strengthening (secondary dynamic stabilisers) + mechanics, peri-scapular + core → progressive throwing program

Outcome42% return to pre-injury sport at avg 24 wk · most heal without surgery in non-high-level athletes

Adolescent acute partial (14-y basketball)activity avoidance 6 wk
✗ Wrong options: stretching (full ROM) · arthroscopy (unless loose body) · static ex-fix (brace OK) · rheumatology work-up

Persistent at 6–12 wkadvanced imaging (MRI, MR arthrogram, US, stress X-rays)

Operative criteria

Procedure Indication
UCL reconstruction (Tommy John) High-level throwers wanting to continue · failed nonop partial tears willing to rehab · midsubstance tears · attritional tears with calcification (excision leaves void)
UCL repair Young athletes, avulsion-type tears (proximal/distal), no intraligament calcification; ± high-strength suture augmentation
✗ Wrong option: repair Midsubstance tear (reconstruction superior)

Repair historyearly repairs poor → replaced by reconstruction; newer augmented repair promising

Reconstruction technique (docking vs Jobe) & return to play

Goalanatomic reconstruction of anterior bundle (medial epicondyle → sublime tubercle); none stronger than native

Approachflexor-pronator muscle-splitting (✓ ↓ morbidity)
✗ Wrong options: detachment (original Jobe; flexor-pronator avulsion risk) · medial epicondylectomy in throwers

Graftipsilateral palmaris longus autograft most common/standard · gracilis autograft or allograft · PL vs gracilis both successful (PL possibly ↑ high-level return; gracilis does not ↓ laxity) · revision autograft 1.6% vs allograft 2.6%

Technique Humerus Ulna Notes
Original Jobe (1986) Tunnels Tunnel Flexor-pronator tenotomy, figure-of-8, routine submuscular ulnar nerve transposition → abandoned
Modified Jobe 2 connected tunnels, "Y" Single tunnel (2 angled holes, sublime tubercle) Muscle-splitting, no routine transposition; graft sutured figure-of-8
Docking Single socket; sutures tied over bony bridge Two converging tunnels Best: ↑ return to sport, ↓ complications, less nerve handling, better graft tensioning
Hybrid interference screw (DANE TJ) Docking socket Single longitudinal socket + interference screw ↓ iatrogenic fracture; docking + ulnar screw = 95% native strength
Cortical button (Endobutton) — Suspensory Mostly revision

Docking vs Jobe~15% more excellent results · 3× fewer complications · 3–5% less ulnar neuropathy · RTP >90% vs 80–85% (figure-of-8)

Biomechanicsdocking + cortical button stronger than figure-of-8 + interference screw

Calcified attritional UCL in high-level throwerreconstruction (modified Jobe)
✗ Wrong options: original Jobe · repair ± augmentation · arthroscopic debridement + repair

Return to play Rate
Modern reconstruction ~90% (Orthobullets) · 85–95% (OB) — answer 80–95%
All athletes (systematic review) 86%
Collegiate 95%
Surgery overall good results 84–94%
Revision reconstruction Worse

Rehab timelineearly wrist/elbow/shoulder ROM + core/hip · strengthening 4–6 wk · no valgus stress until 4 mo · throwing program 4 mo · competition 9–12 mo

Ulnar nerve management & postoperative neuritis

Pre-op ulnar status At UCL reconstruction
No symptoms No routine decompression/transposition (in situ release at most)
Symptoms (cubital tunnel) Decompression ± transposition
Subluxation Transposition

Routine transpositionavoid → ↑ post-op ulnar neuropathy, worse outcomes

Midsubstance tear + cubital tunnel symptoms + subluxationautograft reconstruction + ulnar nerve transposition
✗ Wrong options: repair · reconstruction without nerve

Ulnar nerve in forearmbetween FCU and FDP
✗ Wrong options: medial to brachial artery / most volar in carpal tunnel = median

Postoperative rehabilitation – forearm position

Repair Elbow extension exercises with forearm in
MUCL reconstruction Supination
LUCL repair (± radial head replacement) Pronation
Combined medial + lateral Neutral

6Complications

Ulnar neurapraxiamost common; 3–26% (Orthobullets, OB) · "<10%" (one OB) — read the options; treat by observation (most resolve weeks–months)

↓ Neurapraxia bymuscle-splitting · more superior exiting proximal humeral tunnels · selective transposition · docking

MABC injurycrosses distal incision

Fractureulna or medial epicondyle; small bone bridge → ORIF / larger fixation

StiffnessHO → early therapy; HO excision ~6 mo

Othersfailure to regain pre-injury level (esp. revision) · infection · flexor-pronator avulsion (detaching approach)

Not MUCL complicationsPLRI / radial head + coronoid tip fractures (terrible triad, LCL)

X vs Y

Anterior band (AOL) Posterior band (AOL) POL (posterior bundle)
Strain Isometric ↑ in flexion Greatest change
Taut 0–85° >55° >90° / max flexion
Role Primary valgus restraint Primary at 120° Secondary; max flexion; cubital tunnel floor
Original Jobe Modified Jobe Docking
Flexor-pronator Detached (tenotomy) Split Split
Ulnar nerve Routine submuscular transposition Not routine Minimal handling
Humeral fixation Figure-of-8 tunnels Y-tunnels, figure-of-8 Single socket, tied over bridge
Outcome Abandoned Good Best RTP, fewest complications

Multidirectional Shoulder Instability (MDI)

Shoulder & Elbow · 28 / 60

1Basics

Definition & epidemiology

MDIsymptomatic instability in ≥2 planes (anterior, posterior, inferior) from capsular redundancy; one plane must be inferior (TO, OB)

Agepeaks 2nd–3rd decades

Whooverhead athletes: swimmers, volleyball, gymnasts, throwers, dancers

Generalised laxityin 45–75% of MDI patients undergoing surgery

Torn loose / worn loose / born loose (TO)

Type (TO) Mechanism Example
Torn loose Trauma Traumatic dislocation (TUBS)
Worn loose Microtrauma / overuse Overhead athletes → MDI
Born loose Lax ligaments / capsule Collagen disorders: Ehlers-Danlos, Marfan → MDI

TUBS vs AMBRI (Matsen) (TO)

TUBS AMBRI
Traumatic dislocation → recurrent instability Atraumatic (minimal trauma)
Unidirectional Multidirectional
Bankart lesion most common Bilateral (frequently)
Surgery mainstay Rehabilitation first
— Inferior capsular shift for nonresponders

Pathoanatomy

Cause (TO)inferior capsular redundancy
✗ Wrong options: Bankart · Hill-Sachs · cuff tear

Hallmarkspatulous inferior capsule (IGHL anterior + posterior bands) on MRI · rotator interval deficiency

Add-on lesions (TO)from traumatic events: Bankart (anteroinferior labrum) · Kim lesion (posteroinferior labral avulsion) · glenoid erosion · Hill-Sachs, chondral, SLAP — less often than in unidirectional; rarely change treatment

Glenohumeral stability

Static restraints Dynamic restraints
Glenohumeral ligaments Rotator cuff — compresses head into glenoid (primary role)
Glenoid labrum Biceps
Articular congruity + version Periscapular muscles
Negative intra-articular pressure (release → head subluxes inferiorly)

MDI = static deficiency → therapy builds dynamic stabilisers to compensate

3Presentation

Symptomspain > instability often · weakness · paraesthesia / transient numbness · crepitus · instability during sleep · atraumatic, self-reduced dislocations, never needed ED

Impingement signs <20 ythink MDI (TO)

Voluntary dislocator"popping shoulders in and out" → PT; contraindication to surgery

Diagnosis – sulcus sign, generalised laxity & capsular redundancy

Test MDI finding
Sulcus sign ≥2+; inferior traction at 0° and 45° abduction (TO) → dimple below acromion; most specific for MDI (2 cm → up to 97% specificity)
ER with arm adducted (and at 90° abduction) ↑ ER = incompetent rotator interval
Anterior + posterior load and shift ≥2+ both directions; less specific
Apprehension / relocation Common in both traumatic + MDI
Jerk / Kim tests Posterior traumatic and MDI
Neer / Hawkins Impingement in <20 y → MDI
Sulcus grade (TO) Acromiohumeral interval
1+ <1 cm
2+ 1–2 cm
3+ >2 cm

2+/3+ sulcus + ↑ ER at side (TO)pathologic rotator interval + patulous inferior capsule

Sulcus reflectspatulous inferior capsule + rotator interval (TO, Orthobullets) · "incompetent rotator interval" (OB)

Beighton score (generalised laxity)

Item (9 points) Points
Palms to floor, knees straight 1
Genu recurvatum 2
Elbow hyperextension 2
Small-finger MCP hyperextension (passive >90°) 2
Thumb to ipsilateral forearm 2
Not included Excessive forearm supination

Cut-offsgeneralised laxity >4/9 (Orthobullets) · >6 associated with connective tissue disorder (Marfan, Ehlers-Danlos; OB)

✗ Exam distractorscross-body adduction (AC joint) · O'Brien (SLAP) · axillary webbing (pec major rupture) · Jobe's (supraspinatus)

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Modality Finding
X-ray Trauma series (AP-IR, AP-ER, true AP, axillary, scapular Y); often normal
MR arthrogram Needed to assess capsular volume; patulous inferior capsule / capsular redundancy (e.g. posterior), intact labrum
MRI add-ons Bankart (traumatic anterior) · Kim lesion (traumatic posterior) · glenoid bony erosion (chronic anterior)
Arthroscopy Drive-through sign: scope passes easily between head + glenoid at anterior band of IGHL (also laxity)

Diagnostic criteria

MDI requires
Instability in ≥2 planes One inferior
Sulcus ≥2+ ± ↑ ER at side
Load and shift ≥2+ Anterior + posterior

Differential diagnosis

Diagnosis Clue
Anterior / posterior (traumatic) instability TUBS, Bankart, glenoid bone loss, inverted pear
Long thoracic nerve palsy Serratus weakness, medial winging
Buford complex Normal variant: absent anterosuperior labrum + cordlike MGHL to base of biceps anchor
GIRD IR deficit 25° (OB) · >20° (TO, Orthobullets) vs contralateral → sleeper stretches
Little leaguer's shoulder Salter-Harris I proximal humeral physis, excessive pitch counts
C-spine disease, brachial plexitis, TOS Neurologic

5Management

MDI
  • All patients first→dynamic stabilisation PT (cuff + periscapular)
    • still within PT trial (e.g. 8 wk)→continue PT
  • Failed extensive PT + pain/instability limiting ADLs/sport→capsular shift / plication + RI closure
  • Voluntary dislocator→no surgery
  • Collagen disorder / refractory→allograft capsular reconstruction

Initial treatment – prolonged rotator cuff & periscapular strengthening

First lineall patients, incl. bilateral, voluntary, collagen disorders: dynamic stabilisation PT → rotator cuff + periscapular (serratus anterior, rhomboids) strengthening, proprioception, humeral head control, scapulohumeral rhythm + home exercises

Early rehabclosed kinetic chain exercises → safe co-contraction of scapular + cuff muscles

Duration3–6 months (Orthobullets, TO, OB) · ≥6 months (several OB) · 6–12 months (one OB) — read the options

✗ Initial distractorsimmobilisation / sling (not effective; comfort only) · posterior capsular stretching (= GIRD) · bracing · steroid injections · labral repair · HAGL repair · thermal capsulorrhaphy · open/arthroscopic shift before PT trial

Outcomemost patients satisfactory with nonop (pain + recurrence)

Operative criteria

Surgery for MDI
Indications Failure of extensive PT (sole indication, TO) · pain + instability interfering with ADLs / sport
Contraindication Voluntary dislocators
Procedure of choice Inferior capsular shift (open or arthroscopic)
Results Good, but less predictable than traumatic anterior stabilisation

Surgery – capsular shift & rotator interval closure

Inferior capsular shiftcapsule shifted superiorly → addresses patulous inferior capsule

Capsular plicationloose capsule to labrum, balanced anterior + posterior → ↓ capsular volume

Rotator interval closureplicate SGHL to MGHL (anterosuperior capsule) → eliminates sulcus sign / inferior subluxation · greatest effect = ↓ ER with arm at side (0° abduction) (~10°)
✗ Wrong options: restricts ER in cocking · IR at 90° · flexion/cross-body

Capsule ruletight anterior capsule → ↓ ER · tight posterior capsule → ↓ IR

Do not eliminate sulcusSLAP repair · Bankart repair (anteroinferior only) · supraspinatus repair · SAD

Open approachdeltopectoral; subscapularis tenotomy vs split; also fix any labral pathology

Allograft capsular reconstructionrare; refractory, collagen disorders

Arthroscopic vs opensimilar outcomes; arthroscopic advantages

Post-op rehab
0–4/6 wk Sling / immobiliser
6–10 wk ADLs, 45° limit abduction + ER
10–16 wk Gradual ROM
>16 wk Strengthening
>10 months Contact sports (only after normal strength + motion)

Recurrent instability with glenoid bone loss – bony augmentation

Clues to bone lossmultiple recurrences · long history · instability in mid-range (45–60° abduction + ER)

Glenoid bone loss Management
10% Arthroscopic repair still OK
15% + labral tear, first-time (contact athlete) Surgical stabilisation (✗ Wrong options: prolonged PT)
>20–25% Bony augmentation (Latarjet: coracoid + conjoint tendon) — arthroscopic/open Bankart fail

✗ Bone loss distractorsarthroscopic Bankart · subscapularis advancement · open capsular shift · hemiarthroplasty (no arthritis)

6Complications

Thermal capsulorrhaphy – complications & failure

Statushistorical / contraindicated; abandoned for high complication + failure rates

Failurehigh failure for anterior, posterior and MDI at 2 + 5 y · recurrence peaks 2–3 wk post-op (capsule weakest) · good 1-y result does not protect from later recurrence

Capsulerevision finds capsule thin + patulous · capsular necrosis / attenuation / insufficiency
✗ Wrong options: thick fibrotic

Shrinkagedepends on total thermal energy + rate of delivery · denatured tissue does heal
✗ Wrong options: fixed for peak temp

Revision after thermal failureopen revision → capsular attenuation = contraindication to arthroscopic revision
✗ Wrong options: arthroscopic

Axillary nerve injuryheat-induced; can't actively raise arm, full passive ROM, normal X-ray

Chondrolysisheat from monopolar RF / laser → progressive pain, ROM never regained, joint space loss

✗ Chondrolysis distractor Actually causes
Supraspinatus tear Cuff tear arthropathy, superior head migration
Subscapularis dehiscence Open deltopectoral → anterior instability
Anterior humeral circumflex coagulation Osteonecrosis (main head supply)
Non-compliance with PT Stiffness, pain (✗ Wrong options: chondrolysis)

Surgical complications

Recurrencemost common after arthroscopic or open capsulorrhaphy

Subscapularis deficiencyafter open anteroinferior shift; + lift-off, excessive ER; late anterior subluxation on axillary view

Loss of motionover/asymmetric tightening → ↓ ER; treat Z-lengthening subscapularis; rare

Axillary nerveiatrogenic neurapraxia → observe; abduction + ER moves nerve away from glenoid

Capsulorrhaphy arthropathyposterior glenoid wear, posterior head subluxation, glenoid retroversion, IR contracture; Putti-Platt, Magnuson-Stack

X vs Y

TUBS (traumatic) AMBRI (MDI)
Onset Trauma Atraumatic
Direction Unidirectional ≥2 incl. inferior
Lesion Bankart, bone loss Capsular redundancy, RI deficiency
Side Unilateral Bilateral often
Treatment Surgery Rehab first → inferior capsular shift
MDI GIRD / internal impingement
Exam Sulcus, ↑ ER, load-shift both ways, Beighton + IR deficit ≥25° vs other side
Treatment Cuff + periscapular strengthening Posteroinferior capsular (sleeper) stretching

How it's asked

"Cause of MDI?"inferior capsular redundancy (TO)
✗ Wrong options: Bankart · Hill-Sachs · cuff tear

"Atraumatic recurrent dislocator, hyperextensible MCP — etiology?"capsular redundancy
✗ Wrong options: inverted pear · LTN palsy · Bankart · Buford

"Connective tissue feature EXCEPT?"excessive forearm supination (not Beighton)

"Gymnast, self-reduced dislocations, normal MRA — exam finding?"↑ ER in adduction
✗ Wrong options: cross-body · O'Brien · axillary webbing · Jobe

"Most specific exam for MDI?"sulcus sign
✗ Wrong options: apprehension · load-shift · jerk · Kim

"Voluntary popper, 2 cm bilateral sulcus — initial treatment?"cuff + periscapular strengthening
✗ Wrong options: posterior stretching · plication · thermal · HAGL repair

"Swimmer, 2+ load-shift, 1.5 cm sulcus — next?"dynamic stabilisation therapy
✗ Wrong options: bracing · labral repair

"Bilateral MDI volleyball, impingement signs?"physical therapy
✗ Wrong options: injections · staged surgery

"17-y ♀ MDI — initial?"PT + home exercises
✗ Wrong options: sling · thermal

"Swimmer, 2+ translation, elbow hyperextension, thumb to forearm?"PT cuff + scapulothoracic
✗ Wrong options: open shift · thermal · sling

"13-y pitcher, Beighton signs, sulcus, 10° IR deficit?"MDI; periscapular training
✗ Wrong options: GIRD sleeper stretches · little leaguer's shoulder

"Who gets prolonged PT rather than surgery?"17-y swimmer, Beighton 5 + sulcus
✗ Wrong options: 15% bone loss dislocator · cuff tears

"Dancer, grade III sulcus, 8 wk PT done?"continue PT
✗ Wrong options: shift · Bankart · Latarjet

"Rotator interval closure — true?"restricts ER at 0° abduction

"Failed nonop MDI — successful surgery includes?"rotator interval closure
✗ Wrong options: SLAP repair · capsular advancement into Hill-Sachs · IGHL repair

"Procedure that eliminates sulcus sign?"rotator interval closure
✗ Wrong options: Bankart · SLAP · SAD

"Contraindication to arthroscopic revision?"capsular attenuation from thermal capsulorrhaphy
✗ Wrong options: 10% bone loss · ALPSA · GLAD · SLAP + Bankart

"Can't actively elevate after thermal capsulorrhaphy, normal X-ray?"axillary nerve injury
✗ Wrong options: chondrolysis

"Stiff painful shoulder 3 y after MDI scope, joint space loss?"monopolar RF thermal capsulorrhaphy (chondrolysis)

"Thermal shrinkage — true?"high failure for anterior, posterior and MDI
✗ Wrong options: thick fibrotic capsule · no healing

"6-y recurrent instability, mid-range apprehension, 3D-CT bone loss?"bony glenoid augmentation
✗ Wrong options: arthroscopic Bankart · hemiarthroplasty

Neuropathic (Charcot) Joint of Shoulder

Shoulder & Elbow · 29 / 60

1Basics

Epidemiology

Incidencevery rare (~70 cases reported)

Demographicsmean age ~50 · ♂:♀ 2:1

Sitesshoulder · elbow · foot & ankle

Syrinx → Charcot25% of syrinx patients develop neuropathic arthropathy, 80% in upper limb (Orthobullets, OB) · 25% of all Charcot joints due to syringomyelia (Orthobullets associated conditions) — read the options

Syringomyelia – most common cause & MRI work-up

Cause Note
Syringomyelia #1 cause of upper-limb (shoulder) Charcot; cervical syrinx = 75% of Charcot shoulders; monoarticular (shoulder > elbow); Hatzis: syrinx in 5/6 shoulders
Arnold-Chiari malformation #1 cause of syringomyelia
Hansen's disease (leprosy) 2nd most common cause in upper limb
Neurosyphilis (tabes dorsalis) Usually knee; can be polyarticular; no longer the commonest
Diabetes #1 cause in foot & ankle; reported in shoulder but less common; always rule out
Chronic alcoholism Reported (Hatzis: 1/6)
Others MS, ESRD, adhesive/TB arachnoiditis, meningomyelocele, traumatic SCI, familial sensory neuropathy
✗ Wrong option: uremia No documented association (OB)

Pathophysiology

Syrinxfluid-filled cavity in spinal cord → damages decussating fibres of lateral spinothalamic tract → loss of pain + temperature

Dissociated anaesthesiapain/temperature lost · proprioception + motor preserved (early)

Syrinx enlargesdorsal column + anterior horn → areflexia, weakness, atrophy

Neurotraumatic theory↓ sensation/proprioception → repetitive microtrauma + abnormal joint pressures

Neurovascular theorydysregulated reflexes → ↑ blood flow (hyperaemia) → ↑ osteoclastic resorption

Genes & lab markers

MolecularRANK/RANKL/OPG pathway implicated

LabsESR + WBC may be ↑ → hard to separate from osteomyelitis · can be normal (OB stem: CBC, ESR, CRP normal)

Histologysynovial hypertrophy · detritic synovitis (cartilage + bone fragments in synovium)

3Presentation

Historytrauma as inciting event in 30%

Symptomsswollen shoulder · 50% painless · loss of function · instability · progressive painless weakness + ↓ ROM

Inspectionswollen, warm, erythematous (intermittent) → mimics infection

Motionloss of motion = most common finding (90%) · crepitus · laxity/mechanical instability

Neuro↓ strength · cape-like sensory + temperature loss (back + arms) · asymmetric reflexes · areflexia late

Most common findings (OB)pain, loss of motion, instability

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

X-ray (AP + scapular Y)gold standard / initial diagnosis

Stage X-ray finding
Early Degenerative changes mimic OA
Late Superomedial flattening of humeral head
Late Periarticular soft-tissue calcifications
Late Glenoid sclerosis
Late Extensive bone resorption (humeral head "amputated"), fragmentation
Late Destruction of both sides of joint → subluxation/dislocation

MRI cervical spinenext step in every Charcot shoulder → syrinx (signal ≥ CSF on T1)

CTif concern for osteomyelitis: intraosseous gas, cortical destruction, sequestra

Scan Charcot Osteomyelitis
Technetium bone scan Hot Hot
Indium-labelled WBC scan Cold (negative) Hot (positive)

Best test to separate from osteomyelitisindium WBC scan

Differential diagnosis

✗ Distractor (OB) Why not
AVN (loss of humeral head blood supply) Sclerosis + flattening of head only
Metastasis (distant primary) Variable; no obliteration of both sides of joint
Cartilage tumour ↑ calcification throughout lesion
Bone-forming tumour ↑ ossification throughout lesion
Osteomyelitis / septic joint Same swelling, warmth, ↑ WBC/ESR, hot Tc scan → indium scan hot

Otherssynovial chondromatosis · soft-tissue sarcoma · tumoral calcinosis · Winchester syndrome · Gorham's disease · Milwaukee shoulder

5Management

Charcot shoulder
  • All→MRI C-spine + treat underlying disease
    • cervical syrinx→neurosurgical decompression
  • First line→rest, NSAIDs, sling, activity restriction, gentle PT
    • severe pain→GH corticosteroid injection
  • Failed nonop
    • classic→shoulder arthrodesis
    • underlying condition controlled→off-label arthroplasty

Nonoperative

First linerest, NSAIDs, sling immobilisation (slows ligamentous laxity), activity restriction, treat cause, gentle PT/passive stretching · 50% improve

Corticosteroid injectionsevere pain · glenohumeral most effective · temporary 80% pain ↓ (case reports)

Operative criteria

Procedure Indication Outcome / technique
Neurosurgical decompression Cervical syrinx present Slows progression, improves function + bone (glenoid regrowth); posterior fossa decompression, craniotomy, syringoperitoneal shunt, laminectomy
Arthrodesis Severe pain, failed nonop; historically only option S-shaped incision scapular spine → over acromion → anterolateral arm
Arthroplasty (hemi, TSA, rTSA, resurfacing) Failed nonop + underlying condition treated Off-label (Charcot = strict FDA contraindication, loosening) · 70% improved function at 5 y

Fusion position ("30-30-30")20–30° abduction · 20–30° forward flexion · 20–30° internal rotation → hand to mouth

No emergent ORIF / I&Dnot indicated (afebrile, normal labs) → C-spine MRI first

6Complications

Complication Risk factor
Infection Surgery without managing underlying condition
Upper-limb DVT Any surgery
Acromial stress fracture Reverse TSA for Charcot
Progressive glenoid erosion Hemiarthroplasty

Missed diagnosisoften missed → inappropriate surgery (Hatzis)

X vs Y

Charcot shoulder Osteomyelitis AVN humeral head
Pain Often painless (50%) Painful Painful
Warm, red, swollen Yes (intermittent) Yes No

Olecranon Stress Fracture

Shoulder & Elbow · 30 / 60

1Basics

Epidemiology & location

Frequencyrare; predominantly throwing athletes (baseball pitchers), other high-level athletes; overuse injury

Locationpredominantly the olecranon epiphyseal plate (persistent apophysis); line propagates transverse or oblique

Ageadolescent pitchers; may persist into late adolescence (delayed closure of olecranon epiphysis, 16–20 y; other elbow physes closed)

Associated throwing injuriesUCL tear · medial epicondyle avulsion fracture

2Mechanism

Theory (3 accepted) Note
Posteromedial olecranon impingement —
Triceps traction force Repetitive forceful triceps contraction
Valgus extension overload Part of valgus-extension overload syndrome

Torg & Moyertriceps contraction + varus and valgus torques → olecranon epiphysis separates from epiphyseal plate

3Presentation

Painposteromedial olecranon pain of throwing arm; worse with throwing (after several innings), better with rest

Exammild swelling, localised tenderness over proximal olecranon (medial, distal to epicondyle); full ROM; no mechanical symptoms

Valgus stress testinstability → associated UCL injury; normal in isolated stress fracture

Late pictureacute worsening + inability to throw after failed nonop

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Modality Detail
X-ray AP, lateral, oblique; optional valgus stress + contralateral comparison
X-ray findings Physeal widening, delayed fusion, fragmentation; medial joint space widening if UCL injured
CT Early confirmation; best on lateral (sagittal) views; originates at articular surface → runs dorsal-proximal
MRI Early confirmation; suspected UCL tear → coronal T2 fat-sat: T-sign = UCL tear

Differential

✗ Distractor Why wrong (11-yo pitcher, posteromedial tenderness, normal valgus stress)
Olecranon bursitis No swelling/infection
OCD capitellum No clicking / mechanical symptoms
UCL insufficiency Valgus stress normal
Medial epicondylitis Tenderness distal to epicondyle, over olecranon

5Management

Olecranon stress fracture
  • First line→NSAIDs + rest ± splint (4–6 wk), no throwing up to 3 months
    • delayed union / failed rest→ORIF
  • Undisplaced→single large compression (cannulated) screw
  • Displaced→treat as olecranon fracture (screw ± TBW or plate)

Nonoperative

Regimenshort-term NSAIDs, rest ± temporary splint; 4–6 wk rest, removal from sport up to 3 months; progressive ROM; avoid valgus loading (throwing)

Adjunctselectrical bone stimulation; vitamin D + calcium

Operative criteria – compression screw fixation

Indication Fixation
Delayed union / failed rest (e.g. 9 months, or two 6-wk rest periods) Large compression screw (intramedullary cannulated)
Undisplaced Single large screw (e.g. 7.0 mm)
Displaced Screw ± tension band wire, or plate

Plate fixationoption once displaced (OB) · not indicated for this injury (another OB) — read the options

✗ Next-step trapselbow arthroscopy · open osteophyte removal · ulnar nerve transposition · cast + strengthening after failed rest · physiotherapy · long-arm cast (stiffness; only reasonable briefly at onset) · hinged-elbow brace (no healing benefit)

Outcomes

Rettig (7.0 mm screw, 5 pitchers)union mean 15.4 wk; return to throwing mean 29.4 wk

Charlton & Chandler (16–20 y, delayed epiphyseal closure)UCL intact in all; ORIF with TBW, screw ± autograft → all asymptomatic at 32 months despite > 30 months pre-op pain

Surgeryreliable results when rest fails

X vs Y

Olecranon stress fracture UCL insufficiency
Pain Posteromedial olecranon —
Valgus stress test Normal (unless UCL also injured) Positive / instability
Imaging Physeal widening, CT fracture line Medial joint widening; MRI T-sign
Undisplaced Displaced
Fixation Single large compression screw Screw ± TBW or plate (as olecranon fracture)

How it's asked

"19-yo pitcher, posterior elbow pain 9 months despite nonop, acute worsening — next?"internal fixation with compression screw
✗ Wrong options: arthroscopy · osteophyte removal · ulnar transposition · cast

"11-yo pitcher, posteromedial pain, tender over proximal olecranon, normal valgus stress — diagnosis?"olecranon stress fracture
✗ Wrong options: UCL insufficiency · OCD · medial epicondylitis · bursitis

"15-yo pitcher, two 6-wk rest periods failed, other physes closed — next?"cannulated screw fixation
✗ Wrong options: plate · hinged brace · long-arm cast · physio

"Mechanism theories?"posteromedial impingement, triceps traction, valgus extension overload

"First-line treatment?"NSAIDs + rest ± brief splint, no valgus loading

"Indication for ORIF?"delayed union

✓ Mechanismfailure of fusion between ossification centres

✗ Mechanism distractor Condition

Modality Use
Axillary lateral X-ray Best view for diagnosis
CT Nonunion site; degenerative change (cysts, sclerosis, hypertrophy)
Axial MRI Shows os (superior pain + overhead vignette)

  • Incidental / mild symptoms→observe, NSAIDs, PT, subacromial steroid
    • fails 6–12 months→surgery
  • Symptomatic os + impingement→two-stage fusion
  • Impingement ± cuff tear, os incidental + nontender→ASD + acromioplasty
  • Small symptomatic pre-acromion / failed ORIF→fragment excision

Durationsurgery only after 6–12 months of nonop

Operative criteria – treatment of symptomatic os acromiale (fusion)

Procedure Indication Detail
Two-stage fusion Symptomatic os + impingement, failed nonop Stage 1: fuse ± bone graft (rigid fixation: TBW, sutures, cannulated screws) → Stage 2: acromioplasty
Arthroscopic SAD + acromioplasty Impingement ± cuff tear, os incidental + nontender —
Fragment excision (open/arthroscopic) Symptomatic pre-acromion, small fragment · salvage after failed ORIF Arthroscopic: less periosteal + deltoid detachment; better results with pre-acromion

Presentation & population (capitellum, gymnasts/throwers)

Definitionlocalised injury → separation of articular cartilage + subchondral bone of the capitellum

Populationgymnasts + throwing athletes (pitchers) · repetitive overhead or upper-limb weight bearing · also cheerleaders
✗ Wrong options: swimmers/divers · linemen · rugby · cyclists

Juvenile vs adultjuvenile OCD better prognosis

Capitellumsupplied by 2 end arteries: radial recurrent + interosseous recurrent → vulnerable to ischaemia

Mechanismrepetitive compression (lateral compression + axial loading) of immature capitellum → vascular insufficiency + repetitive microtrauma → osteochondral necrosis → separation

Throwersrepetitive valgus overload of radiocapitellar joint, late cocking phase

Panner's + OCDlikely a continuum (OB)

3Presentation

Paininsidious, activity-related lateral elbow pain, dominant arm · posterolateral pain with throwing

Sign Timing
Loss of extension (mild, ~15°) Early sign = typical early presentation
Catching / locking / grinding / clicking / popping Late — loose bodies; poorer prognosis
Lateral tenderness, mild effusion, ± crepitus Any
Painful click on passive rotation, painful pronation/supination Unstable lesion

Instability testingnormal

Key radiology findings

X-ray (AP + lateral; slightly flexed-elbow view)confirms diagnosis: well-defined subchondral lesion in capitellum · radiolucency, flattening, sclerosis, fragmentation, loose bodies · initial films may be negative

MRIbest for size, extent of oedema, cartilage status · OCD: separation of cartilage from capitellum + chondral fissuring · stable: intact cartilage + subchondral signal change, T2 no signal around lesion

MR arthrogramcontrast outlining margins of lesion = unstable fragment → poor prognostic sign
✗ Wrong options: good

Os supratrochleare dorsalenormal variant, incidental
✗ Wrong options: prognostic

Classification – radiographic & arthroscopic

Type Findings Image
I Intact cartilage; bony stability may or may not be present
II Cartilage fracture with bony collapse or displacement
III Loose bodies in joint

Stability criteria (Takahara)

Stable (heals with rest) — all of Unstable (surgery better) — any of
Open capitellar physis Closed capitellar physis
Localised flattening or radiolucency of subchondral bone Fragmentation
Good elbow motion Restricted motion ≥20°

Capitellar OCD
  • Type I stable → stop activity 3–6 wk→graded return over 6–12 wk
  • Unstable type I / stable type II→arthroscopic microfracture or drilling
  • Large, incompletely displaced→arthroscopic reduction + fixation
  • Unstable type II / type III→arthroscopic debridement + loose body excision
  • Large type II–III engaging radial head→OATS
    • uncontained→size-matched fresh allograft

Stable lesions – activity cessation

First linecessation of offending activity ± immobilisation · >90% success

Durationcessation of activity 3–6 weeks, followed by slow progression back to activities over next 6–12 weeks (Orthobullets, OB) · "minimum 6 wk" / "6 wk" (other OB explanations) — read the options

Return to playresumption when asymptomatic + examination shows restoration of painless range of motion
✗ Wrong options: wait for complete radiographic healing (residual X-ray abnormality persists even when asymptomatic)

No participation until symptoms resolve + motion recovers
✗ Wrong options: continue until worse

Avoid casting 6–8 wktoo long → stiffness

Avoid immediate throwing programme · no surgery before trial of nonop (stable, no loose body)

Nonop healing>50% of stable lesions heal with activity restriction; smaller lesions without cyst-like change heal better

Operative criteria

Procedure Indication Post-op
Arthroscopic microfracture / drilling (extra- or transarticular) Unstable type I · stable type II · symptomatic lesion with intact articular surface (in situ drilling) Protected ROM; strengthen 2 mo; throw/WB 4–6 mo
Fixation (arthroscopic reduction) Large, incompletely displaced (partial separation) As above; results variable
Arthroscopic debridement + loose body excision Unstable type II · type III · mechanical symptoms Early ROM ± brace; no throwing/WB 3 mo
OATS (autograft/allograft) Large type II–III engaging radial head; uncontained → fresh allograft Strengthen 3 mo; throwing 5–7 mo
Lateral column osteotomy Investigational, salvage (offloads lateral compression) —

Surgery overallfailed extended nonop · mechanical symptoms · loose bodies on imaging · unstable lesions

OATS (single plug)93% graft incorporation, high return to sport, low donor morbidity · large unstable lesions: fixation/reconstruction > simple excision

Microfractureamong the most commonly performed + studied

Best predictorskeletal age / open physes
✗ Wrong options: symptom duration · gender · activity-related symptoms · anatomic variant

Healingmost heal in 6–18 months of nonop (open physes)

Poor nonop healingradial head enlargement · skeletal age difference · closed physis

Long term~50% residual ADL symptoms (Takahara: 50% nonop, 46% fragment removal) · up to 50% arthritis

Complicationsstiffness · pain · failure to return to sport · arthritis

Surgery May be needed Contraindicated

2 Recurrence (7–50%) · ↑ with glenoid bone loss ≥11%, uncontrolled seizures
3 DJD
Other Adhesive capsulitis · overtightening → anterior subluxation / coracoid impingement · axillary / suprascapular nerve

Not after posterior repairanterior instability not expected · acromial stress fracture not typical

Posterior instability Anterior instability
Position Flexion, adduction, IR Abduction + ER
Symptom Pain > instability Instability, apprehension

Dynamic stabiliser Subscapularis Infraspinatus + teres minor

Jerk test Kim test
Positive Clunk Pain
Best for Posterior (mid-range) Posteroinferior

Quadrilateral Space Syndrome

Shoulder & Elbow · 37 / 60

1Basics

Epidemiology

Definitioncompression of axillary nerve + posterior humeral circumflex artery (PHCA) in the quadrilateral (quadrangular) space → posterolateral shoulder pain

Incidencerare; often misdiagnosed as subacromial impingement

Age20–40 y (Orthobullets) · 20–35 y (TO) — young adults

Sidedominant shoulder most commonly (TO)

Risk factorsoverhead athletes (basketball, baseball pitchers), contact/throwing sports, weightlifting (muscle hypertrophy)

Anatomy – quadrilateral space

Boundary Structure
Superior Teres minor (inferior border)
Inferior Teres major (superior border)
Medial Long head of triceps (lateral border)
Lateral Surgical neck of humerus (medial cortex)
Contents Axillary nerve (C5 root, posterior cord) + PHCA (+ vein, TO)

Locationposterior compartment of arm; lateral to triangular space, medial to triangular interval (with lateral + medial triangular spaces, TO)

Axillary nerve suppliesdeltoid + teres minor + sensation lateral arm (upper lateral brachial cutaneous)

Long head of tricepscan have axillary innervation (case report, OB)

Teres minor motor nerve2 variants of fascial envelopment; nerve takes highly angulated course at the fascial sling → stout fascial sling may compress it (OB)

2Mechanism

Etiology – causes of compression

Cause Note
Fibrous bands Oblique fibrous bands = most common cause (TO); compress nerve + artery in abduction/ER
Muscular hypertrophy Weightlifting after a break (OB)
Paralabral cyst Most commonly inferior labral tears (Orthobullets, TO) · posterior labrum ("occasionally", TO) — read the options
Trauma Scapular fracture, shoulder dislocation
Masses Benign or malignant

Position of max compressionlate cocking phase of throwing = abduction + external rotation (TO)

Throwersrepetitive motion irritates nerve → dysfunction; usually self-limited (OB)

3Presentation

Symptoms

Painpoorly localised posterior/lateral shoulder pain; worse at night, overhead activity, late cocking/acceleration

Paraesthesianon-dermatomal, lateral shoulder + lateral arm

Weaknessexternal rotation weakness, esp. arm abducted 90° (throwing position); 5/5 ER with arm at side (OB)

Aggravated byactive + resisted abduction + ER; forward flexion (OB)

Examination

Palpationpoint tenderness over quadrilateral space (near teres minor insertion, TO)

Atrophyteres minor + deltoid (✓ deltoid atrophy, TO)
✗ Wrong options: supraspinatus atrophy · positive apprehension · positive dynamic labral shear

Provocation (TO)arm abducted + externally rotated for 1 min reproduces symptoms
✗ Wrong options: abducted + internally rotated

Detecting weakness (TO)weakness/atrophy difficult to detect unless significant deltoid involvement

Neuro examusually normal; mild sensory change in axillary distribution

Typical negatives (OB)full ROM, negative Hawkins/Neer, belly press/lift-off, O'Brien, normal radiographs, no cuff/labral tear on MRA

4Diagnosis & Classification

Diagnosis – axillary nerve compression & teres minor atrophy

Diagnosisclinical (point tenderness ± teres minor atrophy); MRI may show compression

Key radiology findings

Test Finding
X-ray (AP, lateral, axillary) Usually normal; rules out other pathology
MRI Fatty atrophy of teres minor (✓ OB; T1 streaked white + atrophied) · deltoid fatty infiltration · compression of space · inferior paralabral cyst with labral tear
Arteriogram PHCA occlusion in abduction + ER, normal with arm at side (TO)
EMG Confirms diagnosis; axillary nerve involvement
Lidocaine block Confirms diagnosis (see Management)

Selective teres minor atrophy on MRIhighly suggestive of QSS (TO)

Sandersteres minor fatty atrophy in 3% of shoulder MRIs (OB)

Next step to confirm (OB)subclavian arteriogram with arm adducted + abducted/ER

MRI ✗ distractors↓ intra-capsular volume (= adhesive capsulitis on arthrogram) · ↑ capsular volume · infraspinatus atrophy (suprascapular) · latissimus atrophy

Isolated teres minor atrophy (OB)common, unclear aetiology (axillary nerve variants); clinically distinct from QSS

Brown classification (TO)

Type Cause Who
Vascular QSS Repetitive trauma to PHCA in abduction + ER Professional/collegiate overhead athletes
Neurogenic QSS Fixed anatomic anomalies — fibrous bands most common

5Management

Quadrilateral space syndrome
  • First line→NSAIDs + activity modification + PT
    (most improve in 3–6 months)
  • Diagnosis unclear→lidocaine block into space
  • Fails 3–6 mo / significant weakness / space-occupying lesion→open decompression
    • labral tear + paralabral cyst→± arthroscopic labral repair

Nonoperative

RegimenNSAIDs, activity restriction, physiotherapy (GH mobilisation + strengthening, posterior capsule stretching, massage)

TO regimenactivity modification, NSAIDs, cortisone injections, PT for rotator cuff strengthening — indicated initially for all patients

Outcomemost improve with 3–6 months nonoperative

Diagnostic lidocaine block

Techniqueplain lidocaine into quadrilateral space; start 2–3 cm inferior to standard posterior arthroscopy portal

Positiveno point tenderness + pain-free full ROM after injection

Operative criteria

Indication Procedure
Failed nonop (3–6 mo) Open release of quadrilateral space
Significant weakness + functional disability Open release
Space-occupying lesion (paralabral cyst) Decompression ± arthroscopic labral repair
Isolated teres minor atrophy Release of fascial sling to teres minor → ↓ pain, Hornblower's weakness resolves (OB)

Open quadrilateral space decompression

Approachlateral decubitus; posterior approach, 3–4 cm incision over space; reflect posterior border of deltoid superolaterally; fat between teres minor + major

Techniquefind axillary nerve using humeral neck as reference · avoid cutting PHCA · free fibrous bands (lysis of fibrous bands) · confirm release in abduction + ER

Post-opsling for comfort · early pendulums (avoid new adhesions) · supervised full active ROM

Resultsgood results in overhead athletes after failed nonop (McAdams, 4 athletes, OB); usually symptom relief (TO)

6Complications

Prognosislong-standing cases → atrophy/weakness of teres minor + deltoid

X vs Y

Lesion Atrophy Weakness
QSS (axillary n.) Teres minor ± deltoid ER with arm abducted 90°
Suprascapular notch Supraspinatus + infraspinatus Abduction + ER at side
Spinoglenoid notch (cyst) Infraspinatus only Isolated ER at side
Chronic cuff tear Infraspinatus (retracted tear on MRI) ER
Subscapularis Rare (upper + lower subscapular nerves) IR

QSS vs subacromial impingementQSS often misdiagnosed as impingement; in QSS Hawkins + Neer negative, MRI shows teres minor atrophy

✗ Wrong options (other diagnoses)Parsonage-Turner · long thoracic neuritis · internal impingement · external impingement · scapular dyskinesia

How it's asked

"Posterior shoulder pain, worse in abduction + ER, paralabral cyst in quadrilateral space — exam finding?"deltoid atrophy (TO)
✗ Wrong options: supraspinatus atrophy · apprehension · dynamic labral shear

"True about quadrilateral space syndrome?"most common cause is oblique fibrous band (TO)
✗ Wrong options: anterior pain · abducted + internally rotated · middle-aged diabetic female

"MRI in chronic QSS?"fatty atrophy of teres minor
✗ Wrong options: infraspinatus · latissimus · loss of capsular volume

"Pitcher, pain + lateral arm paraesthesia, T1 fatty teres minor + deltoid — diagnosis?"quadrilateral space syndrome
✗ Wrong options: Parsonage-Turner · long thoracic neuritis · internal/external impingement

"EMG shows QSS — muscle affected along with deltoid?"teres minor
✗ Wrong options: teres major · supraspinatus · subscapularis

"Weightlifter, weakness of resisted ER at 90° abduction only, isolated teres minor atrophy?"QSS
✗ Wrong options: suprascapular notch · spinoglenoid notch · scapular dyskinesia

"Next step to confirm QSS?"subclavian arteriogram, arm adducted + abducted/ER

"Pitcher, weak ER at 90° abduction — muscle and aetiology?"teres minor; axillary nerve at quadrilateral space

"Boundaries of quadrilateral space?"teres minor above, teres major below, long head triceps medial, surgical neck humerus lateral

Reverse Shoulder Arthroplasty

Shoulder & Elbow · 38 / 60

1Basics

Concept & history

Designconvex glenoid hemisphere (glenosphere) + concave humeral cup (semiconstrained)

Historyearly reverse designs failed (COR too lateral → torque → glenoid loosening) · Grammont 1985 = first successful reverse (TO) · popular in Europe; North America since 1990

Grammont's 2 innovations (OB)large glenoid hemisphere with no neck + small, almost horizontal humeral cup at 155° (non-anatomic valgus) covering < half the glenosphere

Indications summarycuff tear arthropathy (CTA), comminuted 4-part proximal humerus fractures, failed arthroplasty

2Mechanism

Biomechanics – medialised/inferior centre of rotation & deltoid tensioning

COR shiftmedial + inferior (distal) (✓ TO, OB)
✗ Wrong options: superior · lateral · ↑ lateral humeral offset · posterior · proximal

Standard prosthesis without cuff (TO)deltoid contraction → humeral head subluxes superiorly; reverse corrects the abnormal vector and re-creates a fulcrum

Medial COR↑ deltoid moment arm (less force for same torque) · ↓ torque/shear at glenoid interface (✓ glenoid stability; force vector passes through component) · ↓ articular shear stress

Distal CORlengthens/tensions deltoid (↑ resting length + tone) · humerus lowered relative to acromion · recruits anterior + posterior deltoid as abductors

Grammont advantages (OB)medialisation of COR + lengthening deltoid + ↑ deltoid moment arm
✗ Wrong options: lateralisation · shortening deltoid

Matched radius of curvatureglenosphere + humeral cup → stable fixed fulcrum for elevation; shear converted to compression

Motions gainedforward elevation + abduction ↑ · IR, ER (at side or at 90°), adduction not significantly improved → latissimus dorsi transfer for ER
✗ Wrong options: not normal

↑ deltoid moment (OB)place glenosphere more inferiorly (✓) · anything moving COR medial/inferior or lengthening deltoid
✗ Wrong options: constrained poly (no effect) · short stem (no effect) · smaller NSA (varus) shortens deltoid

3Presentation

Pseudoparalysisinability to actively elevate arm with free passive ROM, no neurological lesion; irreparable cuff tear (± GH arthritis)

Pseudoparalysis without arthritis (TO)loss of fulcrum when cuff fails → head translates superiorly → deltoid loses lever · first line = rehabilitation (recruit accessory muscles) → RSA only after PT fails

Anterosuperior escapeincompetent coracoacromial arch → humeral head escapes into subcutaneous tissue (esp. after HA + acromioplasty); anterosuperior bulging on attempted elevation

Failed HA (cuff failure)pseudoparalysis, lateral deltoid pain, no crepitus, near-normal passive ROM · weakness of ER at side
✗ Wrong options: infection → passive ROM also ↓

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Investigation Purpose / finding
True AP (Grashey) Extent of arthritis, superior migration of humerus, acetabularisation of acromion
Axillary lateral Posterior glenoid wear
Scapular-Y
CT Glenoid version + bone stock (if axillary inadequate), osteopenia
MRI Cuff integrity + fatty infiltration

Anterosuperior migration on X-raycuff tear + CA ligament deficiency (OB)

Hamada ≥3acetabularisation of acromion
✗ Wrong options: not linked to post-op acromial fracture

RA glenoidcentral wear, glenoid medialisation
✗ Wrong options: posterior wear = primary OA

5Management

Massive irreparable cuff tear ± GH arthritis
  • Balanced shoulder (isolated SST tear + arthritis)→unconstrained TSA
  • Full active elevation retained→no RSA
  • Pseudoparalysis, no arthritis→PT first
    • PT fails→RSA
  • CTA / pseudoparalysis, elderly, working deltoid→RSA
    • also no active ER (abducted)→RSA + latissimus dorsi transfer
Failed hemiarthroplasty / aTSA
  • Infection signs→2-stage revision
  • Cuff failure / anterosuperior escape→convert to RSA
    (not RCR, aTSA or tendon transfer — poor results)
  • Intractable pain / persistent infection→resection arthroplasty

Indications – cuff tear arthropathy, pseudoparalysis, failed arthroplasty or cuff repair, fracture

Indication Detail
Cuff tear arthropathy Severe GH arthritis + superior escape + massive cuff tear; best results
Pseudoparalysis Irreparable cuff tear (± arthritis, TO)
Anterosuperior escape Incompetent CA arch
Proximal humerus fracture in elderly 3- or 4-part, age >70 · head-splitting · osteopenia (GT poor healing)
Cuff insufficiency "equivalent" Tuberosity nonunion/malunion after trauma or arthroplasty
Failed arthroplasty Prior HA or aTSA with cuff insufficiency; options exhausted
Failed cuff repairs Irreparable tear after ≥2 repairs
Rheumatoid arthritis Only if glenoid bone stock sufficient
Others (OB) Proximal humeral tumours, B2 glenoid

Patient factorslow demand · physiological age >70 ("exclusively >70 y", OKU 9) · sufficient glenoid bone stock · working deltoid (intact axillary nerve)

Not ideal40-y labourer (glenoid loosening in young/active) · 40-y painful malunion · arthritis with active overhead motion · intact cuff → aTSA · 30-y locked posterior dislocation

Not indications (TO)massive cuff tear + arthritis with full active elevation · isolated supraspinatus tear + arthritis → balanced → unconstrained TSA

Revision options — wrong (OB)revision SST repair after 2 failed (doesn't address subscap) · HA in subscap + SST insufficiency → instability + anterosuperior escape · latissimus transfer = younger, no arthritis · cortisone/PT (doesn't restore function)

HA best resultsmarked glenoid bone loss, younger, RA with forward elevation >90°

HA failure reasonsprogressive glenoid degeneration + cuff deficiency (✓ cuff failure; not advanced glenoid wear when pseudoparalytic without crepitus)

Instability after HAelderly fall → rotator cuff injury → convert to RSA
✗ Wrong options: labrum

Humeral stem looseningmost commonly linked to infection

Sirveaux (OB)80 shoulders: 96% no/minimal pain, 3 revisions; ↑ forward elevation at 44 mo

Proximal humerus fracture – RSA vs alternatives

Option Elderly 3/4-part fracture
Nonoperative Majority of geriatric fractures
rTSA Best surgical option in osteoporotic elderly; better outcomes + lower reoperation than HA; doesn't rely on tuberosity healing
HA Outcome depends on tuberosity healing (cuff function)
ORIF High demand + expected tuberosity healing; elderly → = nonop function, ↑ complications
IMN 2/3-part; ≈ ORIF; high failure in osteoporosis
PHR Last resort — no bone stock; failed revisions, tumour

Fracture RSA – greater tuberosity healing

GT fixation↑ forward elevation + ER (✓ OB); anatomic GT repair → ↑ ER, function, satisfaction vs resection/malunion · not mandatory (deltoid still powers elevation)

No effect on outcomepress-fit vs cemented stem · inlay stem · LTO (LT already fractured) · suprascapular decompression

Humeral height in fracturecalcar/tuberosity; if calcar missing → pectoralis major insertion 5.6 cm below top of humeral head

Contraindications – deltoid dysfunction & axillary neuropathy

Contraindication Note
Deltoid denervation / axillary nerve dysfunction Absolute; separate permanent vs temporary
Global deltoid deficiency Absolute · partial = relative (reasonable results)
C5–C6 root avulsion · posterior cord palsy → complete deltoid palsy
Acromion deficiency Contraindication (Orthobullets) · relative (OB)
Glenoid osteoporosis / insufficient bone stock
Active infection (glenoid osteomyelitis)
Complete brachial plexus injury · prior arthrodesis
Severely impaired deltoid · isolated SST tear · full active elevation (TO)

NOT contraindicationsRA (sufficient glenoid stock; excellent short/midterm results) · pseudoparalysis (= indication) · prior infection (if not active) · prior partial acromioplasty · absent GH joint-space narrowing · age >70 · incompetent CA arch (= indication)

Deltoid wasting + scapular dysrhythmianot a candidate
✗ Wrong options: "candidate due to CTA" · "not candidate due to age/massive tear"

Operative criteria

Factor Requirement
Deltoid Functioning (intact axillary nerve)
Age Physiological >70, low demand
Glenoid Sufficient bone stock
Cuff Irreparable / deficient (pseudoparalysis)
Failed nonop PT, injections
Fracture 3/4-part, >70 y, osteoporosis

Approach

Deltopectoral Anterosuperior (superolateral)
Deltoid Preserved Anterior deltoid split/violated
Subscapularis Take-down needed Preserved
Glenoid Inferior pole exposed (✓ baseplate position) ↑ exposure; risk excess height / superior tilt
Instability Extensive capsular release → ↑ instability (TO: ↑ vs superolateral) ↓ (anterior stabilisers kept)
Axillary nerve ↓ risk ↑ risk (distal branches)
Notching Not associated ↑ notching (insufficiently inferior baseplate)
Other Extensile; LD transfer possible; poor posterior glenoid access; stiffness (immobilise for subscap) Easier humeral axial prep + GT fixation

Technique

Humerusosteotomy 0–30° retroversion (typically 20°); more retroversion → ↑ post-op ER · LHB tenotomy/tenodesis · ream + broach as TSA
✗ Wrong options: no effect on notching

Glenoidexcise labrum, circumferential capsular release, expose inferior glenoid subperiosteally · central guidewire by best bone stock · baseplate as inferior as possible + inferior tilt (↓ loosening + notching) · navigation

Screwssuperior → coracoid base, inferior → scapular body · unicortical screws to coracoid may ↓ acromial fracture; 2 screws may suffice

Glenosphere size36 mm females/smaller · 40 mm large men

Newer prostheses (OB)locking peripheral screws + 15° inferior tilt · NSA 155° → 143° or 135° → ↓ notching, ↓ instability, ↓ need for subscap repair

Humeral component design (inlay vs onlay)

Inlay (Grammont) Onlay
Stem Straight, horizontal inlay tray Curved
Bone More metaphyseal reaming → ↑ GT fracture risk; ↑ bony contact Preserves proximal bone
Cut More varus cut → preserves GT, minimises cuff damage
Offset ↑ humeral offset / lateralisation
ROM ↑ adduction, extension, ER
Conversion Convertible to/from HA + aTSA
Scapular spine fracture ↓ risk (✓ prevention, OB) ↑ risk (humeral lateralisation)

TO trap"onlay has more valgus cut and more cuff damage" = FALSE (onlay = varus cut, less damage)

Latissimus dorsi transfer with RSA

Indicationloss of active elevation + ER → RSA restores elevation, LD restores ER; primary or revision (✓ failed HA, no active ER with arm abducted)

✗ Wrong optionsdeltoid dysfunction (RSA contraindicated) · brachial plexus injury/arthrodesis · CTA with active ER >50° (posterior cuff functioning → RSA or CTA head alone) · AVN + partial infraspinatus tear (nonop → resurfacing) · OA with 10° retroversion (TSA, ream anterior glenoid)

Rehabilitation

Earlysling; passive / active-assisted only

Sling duration3 wk if subscap NOT repaired · 6 wk if repaired; limit passive ER + active IR

Avoidpushing out of chair (extension + adduction + IR) · TO: avoid these 8–12 wk

Early ROMnot ↑ dislocation vs 6 wk immobilisation (OB)

Subscap re-tearanterior instability → early exploration + repair

Outcomes

Best indicationCTA (failed arthroplasty = highest complications)

Deteriorationradiographic after 6 y, clinical after 8 y

Survivorship~90% at 10 y

Surgeon learning curve & postoperative surveillance

Learning curveearly complications ↓ after 18–45 cases (✓ 40; ✗ Wrong options: 10, 75, 100, 200)

Asymptomatic notchingobserve, routine follow-up with serial X-rays (✓) · (✗ Wrong options: aspirate for C. acnes · sling for acromial fracture · revise baseplate) · IR to L5 = excellent for RSA

6Complications

Overview – which is "most common"

Claim Source
Scapular notching = most common (radiographic) complication OB, TO, Orthobullets incidence
Dislocation = most common complication OB (2 questions) — read the options
Instability/dislocation = most common cause of early failure / early revision Orthobullets, TO, OB
Glenoid loosening = most common mechanism of failure / long-term complication Orthobullets, TO
Glenoid loosening/fracture = most common after revision RSA OB

TO ranking (early)notching > instability > acromion/scapular spine fracture > infection > axillary neurapraxia; overall complication rate ~15%

Complications ∝ indicationhighest for failed shoulder arthroplasty (dislocation, loosening, ↓ function); low for CTA / failed RCR

Scapular notching – superior baseplate, neck-shaft angle & lateralisation

Definitionerosion of axillary border of inferior scapular neck (scapular pillar) from medial rim of humeral cup in adduction; unique to RSA

Incidence44–96% Grammont (Orthobullets) · 51–96% (OB) · 68% (Lévigne, OB) · 62% (Lévigne, 326 pts, OB); appears early (1–2 y), variable progression

Most common technical errorsuperior placement of glenoid component (✓) → inferior scapular notching
✗ Wrong options: "superior notching"

↑ Notching ↓ Notching (protective)
Superior baseplate placement (upper half) Inferior placement / inferior overhang — greatest reduction, least adverse effect
Superior tilt of glenosphere Inferior tilt (more even force, impingement-free arc)
155° NSA (Grammont; medialises humeral component) Varus NSA (135°) — most important factor (Gutiérrez)
Medialised COR / medialised glenosphere Lateralised offset (bone/metal augment) — protective (✓ TO "all except")
Superior glenoid erosion (E2) → base plate in valgus Larger glenosphere (OB)
Anterosuperior / superolateral approach ↓ poly depth (↑ ROM, ↓ notching)
↓ scapular neck length · CTA with narrow AHD · infraspinatus FI grade 3/4 · high BMI · ↑ activity · duration

Gutiérrez (sawbones)NSA = largest effect on inferior impingement → then glenosphere position → lateral offset → glenosphere size · COR offset = largest effect on ROM · 15° inferior tilt → most uniform compression, least micromotion

No effect on notchinghumeral retroversion · stem length · horizontal humeral cut · retentive liner · cemented stem · locking screws · over-reaming

Source conflictsinferior/posterior tilt: protective (Orthobullets, TO, most OB) · minimal effect, may ↑ notching (OB7681; low position = biggest effect) · glenosphere size: larger ↓ notching (OB) · no effect (OB214573) — read the options

Consequences↓ ROM, strength, Constant scores (✓ with preop superior erosion, Lévigne) · "not linked to detrimental outcomes" (same OB item) · particulate debris → osteolysis → implant failure; association with baseplate failure · rarely needs revision · not ↑ dislocation · not ↑ aseptic loosening

Baseplate lateralisation↓ notching but ↑ baseplate loosening (more stress)

Sirveaux grade Extent
0 No notch
1 Limited to scapular pillar
2 Contact with inferior screw of baseplate
3 Beyond inferior screw
4 Under baseplate, approaching central peg

Irreparable / inadequate subscapularis Strongest (Orthobullets); ↑ with medialised prosthesis (OB) · less of an issue with newer implants (OB4801) — read the options
Proximal humeral bone loss / loss of tuberosities

Preventionlateralise baseplate/glenosphere (✓) · ↑ glenosphere size · eccentric baseplate · lateralise/distalise humeral component · constrained implant

✗ Dislocation treatment distractorsEMG (deltoid weakness) · I&D + poly exchange (acute infection) · I&D + antibiotic spacer (chronic infection) · ORIF (periprosthetic fracture)

RSA dislocation (OB algorithm)
  • Closed reduction successful→immobilise in abduction 4–6 wk
  • CR fails→open reduction
    • soft-tissue laxity→thicker PE ± metal spacer ± retentive PE ± glenosphere change
    • adequate tension→immobilise in abduction 4–6 wk
  • Recurrent→work-up: full-length humerus X-ray, CT, WBC, ESR/CRP
Recurrent RSA instability – cause
  • ↑ ESR/CRP + positive aspirate→<3 mo: I&D + PE exchange · >3 mo: 1- or 2-stage revision
  • Humeral shortening
    • <15 mm→thicker PE ± metal spacer ± retentive PE
    • >15 mm→humeral revision ± proximal humeral allograft
  • Humeral medialisation
    • <15 mm→larger glenosphere ± ↑ lateral offset
    • >15 mm→baseplate revision with augment / lateralising graft
  • Acromial stress fracture→immobilise in abduction 4–6 wk

Revision Total Elbow Arthroplasty

Shoulder & Elbow · 39 / 60

1Basics

Epidemiology

Lifetime revision rate~13% · much higher than TKA/THA

TEA survival92% (5 y), 81% (10 y), 71% (15 y), 61% (20 y)

Shift in indicationoriginally RA; with anti-rheumatics (DMARDs) → now mostly post-traumatic (distal humerus fractures)

Risk factors for TEA failuresmoking · medical comorbidities (RA, hypothyroidism, uncontrolled DM, iron-deficiency anaemia, obesity) · non-compliance with activity restrictions · non-constrained (dislocation) or highly constrained (loosening) systems

Failure modes & revision rates by indication

Mode of failure Rate Key facts
Aseptic loosening 15% ↑ with cementation + highly constrained designs; anterior impingement of coronoid into anterior humeral flange in max flexion · most common in OA
Component failure 15% Mostly bushing wear (linked/semiconstrained); younger patients or pre-existing deformity
Infection ~8% → ~3% since DMARDs (Orthobullets) · 3–5% (OB) — read the options Higher than other joint arthroplasties
Periprosthetic fracture 5% Intra-op (preparation, reaming, implantation) · post-op (non-compliance, ground-level falls)
Instability — Most common failure of unconstrained (unlinked) TEA — late ligament insufficiency or malposition

Revision rate by indicationtraumatic < inflammatory arthritis < OA (lowest → highest)

OA patientsaseptic loosening = most common complication (higher demand)
✗ Wrong options: infection · fracture

RA patients↑ tendon + ligament insufficiency

Designunconstrained/unlinked · semiconstrained/linked (e.g. Coonrad-Morrey) = best longevity + function · constrained

Polyethylene / bushing wearlinked + semiconstrained · not the main failure of unconstrained · component fracture uncommon

Gill & Morrey (OB)RA, Coonrad-Morrey, 10–15 y: 97% no/mild pain · arc 28–131° · 92.4% survival · 14% reoperation · 86% good/excellent

Infection – organisms, risk factors & staged revision

Organism Fact
S. aureus (GPC clusters, catalase +, coagulase +) Most common (~40%)
S. epidermidis (GPC clusters, catalase +, coagulase −) 2nd (30–35%); worst outcomes / lowest reimplantation — biofilm / encapsulation → most difficult to eradicate
Cutibacterium (P.) acnes (anaerobic aerotolerant GP bacillus) Most common in TSA, not common in TEA
GPC chains, α-haemolytic, optochin-sensitive S. pneumoniae (pneumonia)
GPC chains, β-haemolytic, bacitracin-sensitive Group A strep → necrotising soft-tissue infection

Infection risk factorsRA on steroids · hypothyroidism (independent) · diabetes · thin soft-tissue envelope · prior elbow infection · prior elbow surgery · psychiatric illness

Not risk factorsfemale gender · Nordic heritage · isolated +RF with −anti-CCP · HbA1c <6.0%
✗ Wrong options: RA

Genes & lab markers

Test Value / meaning
TSH ↑ + free T4 ↓ Hypothyroidism = independent PJI risk (TSH normal 0.5–5.0; free T4 normal 0.7–1.9)
ESR, CRP, WBC Usually ↑ in PJI (WBC may be normal)
IL-6, alpha-defensin Not studied in elbow PJI
Synovial WBC No accepted cut-off for elbow
Aspiration culture + = chronic infection; very high PPV, very low NPV → negative aspirate does not rule out
Intra-op histology Most effective diagnostic test; specificity 93%, NPV 90%, sensitivity 51%
Intra-op cultures Negative in 10% of infected TEA; chronic ~15% vs acute 3%

No definitive testdiagnosis needs high clinical suspicion

3Presentation

Symptomssqueaking / crepitus (bushing wear) · pain · swelling · stiffness

Red flags for infectionpain at night or rest · progressive loss of motion without cause · early unexplained loosening · erythema, sinus tract, persistent wound drainage

Examdiffuse tenderness, swelling, deformity (significant bushing wear), painful limited ROM

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

X-rayAP + lateral of humerus, elbow, forearm → loosening, periprosthetic fracture, bushing wear

Bushing wear angleangle between ulnar and humeral components · >10° = mild–moderate wear (Orthobullets text) · figure labels 7° measurable, 10° extensive — read the options

CTperiprosthetic osteolysis / loosening; cement mantle intact or broken in fracture

MRImetal subtraction + contrast → abscess / soft-tissue infection

Mayo (O'Driscoll & Morrey) classification of periprosthetic fracture

Type Location / features Treatment
I Periarticular — humeral condyle or olecranon; osteolysis + muscle distraction Undisplaced → immobilisation / soft-tissue repair (fibrous union OK) · Displaced → ORIF with heavy non-absorbable sutures or tension band · intact extensor + well-fixed stem → fragment excision
II1 Along stem, well-fixed implant ORIF + component retention ± strut allograft (unicortical screws + cerclage cables)
II2 Along stem, loose implant, good bone stock Revision with long-stem ± strut allograft + impaction grafting (± locking plate / cerclage)
II3 Along stem, loose implant, severe bone loss Revision with extensive allograft; often resection arthroplasty
III Distal to prosthesis Well-fixed → humerus: immobilise, ulna: ORIF (plate) · loose → treat as II2 · CT/X-ray to confirm implant + cement mantle

5Management

Failed TEA
  • Bushing wear, stable implants, no infection→I&D + bushing exchange (retain)
  • Acute PJI (<90 d)→I&D + component retention (63%)
  • Chronic PJI→explant + 2-stage revision (90%)
    • unfit / severe bone loss / poor soft tissue→resection arthroplasty
  • Aseptic loosening / Mayo II2→single-stage long-stem revision

Operative criteria

Procedure Indication Outcome
Nonop (immobilise 2–4 wk → brace) Type I with stable prosthesis · Type III humerus with stable implant (→ Sarmiento) · unfit for surgery —
I&D + bushing exchange, retain Squeaking/crepitus, stable implants, no infection · acute PJI <90 d Bushing exchange 75% good at 5 y · acute PJI 63% eradicated · chronic only 31%
ORIF, retain ± excision ± strut Type I olecranon · II1 · III ulna 80–90% no complications
Single-stage revision ± ORIF/allograft Type II2 · aseptic loosening Chronic infection only 66% eradicated
Explant + 2-stage revision Infected TEA · Mayo II2 Chronic infection 90% eradicated
Resection arthroplasty Salvage: resistant PJI, can't tolerate multiple surgeries, severe bone loss, poor soft tissue · II3 not reconstructable 71% eradication; lowest MEPS function

Chronic P. acnes (6 mo), well-fixed, good bone stock, healthy2-stage revision
✗ Wrong options: IV antibiotics alone · arthroscopic I&D · I&D + poly exchange · single stage

Technique pearls

Bushing exchangeprior approach · ulnar nerve explore/decompress if symptomatic, else identify + protect · uncouple components → inspect integrity, loosening, rotation → exchange bushing

ORIFhumerus: posterior paratricipital muscle-sparing · ulna: posterior + subcutaneous border extension · radial nerve crosses lateral IM septum 14 cm proximal to lateral epicondyle · Type I with extensor disruption → tension band, K-wires dorsal to implant engaging cement + figure-of-8

Single-stage revisionremove all loose implant + cement · long stem in all, 2 cortical widths beyond fracture · cement stem BEFORE struts (extravasation under strut → no incorporation, nerve irritation) · humerus: longer posterior + shorter anterior strut · ulna: dorsal strut under anconeus or FCU
✗ Wrong options: flexion impingement

2-stage (infection)posterior triceps-sparing · humeral removal: burr + flexible osteotomes, slap hammer; stuck → posterior humeral cortical split · well-fixed ulna → extended olecranon osteotomy (repair with cables) · antibiotic spacers/beads in both canals; no cement in subcutaneous tissue · ± static ex-fix · ≥6 wk IV culture-specific antibiotics → reimplant when markers normalise, long stem + antibiotic cement

2-stage (fracture)stage I: union with ICBG + plate · stage II: longer stem + impaction graft

Resection arthroplastythick flaps; nerves in unpredictable places; remove all cement; stabilise with heavy sutures/wires if needed

6Complications

Complication Rate / risk factors Treatment
Persistent deep infection ~10% after 2-stage, ~30% after single stage · polymicrobial, S. epidermidis, RA on steroids, extensive bone loss Resection arthroplasty
Ulnar nerve palsy Cement extravasation, not visualising nerve —
Radial nerve palsy Cement extravasation, long plates impinging —
Symptomatic hardware ORIF of periprosthetic ulna fractures Remove after union

Prognosisdepends on cause of failure, comorbidities, remaining bone stock

X vs Y

Unconstrained (unlinked) Semiconstrained (linked) Highly constrained

Longevity — Best (Coonrad-Morrey) —
