Rotator Cuff Arthropathy

Shoulder & Elbow · 40 / 60

1Basics

Epidemiology

Demographics♀ > ♂ · 7th decade · dominant shoulder

Risk factorsrotator cuff tear · RA · crystal-induced arthropathy · haemorrhagic shoulder (haemophilia, elderly on anticoagulants)

Historyterm cuff tear arthropathy coined by Neer (1983)

Defining features

3 common features (all patients)non-functioning rotator cuff · GH degenerative changes · superior migration of humeral head

Full picture+ subchondral osteoporosis · humeral head collapse · femoralisation of head · acetabularisation of coracoacromial arch

Why diagnosis mattersdefinitive treatment depends on whether cuff functions

2Mechanism

Pathogenesis – loss of force couples/concavity compression & anterosuperior escape

Concavity compressioncuff compresses head into glenoid → concentric rotation → primary mechanism centring head against upward pull of deltoid

Force couplingmuscle balance centres the net force vector on glenoid → stable fulcrum for deltoid + periscapular muscles · loss → instability, eccentric wear, CTA

Supraspinatus + infraspinatusdepress head caudally; dynamic stabilisers

Pathwaycuff deficiency → loss of dynamic compression → abnormal joint forces → superior migration → mechanical cartilage wear → acetabularisation of acromion

✗ Concept trap Truth
Absent supraspinatus → centring impossible Subscapularis + infraspinatus can still centre head
Cuff repair restores stability after concavity lost False — cannot fully restore once effective glenoid concavity lost
Intact biceps prevents migration False — biceps is not a head depressor
Cuff vector optimally depresses head False — not optimally oriented

Mechanical factorsloss of concavity (compression effect), ↓ ROM + function, head migration, instability ± recurrent dislocation

Nutritional factorsloss of watertight joint space → ↓ joint fluid → cartilage atrophy (↓ water + GAG) + subchondral collapse (disuse osteoporosis)

Crystal-inducedsynovial degradation proteins destroy cuff + cartilage → end-stage calcium phosphate crystal deposits

Pseudoparalysis mechanism

Pseudoparalysisinability to actively forward flex/elevate with full passive ROM · cuff can't DEPRESS head → deltoid pulls humerus up → anterosuperior subluxation / escape · deltoid lever arm ↓
✗ Wrong options: can't elevate

Injection testno change in active elevation after GH local anaesthetic → pain is NOT the cause → mechanical (RSA)

✗ Pseudoparalysis distractor Why wrong
Posteroinferior / inferior subluxation Deltoid pulls anterosuperiorly
Deltoid atrophy Not the classic chronic-tear mechanism
Suprascapular nerve palsy Weak supra + infraspinatus but cuff still checkreins head → no pseudoparalysis
C5 radiculopathy Weak deltoid + cuff, paraesthesias, no pseudoparalysis
Fibroblastic capsular thickening Adhesive capsulitis (passive ROM lost)
✗ Pathogenesis distractor Diagnosis
Haemosiderin, synovial hyperplasia, cytokines Haemophilic arthropathy (can cause massive cuff tears)
GPC proliferation, PMNs Septic arthritis (P. acnes = gram + bacillus, may have normal markers)
Microcirculation occlusion, osteocyte death AVN (subchondral lucency/collapse, no superior migration)
T-cell autoimmune RA (central glenoid erosion, periarticular osteopenia)

3Presentation

Symptomspain incl. night pain · subjective weakness + stiffness

Inspectionsupra/infraspinatus atrophy · anterosuperior escape (head prominence anteriorly on elevation) · subcutaneous effusion (capsular fluid leak, "geyser")

ROM↓ active ± passive · crepitus GH/subacromial · pseudoparalysis

Acute-on-chroniclow-energy injury → acute decompensation of compensated chronic tear → pain + disability

Test Finding Structure
ER lag sign Can't hold passive ER, elbow 90° Massive infraspinatus tear
Hornblower Can't ER / hold ER at 90° abduction + 90° elbow flexion Teres minor dysfunction
Belly press Normal → subscapularis intact Subscapularis

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

ViewsAP, axillary, Grashey (true AP)

X-ray↓ acromiohumeral interval · acromial acetabularisation · femoralisation of head · asymmetric superior glenoid wear · lack of osteophytes · osteopenia · "snowcap" sign (subchondral sclerosis) · anterosuperior escape

MRIirreparable tear: massive fatty infiltration + severe retraction · not needed if X-ray already shows anterosuperior escape

Labsnormal WBC/ESR/CRP (vs septic, RA)

Hamada classification

Grade Findings
1 AHI ≥6 mm
2 AHI ≤5 mm
3 AHI ≤5 mm + acetabularisation of acromion
4A GH arthritis without acetabularisation (AHI <7 mm)
4B GH arthritis with acetabularisation (AHI ≤5 mm)
5 Humeral head collapse

Hamada versionsstage 2+ AHI ≤5 mm, stage 5 head collapse (Orthobullets) · AHI <7 mm, stage 5 osteonecrosis (TO) — read the options

Seebauer classification

Type Pattern Features
IA Centred, stable Intact anterior restraints; minimal superior migration; dynamic stabilisation; femoralisation + acetabularisation
IB Centred, medialised Intact/compensated anterior restraints; compromised stabilisation; medial glenoid erosion
IIA Decentred, limited stability Compromised anterior restraints; superior translation; minimal CA-arch stabilisation
IIB Decentred, unstable Incompetent anterior restraints; anterosuperior escape; no dynamic or CA-arch stabilisation

5Management

Rotator cuff arthropathy
  • Function preserved / first visit→NSAIDs, steroid injection, PT (deltoid, scapular, cuff)
  • Pain only, intact CA arch + deltoid, young active→hemiarthroplasty
  • Pseudoparalysis / elderly >70 / anterosuperior escape→reverse TSA
    • + ER pseudoparalysis (Hornblower +, ER lag)→+ latissimus dorsi transfer
    • deltoid / axillary nerve dysfunction→no RSA
  • Infection / poor soft tissue→resection arthroplasty (salvage)

Nonoperative care when function is preserved

Indicationfirst-line; esp. good active elevation (e.g. 150°), first presentation

Regimenactivity modification · NSAIDs · subacromial steroid injection · PT (deltoid, scapular, cuff strengthening) · not straight to surgery

Acute decompensationrest, PT, injection often settle the painful phase

Operative criteria

Procedure Indications / facts
Arthroscopic debridement Controversial, unpredictable; preserve CA arch (✗ Wrong options: acromioplasty · CA ligament release)
Hemiarthroplasty Anterior deltoid preserved + CA arch intact (else anterosuperior / subcutaneous escape) · younger, active · relieves pain (good–excellent ~75%) but not function (elevation 40–70°)
Reverse TSA Pseudoparalytic CTA · elderly (>70), low demand · anterosuperior escape · needs functioning deltoid (axillary nerve) + good bone stock · improves pain + function
Latissimus dorsi transfer ER pseudoparalysis · with RSA
Pectoralis major transfer IR deficiency / subscapularis insufficiency (± aTSA for massive anterior tear + arthritis)
Resection arthroplasty Salvage — chronic osteomyelitis, infection, poor soft tissue
Glenoid resurfacing / anatomic TSA Contraindicated — superior glenoid shear / edge loading ("rocking horse") → glenoid loosening (#1 cause of aTSA revision)
Cuff repair Only if no end-stage changes, active, minimal fatty infiltration; not with supraspinatus atrophy
SCR / tendon transfer Younger, irreparable tear, must follow strict rehab
Ream-and-run Young labourer, GH arthritis, intact cuff (✗ Wrong options: CTA)

Reverse arthroplasty for pseudoparalysis & outcomes

Biomechanicsmoves centre of rotation inferior + medial → ↑ deltoid mechanical advantage / lever arm → deltoid powers elevation

Outcomeimproves pain and range of motion even in setting of preoperative pseudoparalysis · low loosening with modern constructs · durability > hemi

Can't elevate after successful local anaesthetic → RSA
✗ Wrong options: biceps tenolysis, open debridement, hemi (pain-reducing only)

Young vs oldyounger: cuff repair, SCR, or hemi · older, less active: RSA

Implant optionsconvertible platform stem, central post or screw baseplate, short cementless stem (osteopenia) all OK · severe osteoporosis / low deltoid tuberosity index → cemented stem · metal-backed polyethylene glenoid (aTSA) = contraindicated

RSA with latissimus/teres major transfer for loss of external rotation

Indication for LDT with RSApseudoparalysis of ER (deltoid restores elevation but not ER) from infraspinatus + teres minor dysfunction

ER dysfunction criteria+ Hornblower · ER lag >15° vs contralateral · teres minor fatty degeneration ≥ stage 2 (Goutallier / Fuchs)

Not LDT indicationsnegative Hornblower · <5° ER lag · IR pseudoparalysis · supraspinatus retraction medial to glenoid · isolated supraspinatus tear
✗ Wrong options: RSA either

RSA contraindicationsaxillary nerve neurotmesis · severe deltoid dysfunction (e.g. stroke)

Post-traumatic arthritis, normal motorTSA, no transfer

Pectoralis major transfer for subscapularis insufficiency – nerve risk

Techniqueupper part or whole pec major tendon → near lesser tuberosity; route deep to conjoint tendon, superficial to musculocutaneous nerve

Nerve at riskmusculocutaneous (tension neurapraxia) → ↓ elbow flexion (biceps, brachialis)

✗ Wrong option: weakness Nerve
Elbow extension Radial
Shoulder ER Suprascapular (infraspinatus), axillary (teres minor)
Shoulder adduction Medial/lateral pectoral, thoracodorsal, lower subscapular
Shoulder abduction Suprascapular, axillary

Traumatic subscapularis tear mechanism

Mechanismfall, grasping to stop fall → forced external rotation against resistance
✗ Wrong options: IR · extension · abduction · flexion

6Complications

Implant choice & complications (superior glenoid wear, metal-backed glenoid)

Scapular notchinghumeral poly abuts inferior glenoid in adduction → bone loss, osteolysis, loosening, lower outcome scores

Notching Factor
↑ Risk CTA with superior glenoid wear → glenosphere too superior / superior tilt · anterosuperior (deltoid-splitting) approach
↓ Risk Lateralised humeral implant with lower neck-shaft angle 132.5° (vs Grammont 155°) · ~10° inferior tilt · inferior-offset glenosphere with ~3 mm inferior overhang · deltopectoral approach

Acromial / scapular spine stress fracturemechanism = deltoid tensioning by implant design · ~4–5%, mean 9 mo · ↑ onlay humeral component, lateralisation, osteoporosis, female, medialised pre-op COR · nonop union 40–50%
✗ Wrong options: bisphosphonate mechanism · C. acnes · superior tilt (= notching)

Complication Note
Instability More common after hemi, rare after RSA
Infection C. acnes → indolent infection
Neurovascular injury Musculocutaneous with pec major transfer
Deltoid dysfunction —
Glenoid loosening aTSA in CTA (rocking horse)

X vs Y

Hemiarthroplasty Reverse TSA Anatomic TSA
Patient Younger, active Elderly >70, low demand Not in CTA
Needs Intact CA arch + anterior deltoid Functioning deltoid (axillary n.), bone stock Functioning supraspinatus + subscapularis
Pain Relieved (~75%) Relieved —
Function Poor (40–70°) Improved, even pseudoparalysis Glenoid loosening
CTA RA AVN Septic (P. acnes)
Glenoid wear Superior, asymmetric Central erosion — —
X-ray ↓ AHI, acetabularisation, no osteophytes, snowcap Periarticular osteopenia Subchondral lucency / head collapse, no superior migration —
Labs Normal ↑ inflammatory markers — May be normal

✗ Wrong options: haemosiderin · GPC · AVN · T-cell

✗ Wrong options: posteroinferior · deltoid atrophy · SSN · failure to elevate

✗ Wrong options: capsulitis, SSN, C5, inferior subluxation

✗ Wrong options: biopsy · aspiration · anatomic TSA · syrinx MRI

✗ Wrong options: resurfacing · hemi · TSA · debridement

"Can't raise arm even after injection relieved pain?"reverse TSA

✗ Wrong options: cuff repair · ream-and-run · hemi · aTSA

"72 y, walks + housework, CTA — implant (figure)?"reverse TSA (Figure F)

"True about best option for CTA, 70° elevation?"improves pain + ROM even with pseudoparalysis
✗ Wrong options: needs CA arch · pain only · high loosening

"Pain on top of shoulder 9 mo after RSA, CT fracture — mechanism?"deltoid tensioning by implant design
✗ Wrong options: bisphosphonates · ↓ lateralisation · C. acnes · superior tilt

"RSA + latissimus transfer most appropriate?"70 F, pseudoparesis of elevation + ER, acetabularisation

✗ Wrong options: aTSA + pec transfer = anterior tears

✗ Wrong options: axillary neurotmesis · negative Hornblower · IR

✗ Wrong options: lateralised 132.5° · 10° inferior tilt · inferior offset · deltopectoral

✗ Wrong options: convertible stem · central post · medialised COR · short cementless stem

Rotator Cuff Tears

Shoulder & Elbow · 41 / 60

1Basics

Epidemiology

FT tear prevalence28% >60 y · 65% >70 y (Orthobullets, OB) · ~1/3 >60 y, >60% at 70 y (OB) · ~30% >60 y (OB) — read the options

Risk factorsage · smoking · hypercholesterolaemia · family history

Burdenleading cause of shoulder disability; ~250,000 RCR/y (USA); 2nd most common reason manual labourers miss work

Age patternmostly >40 y; degenerative/attrition in elderly · acute trauma in young

Genes & lab markers

Inherited / metabolicfamily history + hypercholesterolaemia = risk factors (no gene named in sources)

Indolent post-RCR infection labs (OB)WBC borderline (11.0) · ESR ↑ (40) · CRP mildly ↑ (1.5) · Gram stain negative · culture positive at day 7–21 → Cutibacterium acnes

Natural history – asymptomatic prevalence & tear progression

Fact Value
Asymptomatic tears (FT + PT) >60 y on MRI/US 30–55% (Tempelhof US 30% · Sher MRI 54% = 28% FT + 26% PT)
Asymptomatic ≥60 y (Orthobullets) MRI 55% · US 23% of asymptomatic
Asymptomatic → symptomatic 50% in 2–3 y (Orthobullets) · 30–50% in 2–3 y (OB) — read the options
Symptomatic FT tear enlarges 50% at 2 y (Orthobullets) · ~50% within 2–3 y (OB) · 20–50% at ~2 y, >50% at 5 y (OB)
Asymptomatic tear enlarges ~1/3 within 2–3 y (OB)

Progression ruleslarger initial tears progress faster (linear correlation size ↔ rate) · FT > PT (faster, more atrophy) · ↑ pain = marker of progression · ↑ fatty atrophy / ↓ muscle quality ↔ ↑ pain

✗ Progression trapsFT tears don't progress · symptoms unrelated to size · pain independent of muscle quality · all asymptomatic tears become symptomatic (subset never painful) · "10–15% FT enlarge by 2 y" · "20% symptomatic in 3 y" · PT tears progress faster

Incidental FT tear, minimal symptoms (72 y, 7 mm)observation
✗ Wrong options: repair · debridement · tenotomy

Atraumatic FT tear + PTsubjective functional improvement (↑ PROMs) · ~75% avoid surgery at 2 y · ↑ ROM (forward elevation) · minimal pain long-term · PT aim = strengthen surrounding muscles, not tendon healing

Anatomy – footprint, rotator cable, biceps pulley, innervation & CA ligament

Functiondynamic stability by balancing force couples → stable fulcrum; coronal: inferior cuff (IS, TM, SSc) vs deltoid's superior moment · transverse: SSc (anterior) vs IS + TM (posterior); goal of treatment = restore equilibrium

Footprint Value
Supraspinatus ML width 12.7 mm (Orthobullets) · 12.1–12.7 mm (Dugas, Ruotolo; OB) · 14–16 mm (OB) · ~12–13 mm (OB) — read the options
Infraspinatus · teres minor · subscapularis 13.4 · 13.9 · 17.9 mm (SSc widest)
AP dimension 20 mm (SS + anterior IS)
Max insertional length × width 23 × 16 mm (OB)
Articular cartilage → medial footprint 1.6–1.9 mm
Tendon thickness 10–12 mm
Usual tear site 15 mm posterior to biceps, near SS/IS junction

Footprint ↔ % tear6–7 mm exposed ≈ 50% PT tear

5 histologic layersarticular side = half the strength of bursal side → most tears articular-sided · I CHL fibres (1 mm) · II dense parallel fibres (3–5 mm) · III loose 45° bundles (3 mm) · IV loose CT + CHL · V capsule (2 mm)

Bursal vs articular tissuebursal = tendon bundles → greater deformation + tensile strength · articular = tendon + ligament + capsule complex

Blood supplysubscapular, suprascapular, humeral circumflex aa (layers II–III); bursal > articular (hypovascular); critical zone next to lateral SS insertion

Rotator intervalcapsule + LHB + SGHL + CHL; gap between SS leading edge and SSc superior border

Rotator crescentthin sheet = distal SS + IS insertions (asterisk on arthroscopy)

Rotator cablethickened CHL near its avascular zone, perpendicular to SS fibres, spans SS + IS insertions · >2.5× thicker than crescent · "suspension bridge" · cable disruption → destabilises tendon, tear propagates

Biceps pulley (medial sling)SGHL + CHL (rotator interval tissue) · SSc = anterior wall of bicipital groove → SSc tear tears pulley → medial LHB subluxation

CA ligamentextra-articular · suspension function · restrains anterior translation (with CHL) · contains head in cuff arthropathy · resection → ↑ GH translation (anterior/inferior)

✗ CA resection distractors↑ passive IR · ↑ axillary recess volume · ↓ AC joint forces · ↓ LHB resting tension

Nerve Muscles
Upper + lower subscapular Subscapularis (lower also teres major)
Suprascapular Supraspinatus + infraspinatus
Axillary Teres minor + deltoid
Thoracodorsal (middle subscapular) Latissimus dorsi
Musculocutaneous Biceps, brachialis, coracobrachialis
Lateral pectoral · medial pectoral Pec major (± minor) · pec major + minor
Long thoracic · dorsal scapular Serratus anterior · rhomboids + levator scapulae

Biceps subluxation on MRI → innervation of injured muscle?subscapular nerves (upper + lower) — SSc tear

Sagittal MRI marked muscleinfraspinatus (TO, FNB 2022/2023) · teres minor (OB, sagittal T1 = muscle quality)

Lateral subacromial portal view through FT tearglenoid, labrum, biceps tendon visible

MGHLanterior restraint at 45° abduction; deep to SSc (can be mistaken for it); absent MGHL → suspect SSc tear (MGHL translates medially with retracted SSc)

Posterior lever pushIR arm + posterior stress on head → tensions SSc → shows SSc insertion on lesser tuberosity

2Mechanism

Etiology

Mechanism Features
Chronic degenerative (intrinsic = primary aetiology) Older; SIT; large tears extend to superior SSc
Chronic impingement (extrinsic) Starts bursal surface or intratendinous
Acute avulsion SSc in young (hyperabduction/ER, fall) · SIT >40 y with dislocation
Iatrogenic Failed repair, esp SSc after open anterior surgery (open Bankart)

Disease continuumsubacromial impingement → subcoracoid impingement → calcific tendonitis → RCT → cuff arthropathy

AssociatedAC pathology · proximal biceps subluxation/tendonitis · internal impingement (throwers; PT tears)

PT tear causes (OB)age-related metabolic/vascular degeneration · subacromial impingement · anterior instability · internal impingement · repetitive microtrauma · acute trauma less often · articular side = poorer blood supply

Articular vs bursal originarticular = intrinsic degeneration · bursal = extrinsic (acromial spurs, AC arthritis); degenerative tears "start bursal side" (one OB explanation) vs articular commoner (Orthobullets, TO) — read the options

Throwing athletes – mechanism & management

Phasedeceleration (label E): cuff = principal decelerator → eccentric tensile failure

Sitearticular side of posterior SS or IS; posterior pain after ball release

Overhead-athlete cuff dysfunctionprimary impingement · primary tensile overload · secondary impingement/tensile overload from GH instability; microtrauma (overhead) vs macrotrauma (contact)

FT tear in throwermust be repaired
✗ Wrong options: debrided

Adolescent pitcher, undersurface PT tear, never treatedcessation of all throwing 6 wk → cuff + periscapular strengthening → slow supervised return, pitching mechanics
✗ Wrong options: ↓ pitch count · continued play · arthroscopic/mini-open repair

Cuff tear after shoulder dislocation in older patients

Rule>40 y anterior dislocation → rotator cuff tear (pre-existing degeneration, ↓ elasticity) ≫ recurrent instability; often missed

Which tendonsupraspinatus commonest (TO, OB) · SIT (SS, IS, TM) > SSc · SSc tears more with posterior dislocation or young hyperabduction/ER

Incidence35–86% >40 y (OB) · 54%, rising to 100% >70 y (Simank) · 15% >40 y, up to 40% >60 y (OB) — read the options

Bimodal instabilitypeak <40 y (Bankart, HAGL) · 2nd peak >60 y (cuff tears, fractures); Hill-Sachs common, usually not addressed

Clue (TO)pain lifting in scapular plane (scaption) after 6 wk immobiliser → US/MRI for cuff
✗ Wrong options: LHB entrapment · loose body

Axillary nerve7–10%; far less common than cuff tear; usually too mild for gross weakness; lateral arm sensation intact → nerve palsy/radiculopathy unlikely

(✗ Wrong options: Distractors — posterior Bankart (posterior dislocation)) · HAGL (only ~11% of first dislocations >35 y) · SLAP (throwers, no link to anterior dislocation) · SSN injury (uncommon)

>40 y, first anterior dislocation, can't elevate / weak ER
  • Next step→MRI shoulder (arthrogram if pacemaker)
    • FT cuff tear→early rotator cuff repair
    • MRI negative→EMG (axillary nerve)
  • not CT · sling 6 wk · PT first · diagnostic scope · observation

Arthrogramdye leaks GH → subacromial space (geyser) = cuff tear; normal = dye contained in capsule

Treatmentrotator cuff repair; improved pain + function vs nonop; delay → atrophy + retraction
✗ Wrong options: hemiarthroplasty · ORIF · TSA · RTSA · coracoid transfer · labral repair · PT alone

Most likely to need surgery (52 y)supraspinatus
✗ Wrong options: labrum · GH ligaments · humeral head · biceps

Massive but completely repairableacute tear after dislocation, 45 y (no retraction/atrophy yet) · (✗ Wrong options: RA (attrition, steroids) · prior repair (revision) · SS fossa atrophy · superior humeral migration (→ arthropathy)) · chronic massive repairs retear ~50%

3Presentation

Paininsidious, deltoid region, overhead activity · night pain = poor predictor for nonop

Weaknessactive ROM lost, passive ROM preserved · acute pain + weakness after trauma

Physical examination – external rotation lag sign

Muscle Weakness Test Technique / positive
Supraspinatus Elevation in Jobe position Jobe / empty can, drop arm Abducted, IR, 30° forward in scapular plane, thumb down → resist pressure · drop test: lowers slowly → sudden drop
Infraspinatus ER at 0° abduction ER lag sign Elbow 90°, passive ER → can't actively maintain
Teres minor ER at 90° abd + 90° ER Hornblower 90° abd, 90° elbow flexion, 90° ER → arm falls into IR
Subscapularis IR at 0° abduction Belly press, lift-off, bear hug (upper border), IR lag, ↑ passive ER Belly press: elbow drops back · lift-off: can't lift hand off back

✗ Wrong options (non-cuff tests)Yergason (resisted supination, elbow 90°) = biceps · Jerk = posterior labrum · Wright = TOS · relocation = anterior instability · Hawkins/Neer = impingement · O'Brien = SLAP

Subscapularis tears – belly-press/lift-off tests, biceps instability

Whoyoung, acute avulsion, hyperabduction/ER (fall, wave, door handle) · iatrogenic after open Bankart · degenerative = superior portion; largest cuff muscle, prevalence under-recognised

Symptomsanterior shoulder pain (mimics subcoracoid impingement)

Signs↑ passive ER (e.g. 90° vs 45°, 100° vs 70°) · ↓ active IR · belly press, lift-off, bear hug, IR lag

✗ ROM traps↑ passive flexion/extension/abduction · ↑ active IR · ↑ passive IR

MRISSc discontinuity off lesser tuberosity + LHB out of groove (medial subluxation/dislocation) = near-pathognomonic

LHB dislocated medially → also injured?subscapularis; rare lesser tuberosity injury
✗ Wrong options: MGHL · Bankart (not biceps stabilisers)

Biceps dislocation routesbeneath SSc · within SSc · extra-articular

Arthroscopic findings (all of the above)uncovered lesser tuberosity · retraction to glenoid · avulsed SGHL · medial biceps subluxation

Godenèche (218 scopes)pathologic LHB with intact SGHL/CHL in only 11%; even then medial sheath wall torn in 92% → SGHL/CHL lesion = LHB nearly always unstable

Comma signSGHL + CHL complex attached to superolateral corner of retracted SSc (Lo & Burkhart) · trace it inferiorly → SSc; chronic SSc retracts medially, scarred to deltoid fascia

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Modality Finding / fact
X-ray True AP, AP IR/ER, axillary, outlet view (acromion); GT cysts, calcific tendonitis, CHL calcification, type III acromion, AHI <7 mm = proximal migration (chronic RCT)
Arthrogram When MRI contraindicated (pacemaker); dye GH → subacromial = tear; MR arthrogram ↑ sens/spec
MRI Diagnostic standard; size, shape, retraction; fatty atrophy best on sagittal; medial biceps subluxation = SSc tear; humeral head cysts in almost all chronic RCT
ABER MRI ↓ effacement of articular surface → contrast enters defect → ↑ sensitivity for PT (PASTA) tears
Ultrasound Dynamic, cheap, confirms injections; user dependent; = MRI accuracy for cuff

Tangent signsagittal oblique: line scapular spine top → coracoid top; SS belly below line = positive → SS fatty atrophy → irreparable / poorer outcome after repair (TO)
✗ Wrong options: SSc atrophy · retraction medial to glenoid · biceps dislocation

PASTA on coronal T2articular-sided SS tear; intra-articular contrast delineates

Lesion Imaging / definition
PASTA Partial articular supraspinatus tendon avulsion
ALPSA Labroligamentous complex medial + inferior, rolled under intact periosteum
GLAD Nondisplaced anteroinferior labral tear + glenoid cartilage avulsion
HAGL IGHL avulsed from humeral neck
Bankart Anterior scapular periosteum disrupted
SLAP Superior labrum anterior → posterior to biceps root

Diagnostic criteria – irreparable cuff

Marker Threshold
Size >5 cm (Cofield) or ≥2 tendons
Fatty atrophy Goutallier 3–4
AHI <6 mm (TO) · <5–7 mm (OB) · <7 mm = proximal migration (Orthobullets)
Tangent sign Positive
Retraction Medial to glenoid
Clinical Chronic pseudoparalysis · profound ER weakness · long tear duration
Pattern Posterosuperior (SS + IS) > anterosuperior (SS + SSc)

Pseudoparalysiscan't actively elevate >90° (some authors >45°, TO), full passive; no improvement after lidocaine · SSc + SS complete tear → 80% pseudoparalysis

Anatomic classification

Type Features
SIT (SS, IS, TM) Majority; subacromial impingement; degenerative older or dislocation >40 y
Subscapularis More prevalent than thought; subcoracoid impingement; acute avulsion young (hyperabduction/ER) or iatrogenic failed repair

Cuff tear size

Size cm
Small 0–1
Medium 1–3
Large 3–5
Massive >5 or ≥2 tendons (Orthobullets) · ">2 tendons" (one OB)

Cuff tear shape

Shape Repair
Crescent Little retraction, mobile ML → direct to bone, minimal tension
U-shape Apex at/medial to glenoid → margin convergence side-to-side first (↓ strain on lateral margin)
L-shape One leaf more mobile → margin convergence
Massive immobile U or longitudinal → interval slide

Grade Depth
I <3 mm (<25%)
II 3–6 mm (25–50%)
III >6 mm (>50%)

Grade Fat vs muscle MRI

Type Lesion Surgical approach
I Partial, superior third (articular) Debridement or single-row

Cuff tear arthropathy – radiographic signs (TO)

Sourcil (eyebrow) signsclerosis/erosion of acromion undersurface; superiorly migrated head abuts acromion → rotator cuff tear arthropathy (anterosuperior escape) · sens/spec/PPV/NPV all poor
✗ Wrong options: calcific tendinitis · SS tendinitis · adhesive capsulitis · SLAP · instability

Hamada stage Finding

5Management

Rotator cuff tear
  • Asymptomatic / incidental→observation
  • Atraumatic FT or PT→PT + NSAIDs + subacromial CSI, 3–6 mo
    • fails→arthroscopic debridement or repair
  • Acute traumatic FT (young; >40 after dislocation)→early repair
    (do not delay for PT; better within 3 wk – 3/4 mo)
  • Massive irreparable→partial repair / SCR / transfer / RTSA

Operative criteria

Indication Procedure
Low-grade PASTA (<50%, <5–7 mm footprint) + impingement, failed nonop SAD + cuff debridement
Bursal >3 mm (>25%) Release, debride degenerative tissue + repair
Articular >50% (>6 mm (OB) · >7 mm (Orthobullets, OB) exposed footprint) Completion + repair
PASTA, young, acute, ≥25% healthy bursal tissue In situ repair (bursal tissue left intact)
Intrasubstance tear, intact footprint Trans-tendon repair
Acute (<3 mo) traumatic tear, <60 y Repair (relative indication)
FT or PT failing nonop Repair (relative)
Massive irreparable, intact SSc, no arthritis SCR / LD / lower trapezius transfer
Massive + GH arthritis, intact deltoid RTSA
Relative CI to repair Advanced fatty infiltration/atrophy · significant GH arthritis

Operative vs nonoperative indications (acute traumatic vs atraumatic tears)

Nonop regimenPT + NSAIDs + subacromial CSI = first line; avoid overhead; aggressive cuff + scapular stabiliser strengthening 3–6 mo

Partial tear, improving, never had formal PT (70 y)formal PT
✗ Wrong options: repair · debridement · RTSA · repeat MRI unless unexplained progression

PASTA, full strength, 6 wk (carpenter)physical therapy first
✗ Wrong options: PRP · repair · SLAP repair · SAD

Failed 12 wk PT + injection, PASTArepair or debridement
✗ Wrong options: repeat injection · continued PT · capsular release (full passive ROM) · rotator interval release (for adhesive capsulitis or retracted SSc)

Low-grade PASTA + impingement, 5/5 strength, failed nonopSAD + debridement
✗ Wrong options: SR/DR repair · labral repair · tenodesis

Subacute FT SS tear, weakness, type 1 acromion, no fatty change (47 y)rotator cuff repair alone
✗ Wrong options: repeat CSI · porcine SIS xenograft · + acromioplasty · + remplissage/tenodesis/DCE

AAOS pointsexercise + NSAIDs for PT tears · routine acromioplasty not required · non-cross-linked porcine SIS xenograft not to be used · workers' comp → less favourable outcome

Purpose of repairrestore muscle function; then ↓ pain, prevent irreversible atrophy

Massive tear SS + SSc, 40 y, 5 mo, no atrophyrotator cuff repair; attempt repair before salvage; surgery within 6 mo → better outcome
✗ Wrong options: debridement/SAD/DCE · pec major transfer · 6 wk more PT · SCR

Traumatic FT tear, young — outcome drivertime to surgical repair (repair within 3–4 mo; acute repair within 3 wk best) · (✗ Wrong options: BMI · age · male gender) · higher preop ASES → ↑ VAS improvement only

Atraumatic FT tear — strongest predictor of surgerypatient expectation of PT (also higher activity, non-smoker) · pain not related to anatomic severity · pain ↔ comorbidities, lower education, race

Partial-thickness tears – PASTA, bursal vs articular, debridement vs completion & repair

PASTA (TO)articular side; far more common than bursal or intratendinous

Articular vs bursalarticular more common · bursal more symptomatic (subacromial bursitis) · bursal = higher risk of progression · articular fares better → higher % tolerated before repair

Repair thresholdsbursal >25% (>3 mm) · articular >50%
✗ Wrong options: bursal <25% · articular >25%

Articular >50% tear but poor lateral tissuecomplete the tear → repair
✗ Wrong options: fascial graft · allograft · trans-tendon · biopsy

Bursal tear 4 mm deep, 1.5 cm AP, softeningconvert to FT + repair with suture anchors
✗ Wrong options: debride + acromioplasty · abort · incidental

Footprint exposed 3 mm, bursal intactdebridement + SAD (<5 mm exposure ≈ <50% thickness; ✗ Wrong options: completion · transtendinous repair · tenotomy · synovectomy)

6 mm ML width tear50% of SS tendon

Rotator cable involvedbursal 4 mm tear involving anterior cable → repair · intact cable 3–4 mm → less likely to need repair · articular <7 mm → debridement · SSc upper-border fraying without retraction → no repair (but often-missed tear)

High-grade PASTA (>50%), failed 9 mo PT + PRP (tennis, 51 y)tear completion + repair to footprint
✗ Wrong options: isolated DCE (negative cross-body) · more nonop · SAD ± tenodesis · trans-tendon + DCE

Partial-thickness tear, failed nonop
  • Articular <50%→debridement ± SAD
  • Articular >50%→completion + repair
    • young, acute, healthy bursal tissue→in situ repair
  • Bursal >25% (>3 mm)→completion + repair
  • Rotator cable disrupted→repair

Subscapularis repair – biceps, 3-sided release (TO)

Subscapularis tear
  • Repairable→SSc repair + biceps tenodesis/tenotomy
    (not biceps recentering, groove deepening, tenosynovectomy)
  • Chronic retracted, atrophied→subcoracoid pec major transfer
  • Elderly, irreparable→RTSA

Biceps with SSc tearunstable → tenodesis or tenotomy (recentering unpredictable; prevents recurrent biceps pain/failure) · tenodesis low in groove; address biceps first (rubs/fails repair)

SSc tear after open Bankart (6 mo)subscapularis repair + biceps tenotomy/tenodesis
✗ Wrong options: PT · tenolysis → cosmetic deformity · pec major (tendon repairable)

Which lesion → RCR + biceps tenodesis?SSc tear with dislocated biceps; no significant GH arthritis
✗ Wrong options: Hill-Sachs · GT fracture · bony Bankart · Bankart

Chronic retracted atrophied SSc (55 y carpenter)pectoralis major transfer under conjoined tendon · Achilles allograft alternative for degenerated SSc
✗ Wrong options: fusion = salvage · CSI · arthroscopic/open repair

Lafosse IV — release from coracoid base (TO)coracohumeral ligament
✗ Wrong options: CA ligament · transverse humeral ligament · conjoined origin

3-sided release (TO) Structure
Anterior (subcoracoid space) CHL + adhesions to base of coracoid — key for lateral excursion
Superior Rotator interval; free comma tissue from coracoid base
Posterior (intra-articular) Capsulotomy from capsule + MGHL to 6 o'clock

Repair steps (TO)biceps first → 70° scope, posterior portal for lesser tuberosity → traction stitch at comma via accessory anterolateral portal → anchors inferior first → superior → tie in internal rotation · III/IV → modified double-row

Arthroscopic vs open SSc repairarthroscopic superior motion + pain (Orthobullets)

Repair technique – single vs double row, transosseous-equivalent & failure mode

Mini-opendeltoid-splitting; ↓ deltoid avulsion vs open; immediate PROM; active ~6 wk · arthroscopic = equivalent results

Arthroscopic vs open (medium tear)no difference in retear rate or function · arthroscopic → earlier rehab (no deltoid to protect) · mini-open → worse early pain/function only

Interval slidesanterior = release SS from rotator interval (incise CHL) · posterior = release SS from IS, then margin convergence

Double-row (TOE)medial mattress + lateral simple → more anatomic footprint, larger contact area

DR vs SR Finding
Retear DR lower (esp tears/retraction >3 cm); SR higher (Millett meta-analysis, 7 level I RCTs)
Healing rate DR higher
Biomechanics DR higher ultimate tensile load; = peak-to-peak elongation, stiffness, conditioning elongation
Function, pain, time to heal (short/mid term) No difference (esp <3 cm)
Long term DR may improve function (one RCT)
Cost DR more (more anchors)
Blood loss No difference

Lowest retear riskGoutallier 1 + DR TOE
✗ Wrong options: Goutallier 3–4 · SR

Two DR constructs (B, C)equivalent retear; SR (A) possibly higher; A and B = equivalent outcome scores at 1 y

Vascularityanchor drilling (holes in GT) + peribursal tissue → main supply to repair; ↑ with exercise

✗ Wrong options (false repair "truths")motion restriction ↑ blood flow · DR better clinical results · SAD ↑ healing · non-healing always → poor outcome (~half don't heal, outcomes preserved)

GT trough (cancellous)not stronger repair (animal models)

Failure modesuture pull-out through tendon = tissue failure (most common, early) → gap formation → poor tendon–bone healing

Less common failure Note
Anchor breakage Biocomposite fatigues less than metal
Anchor pull-out Poor BMD, improper placement
Eyelet abrasion suture rupture Metal anchors (sharper)
Knot failure
Infection ~1.9%

Causes of failed RCRfailure to heal (19–94%: poor tissue, vascularity, bone) · surgical (deltoid, infection, foreign body, stiffness, nerve) · diagnostic (missed interval, LHB, SSc) · technical (excess tension, anchor placement); arthroscopic RCR complication rate ~10%

Traumatic retear 3 wk post-op, 1 cm, <65 yrevision RCR (healing >95%)
✗ Wrong options: PT · CSI · sling · debridement (for chronic irreparable)

Revision RCR vs RTSARTSA favoured by older age, static proximal humeral migration; also aetiology of retear, tissue/MRI quality

Massive/irreparable tears – partial repair, SCR & tendon transfers

Massive irreparable tear
  • Elderly / CTA / pseudoparalysis→RTSA
  • Young, posterosuperior, intact SSc + deltoid, no OA→LD or lower trapezius transfer / SCR
    • SSc irreparable→no SCR or LD transfer
  • Chronic irreparable SSc→pec major transfer
  • Part of cuff reaches GT→partial repair

Partial repairSS can't reach GT, posterior cuff can → partial repair (balances coronal + axial force couples) · pain options: acromioplasty + CA release, reverse acromioplasty (tuberoplasty), biceps tenotomy · ✗ RTSA in 48 y · other young options: SCR, transfers, subacromial balloon spacer (none superior)

Pseudoparesis vs pseudoparalysisactive FE >90° (e.g. 100°) after lidocaine injection → pseudoparesis (pain) · no change → pseudoparalysis · arthritis/retraction occur in both

Young (35 y), pseudoparalysis, AHD <6 mm, Goutallier 3, minimal arthritis — least preferred (TO)RSA (✓ LD, ✓ lower trapezius, ✓ SCR)

SCR (TO, Mihata) Detail
Mechanism Passive constraint to superior head translation; space-occupier + tether; restores force couples
Graft Folded fascia lata 6–8 mm · acellular dermal 3–4 mm; anchors superior glenoid rim → medial GT
Indications Failed nonop massive irreparable SS + IS, Hamada 1–2, intact/reparable SSc, functional deltoid; intolerable pain; pseudoparalysis
Contraindications Irreparable SSc (subscapular nerves) · Hamada ≥3 · GH OA
Best candidate 59 y, SS + IS, normal X-ray

SCR caveatirreparability confirmed only after full diagnostic arthroscopy (Hartzler & Burkhart); short-term data only, graft failure risk

Transfer Indication Key facts
Pectoralis major (subcoracoid, under conjoined) Chronic irreparable SSc Replicates SSc vector; restores IR; 4–6 wk rigid immobilisation; not posterosuperior
Latissimus dorsi (± teres major) Irreparable posterosuperior (SS + IS), young labourer, Goutallier ≥3 To cuff/SSc/GT; brace 6 wk, 45° abd, 30° ER; restores ER + elevation
Lower trapezius (± Achilles allograft) Irreparable posterosuperior, middle-aged labourer More anatomic; superior outcomes vs LD (Orthobullets); restores ER

Transfer counsellingpain relief more reliable than function (Omid & Lee)

LD transfer — best candidateyoung labourer, massive posterosuperior tear + SS atrophy/fatty infiltration · some active elevation (90–100°) · intact SSc + deltoid, no OA (e.g. 50 y, FE 100°, ER −10°)

LD transfer — worse outcomespositive lift-off / SSc deficiency (strongest; Gerber, Irlenbusch) · deltoid weakness/detachment · nonsynergistic (out-of-phase) action · stage 3–4 fatty degeneration, poor tendon · female · preop elevation <90° · complete loss of ER · superior escape · salvage after failed repair (vs primary)

Not a worse-outcome factorabsence of CA ligament · other prior surgery

LD relative CISSc deficiency · deltoid deficiency · pseudoparalysis · advanced GH arthritis · CTA (stays painful) · >80 y pseudoparalytic · acute tear in young (repair first) · thoracodorsal palsy · disability claimant

Belly press elbow drops backSSc dysfunction → ↓ LD transfer benefit
✗ Wrong options: ↑ passive IR · drop sign = SS · Hornblower = TM · axillary fold ecchymosis = pec major rupture

Posterosuperior deficiency + intact belly press → transfer?latissimus dorsi
✗ Wrong options: pec major = SSc · pec minor · conjoined = instability · LHB

LD nerves at riskradial nerve deep (anterior) to LD tendon, ~3 cm medial to insertion → IR arm at tenotomy; injury → EPL (extensor pollicis longus) + wrist/digit extensors · posterior branch axillary (deep fascia of posterior deltoid, tendon passage)

Lower trapezius best for45 y manual labourer, irreparable posterosuperior, loss of ER
✗ Wrong options: pitcher SLAP · irreparable SSc → pec major · GH OA → TSA · CTA → RTSA

Retear 2 mo after massive repair (rough PT), ER lagrevision repair SS/IS; failure: intrinsic (age, size, tissue, systemic disease, smoking) + extrinsic (construct, aggressive rehab)
✗ Wrong options: SSc revision · LD first · interval release · anatomic TSA

RTSA mechanismlengthens deltoid lever arm; COR medial + inferior; convex glenoid + concave humerus; ↓ shear · survival 90–95% at 10 y · most reliable for 65 y painter with SS + IS atrophy, no OA
✗ Wrong options: dermal augmentation · SCR · partial repair · trapezius transfer

Other grafts (Orthobullets)xenograft (bovine dermis/intestine; mixed) · allograft (human skin/fascia; good short term) · synthetic (foreign body reaction) · lateral acromionectomy = contraindicated (historic)

Concomitant procedures (acromioplasty, distal clavicle excision, suprascapular nerve release)

Add-on to RCR Effect
Acromioplasty / SAD No difference in PROs, symptomatic retear, ROM, strength, pain · lower long-term reoperation (Level 1, esp type 2–3 acromion; OB) · "routine acromioplasty not recommended" (AAOS, OB) — read the options
Distal clavicle excision No effect on 2-y/long-term outcomes, ROM, revision
SSN release No difference in pain or function; SSN dysfunction in 8–27% of massive tears (traction from retraction → fatty infiltration)
LHB tenotomy vs tenodesis Negligible difference
CA ligament release ↑ anterior/inferior GH translation

No long-term effect eithermini-open vs arthroscopic · starting PT at 6 wk · SR vs DR

Negative predictors of RCR outcomesmoking · severe obesity · tear size · fatty infiltration · age 70+ · pre-existing arthropathy · workers' comp

Postoperative rehabilitation – early vs delayed motion

Healingtendon-to-GT healing 8–12 wk = rate-limiting step · protect ≥6 wk, ~8 wk for large 2-tendon tear

Protocolearly PROM (prevents adhesive capsulitis) → AROM at 6 wk → strengthening ≥2–3 mo · no active strengthening at 1 mo
✗ Wrong options: isometric ER · eccentric SS · resistance · deltoid (can't isolate from cuff)

EMGpassive forward flexion = minimal cuff activation · active, active-assisted, isometric, pulley-assisted all activate cuff (avoid early)

Early (<6 wk) vs delayed (6 wk sling) Result
Functional outcomes Equivalent
Terminal ROM / stiffness at 1 y No difference
Retear / healing No difference (Cuff & Pupello, 68 pts) · delayed may ↑ healing
Short-term PROs Not better with early; early may ↑ pain

PT not available first 6 wkwon't affect ROM at 1 y
✗ Wrong options: peer-to-peer · home band strengthening · strength testing · prophylactic CSI

Scapular plane forward elevation, prone retraction, 2 mo post-RCR (TO)lower trapezius (LT > MT + SA) · SA activity ↑ with elevation angle; LT ↑ steeply at end range · deficit = endurance/control/timing, not weakness → low–moderate repetitive resistance

Trapezius part (TO) Exercise
Upper Shrug ± retraction; overhead shrug
Middle Overhead retraction against wall
Lower Prone scapular setting (retract + depress, lift arm off table)
Lower + middle Prone scapular retraction, arm to ~120°

Return to workfull duty 6–10 mo · light duty after progressive strengthening (earliest 8–10 wk) · labourers later + lower outcomes than desk jobs; most return to full · PROM PT starts 2–6 wk

AnalgesiaNSAIDs improve pain at 1 wk (Orthobullets)

Healing & retear risk factors (age, fatty infiltration, workers' comp, injections)

Retear rate10–90% · massive chronic ~50%
✗ Wrong options: <5%

Factor Effect
Age >65 Highest risk of non-healing (✗ Wrong options: protective); >70 → inferior outcomes
Goutallier grade (3–4) Greatest retear risk (vs age, rehab, technique, gender)
Tear >5 cm, multiple tendons, retraction medial to glenoid ↑ retear
Diabetes · smoking · severe obesity ↑ retear
Poor post-op compliance ↑ retear
Concomitant AC / biceps procedure ↑ retear (Orthobullets)
Workers' comp / work-related ↓ functional improvement + ↓ satisfaction, later RTW

Complications – infection, positioning & regional anaesthesia

Suprascapular nerve (TO)on undersurface of SS + IS; ~2.9 cm from superior glenoid rim, 1.8 cm from scapular spine → no sharp dissection >1 cm medial to glenoid rim · tethered at supraspinous fossa + notch → tension on lateral SS advancement (and medial retraction) · injured during posterosuperior cuff mobilisation in massive RCR, posteriorly directed glenoid-neck sutures (anterior labral repair), glenoid osteotomy
✗ Wrong options: thoracoacromial a. · axillary n. · PCHA

Infection<1% (Orthobullets) · ~1.9% (OB) · 0.006–3.4% (OB) — read the options; S. aureus, strep, C. acnes (formerly P. acnes)

C. acnesdelayed/indolent (10 wk), healed portals, mild ↑ ESR/CRP, Gram negative → anaerobe, cultures positive 7–21 days
✗ Wrong options: Pseudomonas (water-borne, not shoulder)

Pre-op steroid injectionwithin 1 month → highest infection risk (65–75% ↑) · 1–3 mo ↑ · >3 mo = no ↑ risk → delay surgery ≥3 mo · not dose, location, number, steroid type

6 injections, surgery 3 mo later↑ revision, no ↑ infection

Pneumothoraxafter interscalene/supraclavicular block or arthroscopy · risk = smoking/COPD (hyperinflated lungs, high pleural dome) · dyspnoea also from block diaphragm paralysis → CXR
✗ Wrong options: DM · revision · obesity · SSc repair

Beach chairLFCN palsy up to 2%; resolves <6 mo; padding, seatbelt, slight reverse Trendelenburg; BMI >35 risk
✗ Wrong options: femoral · obturator · pudendal (perineal post/hip scope) · sciatic

Othersdeltoid detachment (open) · AC pain · axillary nerve injury · stiffness (early PT/ROM doesn't reduce at 1 y)

Scapular Winging

Shoulder & Elbow · 42 / 60

1Basics

Definition & types

Definitiondysfunction of scapular stabilising muscles → imbalance + abnormal scapular motion; rare, debilitating

Named bydirection of the superomedial corner of the scapula

Medial winging Lateral winging
Muscle Serratus anterior Trapezius (rarely rhomboids)
Nerve Long thoracic (C5, C6, C7) Spinal accessory (CN XI)
Unopposed pull Medialising retraction (rhomboids) + elevation (trapezius) Lateralising protraction (serratus, pec major + minor)
Who Young athletes; more common Iatrogenic (neck surgery)
Commonest cause Repetitive stretch/traction (>50%) Iatrogenic (up to 70%)

Anatomy – scapulothoracic stabilisers

Scapulothoracic articulationnot a true joint; attached via AC joint ligaments; suction by serratus anterior + subscapularis holds scapula to thorax

Scapulaattachment for 17 muscles

Muscle Origin → insertion Action Nerve
Serratus anterior Ribs 1–8 (Orthobullets) · top 8–9 ribs (OB); 7–10 slips → anteromedial (vertebral) border Protraction (+ upward rotation, stabilises vertebral border) Long thoracic (C5–7)
Trapezius Superior nuchal line, EOP, nuchal ligament, C7–T12 spinous → lateral ⅓ clavicle, acromion, spine Upward rotation + elevation Spinal accessory (CN XI)
Rhomboid major T2–T5 spinous → medial border below minor Retraction (+ elevation, OB) Dorsal scapular
Rhomboid minor C7–T1 spinous → medial border at base of spine Retraction Dorsal scapular
Levator scapulae C1–C4 transverse processes → medial border at spine level Elevation + downward rotation C3–C4 cervical plexus + dorsal scapular

Serratus partsupper: downward rotation (glenoid down), stabilises superior scapula · middle: protraction · lower: upward rotation + abduction

Trapezius partsupper: upward rotation + elevation · middle: retraction + adduction · lower: downward rotation + depression

Rootsventral rami C5, C6, C7 · C4 contribution 13% · no C7 in 8%
✗ Wrong options: C8–T1 · C4–6 · C6–8

Coursefirst nerve to branch off brachial plexus · posterior to axillary vessels + plexus · superficial to serratus, branch to each slip

Vulnerabilitylong course, small diameter, little connective tissue · easily injured in axillary dissection

Crow's footwhere LTN crosses the dominant inferior serratus branch of thoracodorsal artery

Spinal accessory nerve

CN XIspinal + cranial parts → accessory trunk → jugular foramen → crosses lateral to IJV → SCM → posterior triangle → trapezius · also ventral rami C2–C4 (OB)

Vulnerabilitysuperficial course in posterior triangle

Dorsal scapular nerve – rhomboid & levator

Medial scapular musclesinnervated by dorsal scapular nerve (TO)
✗ Wrong options: median · ulnar · musculocutaneous · superior/inferior subscapular · thoracodorsal

Dorsal scapular nerve (TO)anterior ramus of C5 → levator scapulae + rhomboids · OB: C4 + C5 (mostly C5); less commonly causes winging

Medial-border origins (TO)posterior surface: levator scapulae, rhomboid major + minor (deep extrinsic) · anterior surface: teres major (TO) · teres minor = lateral border (TO)

Attachments (TO)levator → transverse processes of upper cervical · rhomboids → spinous processes of upper thoracic

Fossa muscles (TO)supraspinatus, infraspinatus, subscapularis from their fossae

Nerve (TO, OB) Origin Muscles Winging?
Dorsal scapular C5 anterior ramus Levator, rhomboids Less common
Suprascapular Superior trunk (C5–6) Supraspinatus, infraspinatus No

2Mechanism

Medial winging – causes

Cause Detail
Traction (>50%) Repetitive stretch = most common (gradual) — head tilted away during overhead activity, throwing, swimmers, weightlifters, volleyball, prolonged abduction · acute high-energy (motorcycle)
Compression – acute Blunt chest/head/neck trauma (contact sports, MMA blows), sudden shoulder depression (fall)
Compression – chronic Scalenes · subcoracoid (coracoid–1st/2nd rib; carrying loads) · inflamed bursae · anteroinferior scapular border
Iatrogenic (10%) Radical mastectomy / axillary node dissection, thoracic surgery (flail chest fixation), chest tube
Penetrating Chest wall
Neuralgic amyotrophy (Parsonage-Turner) Isolated LTN palsy in 22%; no trauma, antecedent immune/inflammatory insult
Mechanical Serratus avulsion · displaced inferior pole scapula fracture
Muscle inhibition Underlying GH pathology (cuff, labrum — Kibler dyskinesia), fatigue from repetitive tensile use

Most common cause conflictrepetitive traction (Orthobullets, OB) · Parsonage-Turner = most often associated (OB6211) · Parsonage-Turner "very rarely" (OB7315) — read the options; nerve = long thoracic either way

Vastamäki (OB)92 isolated serratus palsies: exertion 40%, trauma 24%, surgery/anaesthesia 11% · infection → better recovery, surgery/anaesthesia → poorer

Lateral winging – causes

Iatrogenic (most common)cervical lymph node biopsy, radical neck dissection, posterior cervical surgery, carotid endarterectomy

Traumatictraction (sudden lateral neck flexion, MVA), blunt (deep tissue massage), penetrating neck, fall in elderly

3Presentation

Medial winging – long thoracic nerve/serratus anterior

Symptomsvague, nonspecific shoulder girdle pain + fatigue (base of neck, scapula, deltoid) · spasms · weak lifting away from body/overhead · discomfort sitting against chair · subjective instability (no stable platform) · ± traction plexus symptoms

Deformityinferomedial scapula elevates, protrudes posteriorly + medially; scapula superior + medial with inferior pole rotated medially · worse with forward flexion / wall push-up

Mechanism of deformitycompensatory overpull of rhomboids (major + minor) + levator scapulae (✓ OB) · unopposed trapezius pulls medially (antagonist)

Examabduction often ≤90° · weak forward flexion + abduction · wasting of anterior scalene triangle (SCM atrophy)

Scapular compression testexaminer pushes scapula anteriorly + stabilises chest during flexion → positive = ↑ motion with support

Scapular assistance test (OB)upward pressure on inferomedial angle during elevation → ↓ pain + ↑ arc = positive

✗ Exam distractorsER lag/hornblower (teres minor) · belly press (subscapularis) · apprehension (anterior instability) · Wright's (TOS)

Lateral winging – spinal accessory nerve/trapezius & Eden-Lange transfer

Symptomssimilar to medial + impingement (CA arch translates inferiorly as scapula depresses)

Deformitysuperomedial scapula drops + protrudes posterior and lateral; inferior angle rotates laterally · worse with abduction + resisted ER

Examdrooping/depressed shoulder girdle · trapezius atrophy (flattened superior trapezius) · weak flexion + abduction · manual scapular stabilisation ↓ pain

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

EMG medialLTN palsy vs mechanical (serratus avulsion); serial every 3 mo to follow recovery

EMG lateralisolated CN XI vs wider neurological injury; repeat every 3–6 mo

EMG → which nervemedial winging + abnormal EMG = long thoracic (C5–7); trapezius denervation = spinal accessory

5Management

Medial winging (serratus / LTN)
  • Serratus avulsion / inferior pole fracture→early repair
  • Neurapraxia→PT, observe ≥6 mo (ideally 18–24 mo)
    • no recovery + EMG compression→supraclavicular neurolysis
  • Fails 1–2 y, better with manual stabilisation→split pec major transfer
    • failed transfer / neuromuscular→scapulothoracic fusion
Lateral winging (trapezius / CN XI)
  • Elderly, sedentary, no identifiable injury→nonop
  • Identifiable injury, early (<20 mo)→explore, neurolysis, repair
  • Late (>20 mo) / permanent→Eden-Lange transfer
    • salvage→scapulothoracic fusion

Nonoperative – medial

Regimenobservation, PT (serratus anterior strengthening, stretching), avoid heavy lifting · modified thoracolumbar brace (poor compliance, little benefit)

Duration≥6 months, ideally 18 mo–2 y

Recoverymajority resolve by 2 y (Orthobullets; within 24 mo, Martin, OB) · within 1 y (OB) · ~25% need surgery (OB)

Operative criteria

Procedure Indication
Early serratus repair Mechanical avulsion / inferior pole fracture + symptomatic winging
LTN neurolysis Failed nonop ≥6 mo + EMG compression (distal latency, denervation)
Split pec major transfer Failed nonop 1–2 y + relief with manual scapular stabilisation
Surgery (OB) Symptomatic serratus winging >1 y + EMG denervation → fusion, fascial sling, muscle transfer
Eden-Lange CN XI injury diagnosed late (>20 mo)
CN XI exploration/repair Identifiable injury diagnosed early (<20 mo)
Scapulothoracic fusion Diffuse neuromuscular disorders, failed muscle transfer; not first choice; goal pain relief

LTN neurolysis

Techniquesupraclavicular decompression where nerve traverses scalenes

Outcome98% pain relief + winging resolution after failed nonop · better strength (flexion, abduction) than muscle transfer

Split pectoralis major transfer

Techniquesternal head of pec major → inferior (inferomedial) border/pole of scapula; direct (± bone block) or with hamstring/allograft extension · most effective for medial winging · dynamic stabiliser

Predictor of successsymptom relief with preop manual scapular stabilisation

Outcomepersistent abduction weakness common

Complicationstransfer failure at scapula · breast asymmetry · infection · adhesive capsulitis

Nerve transfer – medial

Donorslateral branch of thoracodorsal nerve → LTN · medial pectoral + sural graft → LTN; preserves muscle biomechanics · nerve/muscle transfers mixed results (OB)

Lateral – nonoperative

Rolecontroversial (most injuries = iatrogenic direct → surgery) · nonop for elderly, sedentary, no identifiable injury · less effective than for serratus palsy

Poor prognosis with nonopcan't raise arm above shoulder at presentation · dominant arm

Delaymarked delay in recognition common

Eden-Lange transfer

Classiclevator scapulae → lateral scapular spine + rhomboid minor + major → infraspinatus fossa (lateralises: medial border → lateral)

Triple tendon transferall three to scapular spine (Rm medial → RM → LS lateral) to reconstruct trapezius

Resultsreliably restores ROM + function · better than scapulothoracic fusion (OB)

(✗ Wrong options: Distractors — split pec major (= serratus/medial)) · long head triceps / infraspinatus transfers (rarely used) · latissimus transfer · levator only

Scapulothoracic fusion

Techniqueanterior scapula to posterior ribs (wire cables, plates/screws)

Outcome~20° gain in abduction · 82% satisfied at 5 y

Complicationsnonunion · pleural effusion · adhesive capsulitis · symptomatic hardware

X vs Y

Medial winging Lateral winging
Scapula Inferior pole medial, scapula elevated Drooping, inferior angle lateral, depressed
Worse with Forward flexion / wall push-up Abduction + resisted ER
Atrophy — Trapezius
Nonop Effective (most recover) Less effective
Muscle transfer Split pec major (sternal head) Eden-Lange (levator + rhomboids)
Nerve transfer Thoracodorsal lateral branch → LTN
Nerve injury Result

Spinal accessory Lateral winging
Thoracodorsal Latissimus weakness, no winging
Suprascapular Supra/infraspinatus wasting, no winging
Upper/lower subscapular Subscapularis/teres major, no winging
Axillary Deltoid/teres minor, no winging
C8–T1 No winging

Scapulothoracic Dyskinesis

Shoulder & Elbow · 43 / 60

1Basics

Definitionabnormal scapular motion during coordinated scapulohumeral movement → impingement + dysfunction · rare

Whoathletes, baseball pitchers · sequela of prior shoulder injury disrupting scapular stabiliser activation

Aetiology

Causes (multifactorial)neurologic injury · thoracic kyphosis · periscapular muscle fatigue · poor throwing mechanics · pain (shoulder, neck)

2Mechanism

Pathoanatomyscapulothoracic power imbalance → scapular protraction → altered GH mechanics → ↑ stress on anterior capsule + posterosuperior labrum

Injury risklabrum · rotator cuff (articular-surface tears) · capsule

Thrower's cascadeposteroinferior capsular tightness + scapular dyskinesis → articular-side cuff tear + posterosuperior labral tear

SICK scapula

SICKmuscular fatigue syndrome of throwers

Letter Meaning
S Scapular malposition
I Inferior medial border prominence
C Coracoid pain + malposition (tender coracoid = pectoralis minor contracture)
K dysKinesis of scapular movement

GIRDloss of internal rotation (e.g. 15°) = posterior capsule tightness

3Presentation

Symptomsshoulder pain/dysfunction worse with arm elevation · loss of throwing velocity · posterosuperior ± anterior pain

Examscapulothoracic crepitus · scapula lower + protracted · symptoms relieved by scapular stabilisation (diagnostic)

Associatedcoracoid tenderness · IR deficit · positive relocation test

4Diagnosis & Classification

Diagnosisclinical

Key radiology findings

X-ray (complete shoulder series)usually unremarkable

MRIoften no intra-articular lesion

5Management

Scapular dyskinesis
  • Mainstay→NSAIDs, PT, local injections
  • Rehab (Kibler, proximal→distal)
    • Stage 1→full scapular motion + coordinate scapula with trunk + hips
    • Stage 2→strengthen scapular muscles
    • Stage 3→shoulder flexibility, closed-chain, sport-specific

Rehabilitation – kinetic chain, pectoralis minor & posterior capsule stretching

Principleproximal → distal (kinetic chain); progress by function, not timetable; acute → recovery → maintenance phases

Initial stagecoordination of scapular motion with trunk + hip movements
✗ Wrong options: isometric · isokinetic · closed chain · axial loading (later)

PT emphasiscore strengthening · scapular stabilisers (serratus anterior, trapezius) · rotator cuff · proper mechanics in throwers

SICK / GIRD initial regimenstretch posterior capsule (IR deficit) + pectoralis minor (coracoid tenderness)

✗ Regimen distractor Why wrong
Posterior capsule + subscapularis strengthening Misses pec minor (coracoid pain)
Posterior capsule + plyometrics Misses pec minor (coracoid pain)
Anterior capsule stretching (any) IR deficit = posterior capsule tightness

How it's asked

"Pitcher, posterior pain, scapular dyskinesis, normal MRI — emphasise first in rehab?"coordination of scapular motion with trunk + hip movements
✗ Wrong options: isometric · isokinetic · closed chain · axial loading

"Pitcher, 15° IR loss, coracoid tenderness, + relocation, normal MRI — initial regimen?"stretch posterior capsule + pectoralis minor
✗ Wrong options: subscapularis strengthening · plyometrics · anterior capsule stretching

"SICK scapula — coracoid pain due to?"pectoralis minor contracture

"Diagnostic exam finding?"symptoms relieved by scapular stabilisation

"Scapular position in dyskinesis?"lower + protracted

Shoulder Arthrodesis

Shoulder & Elbow · 44 / 60

1Basics

Goal

Aimstable base for the upper limb → optimise hand + elbow function

Ideal patientflail shoulder (deltoid + cuff paralysis) with functional hand, wrist + elbow; young, esp. labourer

Anatomy

GH fusion surfacesmall → decorticate GH articular surfaces + humeral head–acromion undersurface to ↑ fusion area

Fixation strengthonly glenoid fossa + base of coracoid strong enough for screws

3Presentation

Symptomsspecific to underlying condition; symptomatic GH dysfunction

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Test Purpose
X-ray AP, lateral, axillary Bone stock for fusion, deformity
CT Glenoid bone loss (esp. failed arthroplasty)
EMG When neurological status of scapular muscles is ill-defined

5Management

Indications – deltoid and rotator cuff paralysis

Indication Note
Paralytic disorders Deltoid + cuff paralysis (post-traumatic), brachial plexus palsy, paralysis in infancy
Irreparable deltoid + cuff deficiency with arthropathy
Failed TSA / failed revision arthroplasty Salvage
Tumour resection Bone deficiency
Chronic infection Painful ankylosis
Recurrent instability Failed previous repairs (severe, refractory)

Rühmann (OB)43 cases: paralysis 74%, OA/humeral head necrosis 35%, infection 16%, instability

Contraindications

Listipsilateral elbow arthrodesis · contralateral shoulder arthrodesis · no functional scapulothoracic motion · trapezius, levator scapulae or serratus anterior paralysis · Charcot in acute inflammatory stage (Eichenholtz 0–2) · elderly · progressive neurological disease

Operative criteria – who benefits vs alternatives

Patient Best option
Flail shoulder (deltoid + cuff paralysis), hand works Arthrodesis ✓
No cuff function No TSA (contraindicated)
No deltoid function No reverse TSA (contraindicated)
Chronic lateral winging Eden-Lange (levator + rhomboids)
Irreparable cuff tear, overhead motion Latissimus dorsi transfer
Young AVN Hemiarthroplasty
Recurrent MDI after arthroscopy Therapy, revision arthroscopic/open stabilisation
Infected TSA removed (70-y) Treat infection → 2nd-stage TSA / HA / reverse
Cleidocranial dysostosis Scapulothoracic (✗ Wrong options: glenohumeral) arthrodesis

Fusion position

Goalhand to mouth (feeding) + groin (hygiene)

Source Abduction Forward flexion Internal rotation
Orthobullets "30-30-30" 20–30° 20–30° 20–30°
OB typical ~40° ~35° ~20°
Rühmann range (OB) 20–60° 20–40° (anteversion) 0–50°; no ER
Orthobullets GH anatomy note 15–20° 20–25° 40–50°

Positions conflict30-30-30 (Orthobullets) · 40-35-20 (OB) — read the options

Technique

ApproachS-shaped incision: scapular spine → over acromion → anterolateral arm

Stepsresect cuff from proximal humerus · tenodese biceps · decorticate glenoid, humeral head + acromial undersurface · position 30-30-30

Fixation10-hole 4.5 mm pelvic reconstruction plate along scapular spine → acromion → humeral shaft · compression screws across GH into glenoid fossa · screw into base of coracoid

Postoperative care

0–6 wkthermoplastic orthosis from day 1

6 wksling if no radiographic loosening

3 momobilisation + thoracoscapular strengthening if no loosening

Recovery6–12 months; marked ↑ pain + function in selected patients

6Complications

Listinfection · nonunion · malposition · prominent hardware (pain) · humeral shaft / periarticular fracture

How it's asked

"45-y, deltoid + cuff paralysis 5 y after motorcycle injury, hand/wrist work?"shoulder arthrodesis
✗ Wrong options: Eden-Lange · TSA · reverse TSA · latissimus transfer

"Who benefits most from GH arthrodesis?"30-y labourer with deltoid + cuff paralysis
✗ Wrong options: AVN · MDI · infected TSA removed · cleidocranial dysostosis

"Position of shoulder fusion?"30° abduction, 30° flexion, 30° IR — hand to mouth (OB: ~40/35/20)

5Management

Positioning

Beach chair Lateral decubitus
Orientation Upright, anatomic Glenoid parallel to floor (non-anatomic)
Traction None → ↓ neurapraxia 10–13 lb (avoid over-distraction) → traction neurapraxia (NV + soft tissue)
Arm Mobile; arm holder possible 30–60° abduction + 20–30° forward flexion
Conversion to open Easy (deltopectoral; no re-prep) Must reposition/redrape
Bleeding ↓ venous pressure + bleeding —

Hypotension / bradycardia ↑ risk No ↑

Anaesthesia Regional + sedation possible Not ideal if regional not tolerated
5 o'clock portal Safer (Gelber) Axillary + MCN closer

Lateral modification (TO)tilt patient 20–30° posteriorly → glenoid parallel to floor → less traction (↓ plexus neurapraxia), labral tears accentuated (pulled away from bed), better access to inferior third of labrum/capsule

Beach chair advantages (TO)faster positioning · ↓ neurapraxia (no traction) · less capsular distortion · arm mobility · easy open conversion

Beach chair disadvantages (TO)difficult posterior portals · ↓ cerebral perfusion with hypotensive anaesthesia → stroke, death

Root Motion Muscle Reflex

Ligament Restrains

4Diagnosis & Classification

Impingement & biceps tests (Hawkins, Speed)

Impingement syndrome (TO)anterior pain in 60–120° abduction (painful arc) · greater tuberosity slides under acromion, bursa smooths it · causes: subacromial bursitis, hooked acromion, cuff pathology (supraspinatus tendinitis, calcific tendinitis, partial tear), GT fracture (TO)

Test Technique Positive / meaning
Neer sign Stabilise scapula, passive forced forward elevation Anterior pain (GT under acromion 70–110°) · needs full ROM · sens 75–86%, spec 50% · also + in stiffness, OA, instability, bone lesions
Neer test Repeat Neer after subacromial lidocaine Marked pain relief = subacromial impingement
Hawkins-Kennedy Flex 90°, elbow 90°, forcible IR (GT under CA ligament) Pain · sensitive, not specific · sens 75–92%, spec 45% · = subacromial bursitis (TO)
Scapular assistance (TO) Push inferomedial scapular angle during elevation (upward rotation + posterior tilt) Relief of impingement pain + ↑ arc
Internal impingement 90° abduction + max ER + extension (late cocking) Posterior throwing pain · relieved by relocation / elbow in front of body

Neer test injectate5 mL 1% lidocaine (TO) · 4 cc 1% lidocaine + 4 cc 0.5% bupivacaine + 2 cc steroid (Orthobullets) — read the options

Biceps test Technique Positive

Yergason Elbow 90°, pronated → resisted supination Groove pain = biceps tendon pathology
Popeye Bulge in arm LHB proximal rupture

Rotator cuff strength & lag tests (lift-off, hornblower, ER lag)

Muscle Tests
Subscapularis Lift-off, belly-press / Napoleon, bear hug, IR lag, ↑ passive ER
Supraspinatus Jobe empty can, drop arm (Codman)
Infraspinatus ER lag sign (specific), drop sign (Hertel), ER resistance stress
Teres minor Hornblower (Patte), ER strength at 90° abduction

Lift-off (Gerber) (TO)dorsum of hand on lumbar spine (IR) → can't lift off = subscapularis tear · specific for IR deficit (TO) · best for inferior subscapularis · more accurate if hand reaches opposite scapula · confounded by other muscles
✗ Wrong options: abduction · ER deficit · anterior instability

Belly-press (Gerber) / Napoleon (TO)palm presses abdomen, elbow in front of trunk · weak → elbow drops behind trunk (shoulder extension) = belly-press · wrist flexes = Napoleon sign · best for superior subscapularis

Bear hug (Burkhart & De Beer) (TO)palm on opposite shoulder, elbow in front, examiner pulls hand away anteriorly · can't resist = positive · most sensitive: detects tears <50% (upper third) missed by lift-off/belly-press (TO) · positive if ≥20% weaker than other side (Orthobullets)

Most sensitive + specific subscap testIR lag sign (Orthobullets, OB) · bear hug most sensitive (TO) — read the options

Not subscap testingisolated IR at side (pec major + latissimus contribute)

✗ Wrong options: GT fracture = drop arm · superior migration = CTA · dislocation can't be positioned · AC separation

Jobe empty can (TO)90° abduction in scapular plane (30° forward), IR thumb down, resist downward push · weakness = supraspinatus tear (TO) · pain only = subacromial bursitis/irritation, tear only with true drop arm (Orthobullets)

Drop arm (Codman) (TO)arm elevated overhead → lower slowly · sudden pain or uncontrolled lowering = supraspinatus tear · passive 90° scapular plane → drop = most specific for full-thickness tear (98%) (Orthobullets)

ER resistance stress (TO)arms at side, elbows 90°, ER 60°, resist examiner's IR push → pain/weakness = infraspinatus + teres minor

ER lag sign (TO)seated, elbow 90°, shoulder 20° elevation in scapular plane, full ER → hold · angular drop = infraspinatus tear (specific)
✗ Wrong options: subscapularis · teres minor · adhesive capsulitis

Drop sign (TO)same as ERLS but 90° elevation in scapular plane · infraspinatus · ERLS slightly more sensitive + specific · not the Orthobullets "drop sign" (= drop arm, supraspinatus)

Hornblower (Patte) (TO)arm 90° abduction in scapular plane, elbow 90° → attempt ER against resistance · can't = hornblower posture · most accurate for teres minor · TO option: "test for infraspinatus and teres minor" · Orthobullets: hold 90° abd + 90° ER → arm falls into IR · also + in posterior supraspinatus tears

Shoulder Hemiarthroplasty

Shoulder & Elbow · 47 / 60

1Basics

Definition

Hemiarthroplasty (HA)humeral articular surface replaced with stemmed humeral component; glenoid left native

Most common indicationGH arthritis with inadequate glenoid bone stock for TSA

Mechanicsrelies on rotator cuff compression for motion + strength; CA arch = barrier to proximal migration

Useless common since RSA; still for young patients/laborers, CTA, osteonecrosis, complex proximal humerus fractures

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Modality Use
True (Grashey) AP 30–40° oblique to coronal plane; extent of DJD, fracture pattern
Axillary Posterior glenoid wear; fracture displacement
CT Glenoid version + glenoid bone stock; unclear fracture pattern
MRI Rotator cuff status

↓ Acromiohumeral distancesuperior head migration → cuff deficiency → evaluate cuff (MRI / CT arthrogram)

5Management

Indications & limitations (cuff integrity, osteonecrosis, CTA head, ream-and-run)

Indication Detail
Primary arthritis Cuff deficient · glenoid stock inadequate · high glenoid loosening risk (young, active laborers)
Rotator cuff arthropathy HA > rTSA if forward flexion > 90°
Osteonecrosis Without glenoid involvement
Proximal humerus fracture 3-part with poor bone · 4-part · head-split · major articular destruction
Contraindication Note
Infection —
Neuropathic (Charcot) joint e.g. syrinx
Unmotivated patient —
CA ligament deficiency CA arch + cuff deficient → superior (anterosuperior) escape
RA · capsulorrhaphy arthropathy Listed as contraindications (one OB)

RA / capsulorrhaphy arthropathycontraindication (OB) · RA results "satisfactory in most, ↓ ROM" (TO) · ream-and-run works in capsulorrhaphy arthropathy (OB) — read the options

Outcomes by diagnosis

Best results (TO)humeral head AVN / osteonecrosis: consistent pain relief in 90%, near-normal ROM

Less good (TO)RA, OA, glenoid dysplasia, post-traumatic arthrosis: satisfactory in most, ↓ ROM

Most influential factor on functionstatus of the rotator cuff
✗ Wrong options: CA ligament · glenoid wear · inferior osteophyte · AC arthritis

Irreparable cuffTSA contraindicated → HA (limited function) or RSA

Fracturesexcellent pain relief in majority; outcome inversely proportional to age + time from injury to surgery

HA vs TSA for GH OA

Statement Truth
HA outcomes with eccentric glenoid wear Inferior to TSA ✓
HA function overall Inferior to TSA
HA revision rate Equal or greater than TSA (mid–long term); higher with eccentric wear
HA outcomes eccentric vs concentric Worse with eccentric wear
Glenoid Progressive erosion may occur

Extended (CTA) head

Theoretic advantagemetal-to-bone articulation with the acromion → greater arc of smooth metal contact with glenoid + acromion

Evidenceunproven; results comparable to standard HA; no other biomechanical advantage
✗ Wrong options: superior stability · fixed fulcrum · ↑ deltoid moment arm · ↑ offset

Ream-and-run

DefinitionHA + concentric glenoid reaming (non-prosthetic glenoid arthroplasty) with nubbed spherical reamer → single smooth concavity

Advantageavoids prosthetic glenoid failure → activity beyond that recommended for TSA

Ideal patientyoung, active, motivated (e.g. 42-yo weightlifter)

Works inOA, capsulorrhaphy arthropathy, post-traumatic arthritis
✗ Wrong options: contraindicated

Rehabtherapy is critical
✗ Wrong options: "TSA needs more therapy"

Outcomesexcellent 2-year functional + radiographic results

Technique

Approachdeltopectoral

Head cutstart at medial insertion line of supraspinatus

Humeral stem version

Version Result
30° retroversion ✓ (broach + stem, TO) Ideal; lateral fin slightly posterior to bicipital groove
Excess anteversion Anterior dislocation
Excess retroversion (e.g. 45°, TO) Posterior dislocation (✗ Wrong options: anterior instability)
✗ Wrong options: neutral · 10° anteversion · neutral–10° retroversion Wrong (TO)

45° retroversion (TO)FNB 2024 item, answer not provided by source; options: anterior instability · limit IR · best function · shaft fracture

Height, head size & fixation

Greater tuberosity height7–8 mm below top of head (Orthobullets) · 6–8 mm (OB) — read the options

Whymaintain cuff + biceps tension; recreate medial calcar contour

Height landmarktop of head → upper border of pectoralis major = 56 mm; cement prosthesis proud

Head sizecontralateral X-ray or measure resected head; too large → overstuffing

Fixationcemented = standard of care (better QoL, ROM, strength vs uncemented)

Tuberosity malposition after fracture hemiarthroplasty

Importancetuberosity migration = commonest cause of failure in fracture HA; non-anatomic placement → variable outcomes, rotation deficit

Techniquesecure tuberosities to each other + to shaft; autograft from resected head → ↓ pull-off, ↑ healing

Malposition Consequence
GT too proximal (above head) GT impingement on acromion in abduction
GT too distal Over-tensioned cuff, stiffness, ↓ motion
LT too lateral (close to GT) ↑ Subscapularis tension → ER deficit

✗ GT position trapsdoes not change nonunion risk · does not cause overstuffing

Rehab

Fracture HAearly passive motion 6–8 wk until healed → strengthening once tuberosity healed

6Complications

Complication Detail Consequence / treatment
Progressive glenoid arthrosis Young, active Conversion to TSA
Tuberosity displacement / malunion Commonest in fracture HA Reposition + bone graft
Overstuffing Head too large → stiffness, accelerated glenoid arthritis
Subcutaneous (anterosuperior) escape Cuff + CA arch deficient RSA > anatomic TSA

Failed hemiarthroplasty – glenoid erosion & conversion to TSA/RSA

Painful hemiarthroplasty
  • Infection excluded? (WBC 1900, 20% PMN, cultures −ve 3 wk)→aseptic
  • Intact cuff + glenoid wear→keep stem, revise head + add glenoid (TSA)
  • Pseudoparalysis + superior escape→convert to RSA

✗ Wrong options: MRI · two-stage spacer · explant stem · RSA

✗ Wrong options: MRI (cuff failure implied) · cuff repair + TSA · fusion if glenoid stock good · revision HA · PT

Why not TSA for cuff-deficient failed HApoor function, continued superior migration, glenoid loosening (rocking-horse)

Cuff arthropathy after HAbony erosion, superior head migration, acromion + AC joint erosion

Glenoid Native Prosthetic Prosthetic (reverse)
Cuff needed Yes Yes No
Best for AVN, 4-part fracture, young/laborer, poor glenoid stock OA, eccentric glenoid wear Cuff deficiency, superior escape
