Shoulder Periprosthetic Fracture

Shoulder & Elbow · 49 / 60

1Basics

Epidemiology

Incidence0.6–3% of shoulder arthroplasty (Orthobullets, OB) · 1.5–3% in stemmed anatomic TSA (OB) · age 50–85

Share of complications20% of all complications (intra-op fractures, Orthobullets) · overall arthroplasty complication rate 11%; post-op periprosthetic fractures = 6.6% (reverse) vs 1.2% (anatomic) of complications

Timingmost are intra-operative, at the index implant (anatomic + reverse); stemless: few post-op reports

Locationadjacent to stem tip · greater tuberosity (esp. revision TSA)

Risk factorsosteoporosis · aggressive reaming · endosteal notching · incorrect reaming entry (ideal 9 mm lateral to anatomic centre of rotation) · press-fit > cemented stems · revision · soft-tissue contracture · instability history · ♀ · post-traumatic arthritis · ↑ comorbidity · osteonecrosis (steroid > alcohol, post-traumatic)

2Mechanism

Intra-operative

Revision TSAhighest risk: greater exposure, subacromial/cuff scarring → ↑ retraction + torque

Intra-op step (revision) Share of intra-op fractures
Removing previous implant Up to 81%
Reaming / broaching Up to 31%
Trialing / insertion Up to 19%
Exposure (forceful retractor) Up to 15%

Implant removalmetaphyseal-filling → GT fracture (cement removal, interface disengagement) · diaphyseal-engaging → GT fracture (metaphyseal stress shielding) · prevent: clear lateral soft tissue, implant-specific tools, controlled corticotomy

Primary TSAlower risk · endosteal notching from reaming · excessive humeral ER during exposure · cortical breach, esp. osteopenic bone

Post-operative

Fall (FOOSH)stem tip = stress riser → most post-op fractures at/adjacent to stem tip · fatigue fracture through stress riser

Atraumaticloosening → implant "rattling" weakens cortex

Nonunion risk ↑prosthesis disrupts endosteal blood supply · stem distracts fragments (no end-to-end healing)

Nonunion factorsosteoporosis · RA · ♀ · displacement >2 mm · cement at fracture site

3Presentation

Historyfall on outstretched hand · prodromal / worsening pain = mechanical loosening

Examvarus/valgus deformity, ecchymosis, shortening, diffuse tenderness · can't move elbow/shoulder (pain) · document full NV exam

Radial nervecheck status; palsy common with distal humerus fracture, mostly neurapraxia
✗ Wrong options: surgery for it

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

X-rayorthogonal humerus: AP, axillary lateral, Grashey, scapular Y · fracture at stem tip, usually oblique · decide on stem stability + zones of lucency (no ingrowth / osteolysis)

CT (metal suppression)concern for loose stem (pattern, prodromal pain) or comminution · morphology, bone stock, cuff muscle quality, glenoid version (if revising)

Wright and Cofield classification

Type Fracture Diagram
A Centred near stem tip, extends proximally ("proximal to stem tip" — OB)
B Centred near stem tip, extends distally (at level of tip)
C Distal to stem tip (into distal metaphysis)

Wright series (Mayo)499 arthroplasties → 9 fractures (1 A, 5 B, 3 C) · 3 splinted → failed to heal

5Management

Post-operative periprosthetic humerus fracture
  • Loose stem (any type)→revision arthroplasty + supplementary fixation
    (poor stock → long stem bypassing 2–3 cortical diameters; good stock → shorter stem + fixation)
  • Stable stem, type A/B→ORIF: hybrid locking plate + cerclage cables
    (long spiral/oblique A/B → bracing possible, union <50%)
  • Type C→fracture brace (nonop)
    • fails / nonunion→ORIF ± allograft strut
Intra-operative fracture
  • Type A→stem spanning fracture by 2 cortical diameters
  • Type B / C→proximally porous-coated long stem, 2–3 cortical diameters
  • Type C unsuitable for long stem→ORIF

Operative criteria

Situation Treatment
Long oblique / spiral A or B, stable stem · type C Immobilisation (coaptation → functional brace); union <50%
Intra-op type A Longer stem spanning 2 cortical diameters ± supplementary fixation
Intra-op type B or C Proximally porous-coated long stem, 2–3 cortical diameters; distal cement
Post-op transverse A/B, stable stem · C failed nonop · can't tolerate nonop ORIF
Loose prosthesis, any type Revision arthroplasty + supplementary fixation
Poor bone stock (loose) Long stem bypass ≥2–3 cortical diameters ± allograft
Good bone stock (loose) Short stem (ends proximal to original) + fixation; tip doesn't distract fracture

Source nuancelong spiral type B, stable stem: bracing possible (Orthobullets) · ORIF hybrid plate + cables best for active patient (OB) — read the stem

Stable-stem fractures – ORIF with plate/cerclage & radial nerve risk

Best for stable stem A/BORIF hybrid locking plate + cerclage cables
✗ Wrong options: revision (stem well fixed) · lag screw + neutralisation · nonop near stem tip → nonunion

Constructplate placed eccentrically → locking screws skive past stem (bicortical) · cables proximal to stem tip · screws distal · usually 4.5 mm LC-DCP · alternatives: dual plates, 3.5 mm attachment plates · deficient cortex → cortical strut allograft + cables (2 hemicylinders = "sarcophagus")

Approachanterolateral (extend deltopectoral: coracoid → DP groove → lateral biceps) · biceps–brachialis interval, split brachialis (medial = musculocutaneous, lateral = radial) · posterolateral for distal fracture with stable stem

GT / calcar fracturesuture or cable fixation

No nonop with sling / hanging arm castbracing is the nonop method; active patient wants fast return → ORIF

No APC (allograft-prosthetic composite)not with good bone quality + no bone loss

EvidenceKurowicki: 7 type B ORIF without revision → all united · Andersen: ORIF 17/17, revision 18/19 united · stable IM stem + supplementary fixation > loose stem

Radial nerve and cerclage

Landmark Distance to radial nerve at spiral groove
Coracoid ~13 cm
Distal lesser tuberosity ~10 cm
Superior latissimus insertion ~8 cm
Inferior latissimus insertion ~4 cm

Cable 4 cm below inferior LD insertion → iatrogenic radial nerve injury
✗ Wrong options: median (medial septum) · axillary (proximal) · subscapularis · brachial artery (superficial, anteromedial)

Safe zonecables just inferior / proximal to inferior edge of LD insertion

Long stem technique

Porous-coated long stemproximal coating = metaphyseal stability · pack cement distally, avoid cement extrusion into fracture · strut + cables if deficient · olecranon fossa may prevent it

6Complications

Complicationsnonunion · delayed union · GH stiffness · radial nerve injury (fracture or iatrogenic cerclage)

Prognosishigh union when treated appropriately; union 2–8 months · significant ↓ shoulder ROM

X vs Y

Stable stem Loose stem
Clues No lucency, no prodromal pain Lucent zones, prodromal pain, "rattling"
Type A/B ORIF hybrid plate + cables Revision long stem + fixation
Type C Brace → ORIF if fails Revision

How it's asked

"Fall, stable rTSA stem, type B fracture — best treatment?"ORIF hybrid locking plate + cerclage cables
✗ Wrong options: revision cemented/cementless long stem · lag screw · nonop

"Cable placed 4 cm inferior to latissimus insertion — complication?"iatrogenic radial nerve injury
✗ Wrong options: median · axillary · brachial artery

✗ Wrong options: sling · hanging cast · revision · APC

"Intra-op fracture — stem should bypass by?"2 cortical diameters (2–3 for type B/C)

"Most common step causing intra-op fracture in revision?"implant removal (up to 81%)

"Type C fracture, stable stem?"fracture brace
✗ Wrong options: sling

Shoulder Prosthetic Joint Infection

Shoulder & Elbow · 50 / 60

1Basics

Epidemiology

Significancemajor cause of revision within first 2 years after shoulder arthroplasty

Incidence~4% primary TSA + RSA (Orthobullets, OB) · 3–4% · 0–5% · up to 4–5% (other OB explanations) — read the options · ~15% revision TSA/RSA

aTSA vs rTSAno difference in primary shoulders without prior surgery · ↑ in primary rTSA after ≥1 prior non-arthroplasty operation (Florschütz)

Risk factors & prevention (smoking, steroid injection, nasal decolonisation)

Risk factor Note
Male 2.5× PJI rate · ↑ C. acnes colonisation
Arthroplasty for fracture / trauma 3× vs elective
Revision surgery ~15%
Intra-articular steroid injection within 3 months Injection 4 months (or 15 months) before = not a risk factor
Smoking ↑ infection + fracture + loosening
Young age —
Postoperative haematoma —
Coagulopathy, ESRD, lupus, RA, uncontrolled comorbidities Medical comorbidities

Pre-op smokersmoking cessation programme next (smoking = suggested contraindication to TSA/RSA)
✗ Wrong options: PT trial (pseudoparalysis CTA) · tramadol (= 1st line knee OA) · CBC/ESR/CRP (infection unlikely) · rheumatology referral

Complication risk (patient)younger age · ↑ BMI · RA · diabetes · smoking

C. acnes colonisation correlatesmale · native hair at surgical site · humeral loosening
✗ Wrong options: age >70 · CKD · female · glenoid lucent lines

✓ Validated prevention Detail
MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) screening + nasal decolonisation If nares colonized → application of 5% povidone-iodine solution to each nostril pre-operatively (10 s/nostril, 1 h pre-op) · or 2% mupirocin BID × 5 days
IV antibiotic prophylaxis Within 30 min of incision, continue 24 h
Penicillin allergy prophylaxis Clindamycin for C. acnes (Orthobullets, OB) · vancomycin, not clindamycin (OB) — read the options
Skin prep Chlorhexidine (ChloraPrep) · hydrogen peroxide prep
Hair removal Electric clippers
Intra-op Frequent saline irrigation · dilute povidone-iodine before closure
Closure / dressing Dermabond · silver-impregnated dressings
Not validated Note
Axillary hair shaving No meaningful ↓
Sterile helmets/hoods May ↑ infection
Laminar flow Not validated

2Mechanism

C. acnes – microbiology, prolonged culture & antibiotic choice

Most common organismCutibacterium acnes (formerly Propionibacterium acnes) · others: S. aureus, S. epidermidis

Descriptiongram-positive, anaerobic rod (OB) · gram-positive rod, facultative anaerobe (OB) · "gram-positive, facultative, aerotolerant, anaerobic rod" (Orthobullets) · ferments lactose → propionic acid · non-spore-forming

Habitataxilla, dermal sebaceous glands; commensal skin flora

Biofilmforms in 18–90 h on implant + synovium (>> planktonic) → aspiration only 17% sensitive

Behaviourindolent, low-grade, low virulence · usually no swelling, erythema, fever, pus · inflammatory markers often normal

Culturemean incubation 7–21 days · usually negative in first 3–5 days · may take up to 3 weeks

✗ Organism distractor Description
S. aureus GP cocci, facultative anaerobe, coagulase + · commonest in hip/knee PJI
S. epidermidis GP cocci, facultative anaerobe, coagulase −
E. coli GN rod, facultative anaerobe · rare in shoulder
Klebsiella GN encapsulated rod
N. gonorrhoeae GN diplococci
C. diphtheriae GP club-shaped, nonmotile, noncapsulated bacillus
Streptococci · fungi Rare · exceedingly rare

Biofilm & timing

Biofilm (all bacteria)on implant within 4 weeks · 15% cells + 85% polysaccharide (glycocalyx) → adherence + immune protection · no safe removal → explant if >4 wk

Sourcedirect (sinus tract, wound dehiscence) · haematogenous (dental work, gallbladder) in longstanding infection-free joint

3Presentation

Symptomspersistent pain (most common) · draining sinus (2nd) · systemic (fever, chills, sweats) · stiffness

Sinus tract to jointdiagnostic

Typical C. acnes stemmonths–years after arthroplasty, gradually ↑ pain, normal WBC/ESR/CRP, humeral lucency

4Diagnosis & Classification

Classification – time of onset

Acute Chronic
Timing <3–6 wk (CDC <90 days) >3–6 wk (CDC >90 days)
Biology Confined to joint; no bone–implant invasion; less biofilm Biofilm; invades prosthesis–bone interface
Treatment I&D + retention (DAIR) 2-stage revision

DAIR window<4 wk (Orthobullets treatment) · within 5–6 wk (OB) · <3–6 wk (Orthobullets classification) — read the options

Key radiology findings

X-raynormal early · osteopenia · periprosthetic lucencies · pseudosubluxation of head · effusion · endosteal scalloping · bony resorption

Humeral vs glenoid looseningglenoid loosening = most common cause of TSA failure, not specific for infection · humeral loosening → suspect PJI

US / MRIfluid collections (US: loculated away from GH joint)

Bone scannot routinely (efficacy not shown)

PETadjunct; 98% sensitivity + 98% specificity

Genes & lab markers

Marker Fact
WBC Not sensitive/specific; normal in C. acnes
CRP Peaks 2–3 d post-op → normal 14–21 d; may be normal in C. acnes
ESR Peaks 5–7 d → normal 90 d; may be normal
ESR/CRP overall Insufficient sensitivity/specificity for PJI
Alpha-defensin Investigational
Synovial WBC >50,000
Crystals Don't exclude infection
Gram stain Often negative; + in ~75%

Diagnostic work-up – aspiration

Synovial tissue culturegold standard (+ ~80%) · ≥4 specimens at surgery · aerobic + anaerobic + broth media

Hold cultures14–28 days (Orthobullets) · 14–21 days / 2–3 weeks (OB) — read the options · fungal 4 wk · mycobacterial 8 wk

Aspirationlow sensitivity + low NPV · dry tap common → does not rule out · + S. aureus culture = high specificity + PPV

Fluoroscopic / US guidanceensures intra-articular placement · no ↑ PPV/NPV or yield, operator-dependent, ↑ cost

Antibioticsstop 2 weeks before aspiration
✗ Wrong options: current antibiotics don't affect yield

No growth at 5 daysobserve cultures additional 2 weeks before revision
✗ Wrong options: revision · arthroscopic I&D

5Management

Shoulder PJI
  • Unfit / unwilling→antibiotic suppression (fails 60–75%)
  • Acute (<4 wk; 5–6 wk OB)→I&D + component retention (DAIR)
    • exchange mobile parts (glenosphere, poly liner, tray)
  • Chronic
    • fit, unknown organism, adequate bone→2-stage exchange (gold standard)
    • low-virulence known organism, healthy tissue→1-stage revision
    • frail / poor bone / recalcitrant→resection arthroplasty

Antibiotics

C. acnes drug of choicepenicillin (low MIC) · penicillin G, amoxicillin
✗ Wrong options: TMP-SMX · meropenem · vancomycin (not 1st line)

Penicillin allergyceftriaxone or clindamycin

Durationprolonged IV; guided by cultures + ID consult

Mechanism of action Antibiotic
Binds transpeptidase (PBP) → inhibits cell wall synthesis Penicillin ✓
Reversibly binds 50S Macrolides
Irreversibly binds 30S Aminoglycosides
Blocks 30S–50S initiation complex Linezolid
Binds cell wall, disrupts peptidoglycan cross-linking Vancomycin

Operative criteria

Option Indications Outcome
Antibiotic suppression Severely ill, unwilling, multiple comorbidities Fails 60–75%
I&D + retention Acute infection 50% failure
Single-stage revision Uncommon; low-virulence organism with good sensitivity; healthy patient + soft tissue Up to 90%; ↓ stay, cost, antibiotic time · consider RSA (cuff sacrificed)
2-stage exchange Gold standard; medically fit; unknown organism; adequate bone stock; eradication before stage 2 60–90%; some keep spacer
Resection arthroplasty Frail/complex, insufficient bone stock, recalcitrant Poor function; pain relief >50%; tuberosity preservation predicts better result
Arthrodesis Rare (bone stock poor) Pain ↓
Amputation Life-threatening infection —

Spacerantibiotic-PMMA; local antibiotics, pseudocapsule, maintains soft-tissue tension, ↓ pain, allows PT · stem from Steinmann pin + chest tube

Resectionantero-superior subluxation if tuberosities + cuff removed

ArthrodesisS-shaped incision · resect cuff, biceps tenodesis, decorticate glenoid/head/acromion undersurface · 10-hole 4.5 mm pelvic recon plate · 30° abduction, 30° flexion, 30° IR · complications: infection, nonunion, malposition, prominent hardware, humeral shaft fracture

Approachdeltopectoral for all

6Complications

Complicationsfailure to eradicate (inadequate clearance after suppression, I&D, 1-stage) · recurrent infection (2-stage) · humerus/glenoid fracture · poor bone stock

X vs Y

Shoulder PJI Hip/knee PJI
Commonest organism C. acnes S. aureus / S. epidermidis
Inflammatory markers Often normal (C. acnes) ↑ with S. aureus / MRSA
Aspiration value Less clear: low sensitivity, dry taps Clearer
Gold-standard treatment 2-stage 2-stage

How it's asked

"rTSA, drainage at 4 wk, I&D + poly exchange, cultures negative at 10 d — MOA of best antibiotic?"binds transpeptidase, inhibits cell wall synthesis (penicillin)
✗ Wrong options: 50S macrolide · 30S aminoglycoside · linezolid · vancomycin

✗ Wrong options: GP aerobic cocci · GN rods · diplococci · club-shaped

✗ Wrong options: arthroscopic I&D · revision

"Independent correlate of P. acnes colonisation?"native hair at surgical site
✗ Wrong options: age >70 · CKD · female · glenoid lucent lines

"aTSA 2 mo ago, infection confirmed — organism characteristics?"gram-positive rod, facultative anaerobe
✗ Wrong options: coagulase + / − cocci · GN rods

"C. acnes grown — antibiotic of choice?"penicillin
✗ Wrong options: TMP-SMX · clindamycin = allergy only · meropenem · vancomycin

"Smoker with CTA planned for arthroplasty — next step?"smoking cessation programme

"rTSA infection — NOT a risk factor?"steroid injection 4 months before surgery (✓ risk: coagulopathy, fracture, male, smoking)

"Validated PJI prevention before rTSA?"5% povidone-iodine to each nostril if MRSA-colonised
✗ Wrong options: axillary shaving · helmets · laminar flow · clindamycin for allergy

"rTSA 2 y, ↑ ESR/CRP — most common organism (Gram picture)?"gram-positive rod (C. acnes)
✗ Wrong options: staph · strep · E. coli · fungus

"Shoulder aspiration — true statement?"positive S. aureus culture = high specificity
✗ Wrong options: high sensitivity/NPV · dry tap rules out · fluoroscopy ↑ PPV/NPV · antibiotics don't matter

"Gold standard for chronic shoulder PJI?"2-stage exchange

SLAP Lesion

Shoulder & Elbow · 51 / 60

1Basics

Epidemiology

Incidenceuncommon: <5% of shoulder injuries · yet a common cause of pain + weakness in throwers

Whodominant shoulder of overhead/throwing athletes · older patients after traumatic falls

Risk factorGIRD

Associationsinternal impingement · GIRD · articular-sided cuff tears · (subtle) instability · scapular dyskinesis · paralabral cyst · sublabral clefts, Buford complex

Anatomy – biceps anchor, Buford complex & vascularity

LHB attachment~50% to supraglenoid tubercle, ~50% to labrum (predominantly posterior labrum) · tubercle >6 mm medial to glenoid surface

Posterior / posterior-dominant attachment~70% of shoulders (✗ Wrong options: 15% · 30% · 100%) · most common: posterior to 12 o'clock (✗ Wrong options: "anchored anteriorly")

Tuoheti type Biceps attachment Share
I Completely posterior I + II >70%
II Predominantly posterior
III Anterior + posterior 25%
IV Anterior 5%

Biceps functiontorsional + horizontal stability in late cocking · poorest blood supply in intra-articular course

Labrumfibrocartilage; chock block to subluxation · superior labrum attaches more medially + anchors biceps = weak link

Labral blood supplysuprascapular, circumflex scapular, posterior humeral circumflex arteries via capsule + periosteum · anterosuperior labrum = poorest → degenerative tears, poor healing
✗ Wrong options: bone · single source

Variant Feature Pitfall
Sublabral recess / foramen ± thickened MGHL Mistaken for tear on MRI
Buford complex Cord-like MGHL + absent anterosuperior labrum; normal variant, 1.5% Do not repair → significant loss of ER + pain
Meniscoid labrum 1% —
Superior MGHL attachment On glenoid —

Arthroscopy tellerythema + tearing under labrum = tear (vs normal recess)

2Mechanism

Mechanismsrepetitive overhead activity · FOOSH with tensed biceps · traction on arm

Thrower pathoanatomytight posterior IGHL → GH contact shifts posterosuperiorly → ↑ shear on superior labrum → "peel-back"

ConsequenceSLAP ↑ strain on anterior band IGHL → ↓ stability

3Presentation

History"pop" during overhead activity or trauma · lag between injury + symptoms

Symptomsvague deep shoulder pain · popping/clicking · weakness, fatigue, ↓ performance

Exambicipital groove tenderness · check IR + total arc vs contralateral · SS ± IS atrophy (suprascapular neuropathy from cyst) · apprehension positive in 85%

Testsno single specific test

Test group Tests
Biceps provocation Speed's, Yergason's, Kim biceps load
SLAP O'Brien (active compression), crank (full abduction, load + rotate), dynamic labral shear, Kibler anterior slide

Related topics (distal clavicle excision, biceps dislocation)

Arthroscopic vs open DCEadvantage = evaluate GH joint · failed open DCE: 15/20 had SLAP (9/15 good–excellent after arthroscopic treatment)
✗ Wrong options: fewer complications · infection · time

Arthroscopic DCEsacrifices inferior AC ligament, preserves superior AC ligament

Medial LHB dislocationsubscapularis tear
✗ Wrong options: supraspinatus (LHB rupture) · transverse ligament · shallow groove · type I SLAP; type II SLAP can cause instability

Diagnosis – MR arthrogram

X-rayusually normal

Study of choiceMR arthrogram · gold standard = arthroscopy
✗ Wrong options: US · EMG · labs · PT first when suspicious

Accuracysens ~50%, spec ~90%, ↑ with arthrogram (Orthobullets) · linear high signal on oblique coronal T2: sens 41%, spec 86%, accuracy 63% (OB) — read the options

Paralabral ganglion cysthighly specific for labral tear; usually spinoglenoid notch
✗ Wrong options: suprascapular notch

Overdiagnosisconcern (↑ SLAP repairs in ABOS case logs)

Arthroscopic peel-back testlabrum peels back at 90° abduction + ER

Dynamic labral shear + tear 11–1 o'clock, intact biceps (TO)type III SLAP
✗ Wrong options: type II = biceps anchor detached · Bankart

✗ Wrong options: SLAP II · posterosuperior · anterior + posterior · posterior IGHL avulsion

5Management

SLAP lesion
  • First line→rest + PT + NSAIDs (scapula, cuff; treat GIRD)
  • Failed nonop, type I / III / IV <1/3 biceps→arthroscopic debridement
  • Failed nonop, type II, young overhead athlete→SLAP repair
    • >40 y (failure >36 y)→debridement + biceps tenodesis/tenotomy
  • Type IV >1/3 biceps→biceps tenodesis/tenotomy ± labral repair/debridement

Treatment – nonoperative vs repair vs tenodesis (age, type IV) & return to sport

Initial ✓rest + rehab for scapular mechanics + cuff strengthening (+ NSAIDs; address GIRD)
✗ Wrong options: aggressive concentric biceps strengthening (aggravates) · surgery first

Labral tear in throwerinitial: posterior capsular stretching + cuff strengthening

Situation (failed nonop, severe symptoms) Procedure

Group / treatment Rate

✗ Wrong options: IR

1Basics

Joint anatomy

Ligament Function
Posterior SC capsular ligament Primary restraint to anterior–posterior stability

First to ossifyclavicle, 5th–6th week of gestation

Before 25 ymost "SC dislocations" are medial clavicular physeal fractures → distinguish

1Basics

Epidemiology

Frequencymost common cause of shoulder pain · 44–65% of shoulder disorders · with biceps tendinitis, among commonest causes

Type Shape Diagram
I Flat
II Curved
III Hooked → associated with impingement

Typespre- · meso- · meta- os acromiale (named by unfused centre)

5Management

Subacromial impingement (no cuff tear)
  • First line→PT (cuff + periscapular) + NSAIDs ± subacromial steroid
    (scapular dyskinesia → integrated kinetic-chain rehab)
  • Failed ≥4–6 months nonop→subacromial decompression ± acromioplasty
  • Os acromiale → stage 1 fuse with graft→stage 2 acromioplasty

Nonoperative management – physical therapy & PRP

MainstayPT (aggressive cuff strengthening + periscapular stabilisation), NSAIDs, subacromial injection

Benign exam (full strength, Jobe/Speed painful)PT before imaging
✗ Wrong options: AC injection · ASD · MRA · MRI

Outcomemost improve with PT alone (even with type III acromion) · but tendinitis tends to recur
✗ Wrong options: "most fail nonop"

PT vs surgeryPT as effective as subacromial decompression ± debridement (tendinitis, partial tears) · ASD + PT not better at 2 y

PRPno effect on pain, function, ROM at 1 y vs therapy alone · not harmful · does not prevent arthropathy · meta-analysis: insufficient evidence

Operative criteria

Procedure Indication
Subacromial decompression / acromioplasty Impingement failed ≥4–6 months nonop
Two-stage os acromiale Fuse with bone graft → later acromioplasty (✗ Wrong options: direct excision → deltoid dysfunction)
Avoid acromioplasty + CA ligament release Massive irreparable cuff tear (preserve CA arch → avoid anterosuperior escape)

Technique – acromioplasty

Step 1anterior acromionectomy (arthroscopic: limited by anterior deltoid origin, keep intact)

Step 2anteroinferior acromioplasty smooths undersurface (rasp open; shaver/burr arthroscopic) · open → meticulous deltoid repair to bone

Subacromial decompression outcomes (workers' compensation)

Lower satisfactionworkers' compensation (also longer return to work) · anxiety + depression
✗ Wrong options: dominant arm · male · smoker · age <60

Irreparable (TO)can't reach tuberosity despite release (size, retraction, atrophy, fatty infiltration)

Fatty atrophy Goutallier III–IV

MRI Positive tangent sign

Tangent sign (TO)sagittal oblique; line top of scapular spine → top of coracoid · SS belly below line = positive → fatty atrophy, irreparable supraspinatus / poor repair outcome

Suprascapular Neuropathy

Shoulder & Elbow · 54 / 60

1Basics

Anatomy – suprascapular nerve course

OriginC5–C6, superior (upper) trunk of brachial plexus → across posterior triangle of neck → superior border of scapula

Courseunder superior transverse scapular (suprascapular) ligament at suprascapular notch → supraspinous fossa (supraspinatus) → around lateral border of scapular spine through spinoglenoid notch (under spinoglenoid ligament) → infraspinous fossa (infraspinatus)

Suprascapular ligamentfrom medial base of coracoid over notch · artery ABOVE, nerve BELOW

Functionmotor only (SS + IS) · no sensory → no sensory deficit

Transglenoid fixation risknerve lies 1.5 cm medial to glenoid labrum at spinoglenoid notch

Site Level Muscles weak
Suprascapular notch Proximal Supraspinatus + infraspinatus
Spinoglenoid notch Distal (SS branch already given off) Infraspinatus only

TO wording"infraglenoid notch" compression → infraspinatus only (= spinoglenoid notch)

Atraumatic compression sitessuprascapular + spinoglenoid notches (fascial bands, ganglion cysts)
✗ Wrong options: scalenus anterior · cervical rib · conjoined tendon · subcoracoid

Epidemiology & associations

Whooverhead athletes: volleyball (classic), baseball pitchers/catchers, tennis · also weightlifters, rowers, linebackers

AssociatedSLAP tears · posterior labral tears · internal impingement

2Mechanism

Suprascapular notch – causes

Causesganglion cyst (often with labral tear) · transverse scapular ligament entrapment/thickening · fracture callus

Spinoglenoid notch – causes

Causesposterior labral tear → cyst · spinoglenoid ligament · spinoglenoid notch ganglion · traction (45% of volleyball players) · transglenoid fixation

Cyst mechanismlabral tear = one-way valve → synovial fluid exits joint, can't drain → paralabral cyst

Cyst frequencyganglion cysts at spinoglenoid notch > less commonly suprascapular notch · cyst origin: transverse scapular ligament, scapular fibrous tissue, or GH joint

Labral sourceSLAP most often, posterior labrum less (OB) · posterior labral tear (Orthobullets, OB) — read the options; posterior SLAP / posterosuperior labral tear fits both

3Presentation

Symptomsdeep, diffuse, posterolateral shoulder pain · weakness, fatigue with overhead activity · ↓ velocity · no numbness

Suprascapular notchtender notch · supraspinatus weak: abduction 90° + 30° FF + IR (Jobe +) · infraspinatus weak: ER with elbow at side · atrophy above + below spine

Spinoglenoid notchisolated weak ER with arm at side · atrophy below scapular spine (posterior shoulder) · supraspinatus normal (empty can negative) · O'Brien + (associated SLAP)

Most specific exam finding (spinoglenoid cyst)weakness of ER
✗ Wrong options: impingement sign · apprehension · active compression · abduction weakness

ER in elevationisolated IS palsy: full ER with arm elevated · combined SS + IS: can't ER in forward elevation

Distinguishing shoulder tests

Test Muscle / lesion In SSN entrapment
Jobe / empty can Supraspinatus Abnormal at suprascapular notch ✓
ER with arm at side Infraspinatus Abnormal at both sites ✓
Hornblower (90° abduction + 90° ER, falls into IR) Teres minor (axillary) Normal
Belly press · bear hug · lift-off Subscapularis Normal
Anterior load and shift (supine, 40–60° abduction + FF) Anterior instability Normal
Kim test (seated, 90° abduction → 45° FF + axial + posteroinferior force) Posterior instability Normal
Jerk test Posterior labral tear May be + (cyst source)

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

MRIidentify compressive mass / cyst + associated labral lesion · cyst: well-defined, low T1, high T2 · denervation: ↓ bulk + fatty infiltration (SS ± IS)

Paralabral cystmost commonly with labral tears

Diagnosis – EMG & compression sites

EMG/NCVdiagnostic; with MRI = investigations of choice · localises compression

Isolated ER weakness + atrophy, MRA normal (no cyst, no tear)EMG/NCV first → found notch entrapment with early SS denervation
✗ Wrong options: cervical MRI first · subacromial steroid · notch release before EMG · CRP/ESR

C5 radiculopathyweakness out of proportion; not when specific SSN pattern

Lesion (distractor) Nerve / site Deficit
Quadrangular (quadrilateral) space Axillary + PHCA Teres minor atrophy, deltoid (forward elevation, abduction)
Triangular interval Radial nerve + profunda brachii Elbow + wrist extension
Subscapular recess Anterior to subscap, below coracoid Loose bodies
Upper/lower subscapular nerves Subscapularis IR (lift-off)
Long thoracic (C5–7 roots) Serratus anterior Not affected by spinoglenoid cyst

Brachial plexus figuresuprascapular = A (upper trunk) · dorsal scapular · medial pectoral · lower + upper subscapular = wrong options

5Management

Suprascapular neuropathy
  • No structural lesion on MRI→activity modification + rehab ≥6 months
    • fails ~1 year→surgical decompression (notch release / spinoglenoid ligament release)
  • Suprascapular notch cyst→decompression at suprascapular notch
  • Spinoglenoid cyst + labral tear→arthroscopic labral repair + cyst decompression

Operative criteria

Situation Treatment
No structural lesion Nonop ≥6 months (posterior capsule stretching for spinoglenoid)
No lesion + failed ~1 year nonop Suprascapular notch release · or spinoglenoid ligament release (posterior approach)
Structural lesion (cyst) at suprascapular notch Nerve decompression at notch
Labral tear + spinoglenoid cyst Arthroscopic labral repair + cyst decompression ✓

Treatment – labral repair with cyst decompression

Young competitive athlete, posterior labral tear + spinoglenoid cystcyst decompression + posterior labral repair
✗ Wrong options: 6 wk rest · PT · suprascapular notch decompression · cuff repair + acromioplasty

Catcher, posterosuperior tear + large cyst, severe ER weaknessarthroscopic repair + decompression
✗ Wrong options: aspiration + steroid · rest · acromioplasty · rehab

Labral tear keyaddress tear (cause of cyst) · no isolated cyst decompression when tear present

Labral repair alonenot enough (doesn't decompress cyst, atrophy may progress — OB) · "good outcomes with labral repair alone; needle aspiration also used" (one OB explanation) — read the options; best answer = repair + decompression

Failed 6 wk PT with cyst + IS atrophyoperate
✗ Wrong options: another 6 wk PT · cervical MRI + EMG · tenodesis

Mechanical compressionsurgical decompression usually required

6Complications

Iatrogenic injury

Arthroscopic SSN release at suprascapular notch → injured nerve → weak abduction, forward elevation + ER, wasting above + below scapular spine = suprascapular notch level
✗ Wrong options: spinoglenoid = IS only · axillary · spinal accessory · dorsal scapular

SLAP repairanchors/instruments medial to glenoid → SSN injury

Atrophy Above + below spine Below spine

Thoracic Outlet Syndrome

1Basics

Epidemiology

Definitioncompression of brachial plexus ± subclavian vessels between neck and axilla (first rib–clavicle); heterogeneous, potentially disabling

Incidence1–2% of population

Demographics♀ > ♂ (3:1); thin, long neck, drooping shoulders; age 20–60

Type Frequency Note
Neurogenic 95% (most common) Lower plexus
Venous 4% Paget-Schroetter; athletic ♂ > ♀
Arterial <1% Aneurysm, emboli; athletic ♂ > ♀

Anatomy – thoracic outlet spaces

Boundaries (OB)clavicle, first rib, subclavius, costoclavicular ligament, anterior scalene

Space Borders Contents Test
Interscalene triangle (proximal) Ant: anterior scalene · Post: middle scalene · Inf: 1st rib Plexus trunks + subclavian artery (✗ Wrong options: vein (runs beneath anterior scalene)) Adson, supraclavicular pressure
Costoclavicular space (middle) Ant: clavicle + subclavius · Post: 1st rib + scalenes · Med: costoclavicular ligament · Lat: upper scapular border Divisions + subclavian artery + vein Costoclavicular manoeuvre
Retropectoralis minor (subcoracoid; distal) Sup: coracoid · Ant: pectoralis minor · Post: ribs 2–4 Cords + axillary artery + vein Wright

Most affected (OB)subclavian artery, vein + lower trunk (C8–T1)

2Mechanism

Pathogenesisanatomic predisposition + superimposed neck trauma (acute or repetitive)

Splitsoft tissue 70% · osseous 30%

Soft tissue Detail
Scalene abnormalities Anterior scalene hypertrophy · plexus through anterior scalene · middle scalene anterior insertion on 1st rib
Scalenus minimus Accessory; 30–50% of TOS; C-transverse process → 1st rib between subclavian artery + T1 root
Fibromuscular bands ↑ stiffness, ↓ compliance; congenital band → lower trunk
Costoclavicular ligament Abnormal insertion → Paget-Schroetter
Tumours Pancoast (1–3% lung cancers; lacks cough/haemoptysis/dyspnoea), neuroblastoma, plexus schwannoma
Pectoralis minor Abnormal
Osseous Detail
Cervical rib <1% population; from C7
Prominent C7 transverse process
Clavicle / 1st rib Displaced fracture, hypertrophic callus, malunion
AC / SC injury Dislocation
Tumours 1st-rib metastasis (breast, prostate, kidney), osteoid osteoma

Cervical rib types

Type Description
1 Complete, articulates with 1st rib or manubrium
2 Incomplete, free bulbous tip
3 Incomplete, fibrous band distally
4 Short bar (mm) beyond C7 transverse process

Overuserepetitive overhead lifting, hyperabduction; weightlifting, rowing, swimming

Vascular damageaneurysm, thrombosis, emboli, limb-threatening ischaemia

Paget-Schroetter syndrome

Definitionvenous TOS in well-developed young athletes → upper-limb DVT

Causeintermittent subclavian vein obstruction in costoclavicular space by abnormal costoclavicular ligament or anterior scalene hypertrophy

3Presentation

Neurogenic

Painneck, trapezius (92%), chest, shoulder, arm

Paraesthesia98%; non-radicular, wide plexus distribution · lower plexus (C8–T1) or combined (C5–T1) in 90% → ring + small fingers, medial forearm

Otherweakness, numbness, heaviness with overhead activity · activity-related + night symptoms (↓ pressure → returning sensation felt as pain) · uni- or bilateral

Posturerounded shoulders, ↑ kyphosis, depressed/downward-rotated scapula

Gilliatt-Sumner hand (TO)

Definition (TO)rare, severe sign of true neurogenic TOS; chronic lower-trunk (C8–T1) compression by cervical rib or congenital fibrous band

Patternpreferential APB atrophy, relative hypothenar sparing (TO, ✓) · atrophy of APB + hypothenar + interossei (Orthobullets, TO Elvey list) — read the options

Why APB (TO)T1-innervated muscles hit harder (median + ulnar both get lower-trunk fibres)

Red flag (TO)thenar wasting usually = CTS, but in TOS + medial forearm sensory change + milder ulnar intrinsic involvement

(✗ Wrong options: Distractors (TO) — symmetric interossei/hypothenar wasting sparing thenar) · claw hand from ulnar compression at humerotricipital groove · thumb/index C6 sensory loss

Diagnosis (TO)EDX (neurogenic changes) + MRI/US

Treatment (TO)surgical decompression → stops progression of atrophy + pain; partial motor recovery possible

Differential (TO)CTS, ALS (motor neuron disease), Hirayama disease

Vascular

Venousepisodic cyanosis + swelling, distended veins, deep arm ache, heaviness after activity

Arterialunilateral Raynaud-type: coolness + pallor → cyanosis → erythema, worse in cold; hand predominantly; ulcers/microemboli (rare)

Provocative tests & neurogenic TOS

All provocative testshigh false-positive rate

Test Technique Positive Space
Supraclavicular pressure Squeeze upper trapezius + anterior scalene 30 s, arm at side Pain/paraesthesia Interscalene
Adson Arm slightly abducted + ER (TO: abducted + extended), elbow extended; neck extended + rotated TOWARD tested side; inhale + hold ↓/absent radial pulse ± symptoms; 51% of normals ↓ pulse; TO: low sensitivity + PPV (modified: tilt to opposite side / symptom aggravation) Interscalene

Halstead (TO) Downward traction on arm, neck hyperextended + rotated to opposite side Radial pulse disappears

Implant design (linked, semiconstrained, unlinked) & survivorship

Unconstrained (unlinked, resurfacing) Semiconstrained (linked) Constrained
Example Ewald capitello-condylar Coonrad-Morrey Dee
Hinge None "Sloppy hinge": 7° varus-valgus + 7° axial rotation Rigid hinge
Needs Competent collaterals + soft-tissue envelope, good bone, precise alignment collaterals not needed; radial head not needed —
Use — Most commonly used No longer used
Results No proven superiority Best results of all designs Highest loosening
Commonest failure Instability (5–10% dislocation) Instability (Orthobullets, TO) · bushing wear (OB) Aseptic loosening, then bushing wear

Semiconstrained laxity↓ stress at bone–cement interface → ↓ aseptic loosening, at the cost of bushing wear

Constrainedno coronal/rotational flexibility → high shear stress → early loosening; theoretically most stable

Unconstrained suitshumeroulnar disease with intact collaterals + radiocapitellar joint: OA, post-traumatic arthritis, acute intra-articular distal humerus fracture, distal humerus malunion, bony ankylosis

Unconstrained relative contraindicationlate-stage RA (capsuloligamentous instability + bony erosion); RA → linked
✗ Wrong options: unlinked: tendon injury → instability

Design pearls

Stemshumeral + ulnar stems → better fixation, ↓ loosening

Anterior humeral flangeextracortical; resists posteriorly directed + rotational forces; designs without flange → early humeral loosening; improper flange placement → humeral loosening (TO)

Radial headnot needed for stability in linked designs; often debrided/resected in RA

Grade Humeral bone stock

Type Characteristics Treatment
I (commonest, TO) Periarticular — humeral condyle or olecranon; osteolysis around hinge + muscle distraction Undisplaced → immobilise / soft-tissue repair (fibrous union OK) · displaced → ORIF heavy nonabsorbable suture or TBW
II1 Along stem ORIF, retain components ± strut allograft
II2 Along stem, loose implant, good bone stock Revision long-stem ± strut allograft + impaction grafting (± locking plate / cerclage)

5Management

Operative criteria – RA, elderly distal humerus fracture, failed interposition

Indication Criteria
Rheumatoid arthritis 10–20% of RA have elbow disease; Larsen 3–5 (Orthobullets) · grade III–IV (OB) + pain, functional loss, instability; ideally > 65 y; synovectomy for less advanced disease
Primary OA (advanced) > 65 y; mid-arc pain from ulnotrochlear cartilage loss
Fracture Physiologically elderly (> 70 y): acute complex unreconstructable intra-articular distal humerus fracture, missed fracture-dislocation, poor bone
Post-traumatic OA (advanced) · chronic instability —
Failed interposition arthroplasty End-stage arthritis + instability → semiconstrained TEA

Contraindicationsabsolute: active infection (→ arthrodesis), Charcot joint · relative: poor neurological control (UE paralysis), active patient < 65 y, olecranon osteotomy · RA list (OB): active/historical infection, paralysis, won't follow instructions

Olecranon osteotomycontraindication: preserve extensor mechanism; trans-olecranon approach jeopardises ulnar component stability → never for TEA

Not contraindicationscentral comminution · ulnar nerve transposition · radial head impaction · retrocapitellar comminution (radiocapitellar joint secondary)

Elderly unreconstructable distal humerus fracture
  • Physiologically elderly, low demand, poor bone→TEA (semiconstrained)
    • approach→direct posterior triceps-sparing
  • not ORIF (unstable fixation), acute fusion or anterolateral approach

Fracture TEA vs ORIFfaster recovery + more predictable function; elderly accommodate limits, fewer complications
✗ Wrong options: slower recovery

Anterolateral approachbrachialis/brachioradialis (radial nerve between) → no access for TEA

Prior radial head resection in RAsemiconstrained > unconstrained (both better in native elbows)

Failed interposition, 60-yo sedentarysemiconstrained TEA
✗ Wrong options: unconstrained fails with ligament instability · revision interposition · Outerbridge-Kashiwagi · arthroscopic osteocapsular arthroplasty

Survivorship & outcomes

Indication Outcome
RA Longest survivorship of all indications (> fracture, flail elbow, OA, post-traumatic); 92.4% revision-free at 10 y; > 90% up to 15 y
RA complications 14% (Orthobullets) · ~15% (OB) — triceps avulsion, deep infection, periprosthetic fracture, aseptic loosening (✗ Wrong options: "< 5%")
Primary OA 10-y survival 80–85%; more active → ↑ aseptic loosening + stem fracture vs RA
Overall > 80% at 10 y
Post-traumatic Functional ROM, satisfaction at 5 y; complications 27–43%, re-operation 25%

Longest survivorship combinationRA + semiconstrained

Linked TEA, OA vs RAOA ↑ aseptic loosening; instability equal (linked)

Surgical approach & triceps insufficiency

Approach Technique Key fact
Triceps-reflecting (Bryan-Morrey) Triceps + anconeus reflected medial → lateral; reattached to ulna with nonabsorbable suture through bone tunnels Triceps failure; ↓ extension power up to 30%; delayed ROM
Triceps tongue Fascial tongue raised from olecranon proximally; release collaterals Fractures or TEA
Triceps-splitting Longitudinal split in continuity with forearm fascia; or V-shaped turndown (insertion intact) Allows extensor lengthening
Triceps-sparing (e.g. Alonso-Llames, para-olecranon) Mobilise medial + lateral triceps borders; insertion retained Best for acute fracture TEA; earlier ROM, ↑ final ROM; ↓ ulnar visualisation
Triceps "on" Midline incision; release/protect ulnar nerve; release flexor-pronator + MCL, common extensors + LCL; elevate triceps off posterior humerus; dislocate ulnohumeral joint No triceps release → no insufficiency
Trans-olecranon Osteotomy, triceps stays on olecranon ORIF only, never TEA

Triceps-off vs triceps-sparingtriceps-off: delayed ROM, ↑ triceps failure · no difference: cement mantle, ulnar nerve palsy · sparing: ↑ final ROM

Bryan-Morrey (1982)initial 49 patients no triceps failure; later series ↑ failure

TO approachessplitting/reflecting keep triceps attached to periosteum + forearm fascia (± olecranon wafer); triceps-preserving (bilateral tricipital) = exposure by ulnohumeral dislocation, useful in severe RA; no consensus on best approach

Post-op protection (triceps-reflecting)restrict active extension early; 6–8 wk before resisted extension
✗ Wrong options: active flexion · supination · passive motion

Technique

Positioningsupine (arm over chest, assistant; avoid ETT) or lateral decubitus over bolster (no assistant, ↓ manipulation)

Humerusresect olecranon fossa, keep medial + lateral columns; bone wedge behind anterior flange; orient to posterior flat surface of distal humerus

Ulnaresect olecranon tip + coronoid tip (prevents impingement on flange → axial pistoning + loosening); orient perpendicular to dorsal flat olecranon; centre of greater sigmoid notch, rotation from posterior olecranon cortex (TO)

Alignment (TO)implant–medullary canal parallelism (Figgie); COR displacement limit 5 mm; axis: anterior humeral cortex (AP), roof of coronoid fossa (depth), condylar plane (coronal rotation)

Pistoning (TO)check coronoid, protruding cement, HO on trial motion

Stability check (TO)joint line should separate ≤ 1–2 mm on distraction at 90° flexion + pronation; UCL + extensor mass contribute most

Cementmodern cementing; semiconstrained commonest

Post-op care & lifelong lifting restrictions

Immobilisationall protocols acceptable (immediate motion, or splint 60–90° for 2–5 d, 5–10 d, ≥ 10–14 d → active flexion + gravity-assisted extension); historically 4 wk; immediate motion safe

Evidenceearlier ROM → fewer complications · prolonged immobilisation → higher implant survival (Orthobullets); complications lowest without immobilisation in RA (OB)

Lifting limit5–10 lb lifelong (Orthobullets, OB) · ≤ 5 lb (OB) — read the options

Avoid after TEAimpact sport (golf, tennis) · immediate aggressive triceps strengthening · immobilising wrist/hand 4 wk (mobilise immediately) · avoiding pronation/supination (doesn't stress ulnohumeral implant)

Patient selection> 65 y, low demand, able to obey restrictions ("none do"), medical optimisation

6Complications

Complication Rate / fact
Aseptic loosening Radiographic 17%, clinical 6% (Orthobullets) · clinically significant 7–15% (TO) · < 10%, usually > 10 y (OB); commonest failure of constrained
Infection 8% (Orthobullets) · 3–8% (TO) · 5–8%, within first 5 y (OB); commonest early failure
Instability 7–19%; commonest failure of semiconstrained (Orthobullets, TO) and unconstrained
Bushing wear Constrained + semiconstrained; isolated exchange 1–6%, mean 7.9 y; commonest cause of revision / mechanical failure of semiconstrained (OB)
Periprosthetic fracture 5–30% of primary TEA; trauma commonest cause
Component fracture Humeral 0.65% · ulnar 1.2% (ulna > humerus); usually ulnar, late
Triceps insufficiency 2–8%; complete disruption < 2%
Ulnar neuropathy Paraesthesia < 40%, resolves 2–6 wk; radial nerve less often
Wound healing ↑ with long-term steroids

Total Shoulder Arthroplasty

Shoulder & Elbow · 57 / 60

1Basics

Principles

Definitionreplace humeral head + resurface glenoid; cemented all-polyethylene glenoid = standard of care

vs THA/TKAgreater ROM · success depends on soft tissues (intact cuff, esp. subscapularis) · glenoid less constrained → greater shear stress → mechanical loosening

Requirementsintact + functional rotator cuff · adequate glenoid bone stock + version

Outcomespain relief = most predictable benefit (more than hemi) · preserved IR + ER · survival 93% at 10 y (Orthobullets, OB) · ">90% at 10 y" (OB) · TSA/hemi for OA: good/excellent 95% (Norris) · worse for post-capsulorrhaphy arthropathy

Humeral fixationcemented or press-fit (porous-coated); both good longevity; humeral loosening uncommon without infection

Humeral anatomy & implant design (version, stemless, platform stems)

Parameter Native value
Humeral head retroversion Mean ~20° (transepicondylar axis) (OB) · Boileau & Walch mean 17.9° (−6.7 to 47.5°) · range 0–55° depending on method (TO)
Neck-shaft angle (inclination) 45° ± 5° (range 30–50°); arthritic ≈ 50° (flatter) (TO)
Humeral head height Top of head 8–10 mm above top of GT (TO, native)
Lateral humeral offset (LHO) Lateral base of coracoid → lateral margin of greater tuberosity (TO)
Humeral offset Centre of rotation → humeral canal axis; medial 4–14 mm, AP −2 to 10 mm (TO)
Head thickness 70% of radius of curvature (OB)
Radius of curvature Glenoid 22–28 mm · head 23–28 mm (TO)
Glenoid version 0–3° retroversion (OB) · 1.5° retroversion (10.5° retro to 9.5° ante) (TO) · ~0°, <10° either way (TO)
Glenoid inclination Superior ~4° (4.2°; −7 to 20°) (TO)

LHO (TO)↓ LHO → ↓ lever arm of deltoid + supraspinatus → weak abduction · ↑ LHO → overstuffing → ↓ motion, ↑ poly wear · reconstruct within 4 mm of normal

Retroversion axes (TO)proximal: articular surface plane / COR–articular centre / GT–articular centre · distal: trochlear axis, transepicondylar line, forearm

Restoring CORmay prolong glenoid fixation + ↓ poly wear (TO)

Humeral implant Key fact
Stemless Completely metaphyseal (biological) fixation · more bone preserving · no osteotomy needed for proximal humerus malunion (not constrained by stem) · not for 3/4-part fractures (→ stemmed RSA in elderly)
Stemmed Cemented or uncemented porous-coated
Short stems ↑ varus malalignment (metaphyseal-diaphyseal mismatch)
Large-diameter, high-fill stems ↑ proximal stress shielding
Platform (convertible) stem Modular conversion TSA → rTSA without stem removal → ↓ operative time, ↓ blood loss, preserves humeral bone, ↓ cost

Subscapularis failureindependent of implant design

2Mechanism

Rocking-horse phenomenon & glenohumeral mismatch

Rocking horseeccentric glenoid loading → lifting of opposite unloaded rim → glenoid loosening · causes: superior migration of head (cuff deficiency) · abnormal glenoid version (ant/post translation)

Minimised by (TO)glenoid radius of curvature larger than humeral head radius (2–4 mm) → normal translation without rim loading
✗ Wrong options: perfect congruence · larger head radius

Mismatch (TO)recommended <4 mm (2–4 mm larger glenoid) · "mismatch <4 mm ↑ loosening" (another TO explanation) — read the options · matched within 2 mm: no ↑ loosening reported · too much mismatch → ↑ translation, ↑ poly wear, fracture

Modern glenoidscemented all-poly, radius 2–6 mm larger than head (TO)

Glenoid conformity Effect
Conforming More stable · rim stress + radiolucencies
Nonconforming ↑ polyethylene wear
Overall Neither superior

Osteolysisrare in TSA: larger particle size → harder for macrophages to mount RANK–RANKL reaction (OB)

Indications & contraindications (cuff status, brachial plexus injury, RA, capsulorrhaphy arthropathy)

Indicationspain (esp. night) + ↓ ADL · glenoid chondral wear to bone (primary OA, inflammatory arthritis esp. RA) · posterior head subluxation · OA after primary/recurrent dislocation · complicated proximal humerus fracture not fixable (TO)

TSA vs hemiTSA preferred for OA + inflammatory arthritis (better pain relief + forward elevation in RA) · age <55: TSA > hemi (outcomes, survival, satisfaction)

AAOS CPG (end-stage GH OA)TSA with all-polyethylene cemented glenoid · (✗ Wrong options: humeral head resurfacing · CTA head · metal-backed glenoid (↑ revision/loosening)) · hemi + ream-and-run = option but TSA preferred

Contraindication Note

Active infection "Only absolute contraindication" (other TO explanation) — read the options
Irreparable rotator cuff tear → hemi or rTSA; rocking horse → glenoid loosening
Rotator cuff arthropathy (proximal migration on X-ray) Glenoid resurfacing contraindicated
Insufficient glenoid bone stock Glenoid erosion to coracoid → favours hemiarthroplasty
Deltoid dysfunction e.g. can't abduct past 30°
Relative (TO) Charcot, severe plexopathy, intractable instability, prohibitive comorbidity, cuff + deltoid dysfunction
Isolated supraspinatus deficiency Relative only (TO)
NOT a contraindication Why
Non-retracted isolated supraspinatus tear / 2-cm full-thickness SS tear Reparable at TSA
Passive ER <10° Release at surgery
Eccentric posterior glenoid erosion / retroverted glenoid Eccentric reaming
Poor glenoid bone stock Build up with graft (TO)

Subchondral cysts Normal end-stage OA finding
Age (young) TSA favoured over hemi

Cuff tears at TSAfull-thickness in 5–10% of TSA patients (Orthobullets) · <5% in primary OA (OB) — read the options · + impingement signs → pre-op MRI

RA + good elevation (120°), no superior migrationTSA cemented all-poly
✗ Wrong options: rTSA · hemi · arthroscopic debridement = less advanced disease

Rough humeral surface, intact glenoid cartilage, enough glenoid arc Recent sepsis
Insufficient bone for glenoid Neuropathic joint

Post-capsulorrhaphy arthropathy

Putti-Plattsubscapularis + anterior capsule divided; lateral stump → anterior glenoid neck; medial stump → tuberosity (pants-over-vest) → limits ER → incongruent contact loading → post-capsulorrhaphy arthropathy
✗ Wrong options: no coracoid transfer

Magnuson-Stackmiddle subscapularis + piece of LT transferred lateral to bicipital groove (restrict ER) → subscapularis lacerated during biceps release at TSA → ↑ ER, anterior instability, + belly press

View Look for

Type Description
A1 Concentric, centred head; minor central erosion

B0 Pre-OA posterior subluxation of head

5Management

Implant choice

Glenohumeral arthritis
  • Intact cuff + adequate glenoid→aTSA (cemented all-poly glenoid)
    • retroversion >15°→augment or posterior bone graft
  • Glenoid eroded to coracoid→hemiarthroplasty
  • Irreparable cuff / CTA / proximal migration→rTSA (or hemi)
  • Plexus palsy / active infection→no TSA

Approach

Deltopectoralcephalic vein = interval landmark · detach subscapularis + capsule from anterior humerus → dislocate anteriorly · tight shoulder: release upper half (Orthobullets) · upper 1/3 (OB) of pectoralis major tendon

Superior border of subscapularis (TO)biceps tendon (just medial to pec major insertion → follow up to rotator interval) · biceps ruptured/dislocated → base of coracoid marks medial interval

Inferior border of subscapularislandmark for axillary nerve (anterior → posterior under GH joint → quadrangular space)

Palpate cuff insertion before head cut — ✓ protects cuff

Subscapularis management & failure (peel, tenotomy, LTO; postoperative restrictions)

Takedown optionspeel (off bone) · tenotomy (trans-tendon) · partial tenotomy · lesser tuberosity osteotomy (LTO)

Which is best?no technique superior: no difference in strength, ROM/function, biomechanical strength or failure rates
✗ Wrong options: LTO lower failure · peel more ROM · tenotomy higher failure

LTOinterest due to bone-to-bone healing (biomechanical strength); high union rate · nonunion → very poor outcomes, multiple revisions

Most commonly ruptured muscle after TSA (TO)subscapularis · factors: multiple previous operations, overstuffing, aggressive physio, tendon length compromise (poor technique)

Glenoid morphology & retroversion correction (eccentric reaming, bone graft, augments)

Why correctfailure → glenoid malposition → ↓ contact area → ↑ contact pressure → accelerated loosening

>25° Allograft reconstruction of posterior defect Bone graft
Insufficient bone (to coracoid) No eccentric reaming → posterior bone graft or hemi —
Cuff-deficient / acetabularised acromion rTSA (reaming irrelevant) —

Eccentric reaming not forhumeral anteversion/retroversion (address with head cut + stem) · humeral head collapse · superior inclination 18° (exceeds correctable)

Glenoid deficiencybuild up with iliac crest autograft or resected humeral head · never cement to fill

Glenoid loosening – most common complication & risk factors

Frequencymost common cause of TSA failure: ~30% of primary OA revisions (OB) · 39% (TO) · reoperation 2.9% primary vs 28% revision TSA

Commonest complication at 5 yloosening of glenoid component
✗ Wrong options: humeral loosening · acromial stress fracture · infection

✓ Risk factor Not a risk factor
Glenoid morphology: biconcave (Walch B2), posterior glenoid wear, excessive retroversion Age (incl. >65)
Dysfunctional/deficient rotator cuff (rocking horse) Inferior humeral head osteophytes
Insufficient glenoid bone stock Subtle anterior subluxation (biconcave goes with posterior)
Excessive reaming removing subchondral bone Goutallier/cuff atrophy (not correlated)
Flat-back glenoid Curved-back (↓ loosening) · pegged component
Mismatch (see Mechanism) Stemless humerus · diabetes (infection) · uncemented central peg
Soft-tissue instability · infection · aseptic osteolysis ✗ Wrong options: osteonecrosis · RA · OA (as cause of glenoid loosening)

Radiolucent linespresence does not correlate with symptoms or clinical failure (3 + 7 y) · progression does correlate (50% by 3–4 y)

Treatmentglenoid removal (if bone stock) ± bone graft for later re-implantation · convert to rTSA (salvage) · glenoid morphology not fixable with aTSA → rTSA

Infection – C. acnes & work-up

Risk factor Not
Male (more sebaceous glands, more C. acnes; more TSA for post-traumatic/CTA) Female
Age <65 Age >65
Reverse TSA (vs anatomic) Anatomic TSA
Inflammatory or post-traumatic arthritis Primary OA
Corticosteroid injection within 3 months (e.g. 2 months) Injection 4 months before

RateC. acnes infection 1–2% after primary TSA (Orthobullets) · 4.6% (TO)

C. acnes (P. acnes)gram-positive, facultative, aerotolerant, anaerobic rod; ferments lactose → propionic acid · commonest cause of late/indolent infection + implant failure · >50% of chronic infections; S. epidermidis 2nd (15%)

C. acnes factscolonises shoulder > hip/knee · men > women bacterial burden · biofilm 18–90 h · presentation: early pain + stiffness, later swelling + redness · usually no fever (subtle)

Cultureshold 14 days (OB) · 10–14 days in anaerobic bottles, mean detection 6 days (Orthobullets TSA note) · 14–28 days (Orthobullets PJI note) — read the options · 16S rRNA PCR · sonicate explanted implant

Samplingarthroscopic tissue culture 100% sensitive + specific vs fluoroscopic aspiration 17% sensitive, 100% specific · aspiration may be normal · imaging + in only 24%

New pain after pneumonia / ↑ WBC + ESRhaematogenous → radiographs + aspiration with Gram stain + culture · well-fixed implants → I&D may avoid full revision
✗ Wrong options: wait 2 wk for repeat labs · PT/NSAIDs/stretching · MRI · emergent revision

Timing Treatment
Early (<6 wk) Open I&D
Late (>6 wk) / grossly infected (frozen >10 WBC/HPF, GPC in clusters) Remove components + antibiotic spacer → 2-stage reimplantation · IV antibiotics 6 wk (penicillin G, ceftriaxone, clindamycin, vancomycin) then PO 2–6 mo

Avoid in 2-stage stage 1bone grafting glenoid (won't heal with infection; do at stage 2) · resection arthroplasty (poor function) · head exchange/arthroscopic debridement (won't eradicate)

Musculocutaneous (lateral cord) Retraction on conjoint tendon / strap muscles (short head biceps + coracobrachialis) Weak forearm supination + elbow flexion (biceps)
Radial nerve Latissimus dorsi tenotomy for transfer (with rTSA) —

Anterior humeral circumflex vessels Distal dissection at inferior subscapularis (peel) —

Traumatic Anterior Shoulder Instability (TUBS)

Shoulder & Elbow · 58 / 60

1Basics

Epidemiology

TUBSTraumatic Unilateral dislocation, Bankart lesion, requires Surgery

Frequencyone of the most common shoulder injuries; 1.7%/year general population; shoulder = most commonly dislocated major joint

High-risk groupsmilitary, contact/collision athletes (rugby, American football commonest)

Hyperlaxityglobal hyperlaxity (Ehlers-Danlos, collagen disorders) → OR 2.68 for anterior instability · 3× recurrence · fewer capsulolabral lesions · more often atraumatic instability

Anatomy – static & dynamic restraints

Staticbony anatomy, capsule, GH ligaments, labrum (+50% glenoid depth)

Dynamicrotator cuff, long head of biceps

Concavity-compressioncuff compresses head into glenoid concavity; lost with anterior glenoid rim loss → ↓ effective depth
✗ Wrong options: adhesion-cohesion · negative intra-articular pressure: both preserved in closed capsule

Ligament Taut / restrains in Direction
SGHL Arm at side (0° abduction) Inferior
MGHL 45° abduction + ER Anterior (and posterior, OB)
Anterior band IGHL 90° abduction + ER Anterior – main anterior restraint
Posterior band IGHL 90° abduction Posterior

Main anterior stabiliser (TO)IGHL
✗ Wrong options: MGHL · SGHL · anterior capsule · subscapularis

Main stabiliser above 45° abduction (TO)IGHL

AIGHL glenoid attachmentusually to labrum; less commonly direct to glenoid neck

Pathoanatomy – Bankart lesion, IGHL & mechanism (abduction–external rotation)

Bankart lesionavulsion of anteroinferior labrum + anterior band IGHL from anteroinferior glenoid; labrum separated from the bony glenoid; "essential lesion" of traumatic anterior dislocation (TO)
✗ Wrong options: cartilage–labral junction only

Bankart frequency Source
80–90% of TUBS Orthobullets
85% (Rowe) · 87% (Hintermann) · 97% (Taylor 63/67) · 73.5% (Wolf) OB studies

Most common surgical findinganteroinferior labral tear
✗ Wrong options: anterosuperior · posterior · Hill-Sachs

Hintermann (212 dislocators)Bankart 87% · ventral capsule insufficiency 79% · Hill-Sachs 68% · GHL insufficiency 55% · complete cuff tear 14% · posterior labral tear 12% · SLAP 7%

Lesion Definition Key point
Bankart Labrum + IGHL off anteroinferior rim; medial periosteal hinge undisrupted (TO) Most common
Perthes (TO) Labrum avulsed (not torn), attached by intact but medially stripped periosteum May sit in normal position (neutral-arm MRI) → hard to see arthroscopically; stabiliser function lost → recurrent dislocation
ALPSA "Medialised Bankart": labroligamentous complex displaced medially (+ inferiorly) on scapular neck, intact medial hinge, fluid underneath; anterior labrum absent on rim (TO) Heals medially on glenoid neck · ↑ arthroscopic failure · common in recurrent instability treated nonop
GLAD Partial anteroinferior labral tear + adjacent glenoid articular cartilage defect ↑ arthroscopic failure · debridement relieves pain (Neviaser)
HAGL IGHL avulsed from humeral insertion See HAGL block
Bony Bankart Fracture of anteroinferior glenoid Up to 49% of recurrent dislocators
Kim lesion (TO) Concealed tear at posterior glenoid chondrolabral junction + concealed deep labral detachment Posterior instability; visible chondrolabral junction intact; probing → labral fluctuance; ± glenoid hypoplasia

Association (TO)Bankart, Perthes, HAGL, ALPSA, GLAD → all recurrent anterior instability · Kim → posterior

97% rule97% of recurrent instability have Bankart or ALPSA

Mechanismanteriorly directed force with arm abducted + externally rotated · posterior instability = adduction + internal rotation

Bankart vs positionAIGHL/anteroinferior labrum taut in ER at 90° abduction
✗ Wrong options: 45° = MGHL

Associated lesion in young dislocatorHill-Sachs
✗ Wrong options: full-thickness cuff tear = elderly · reverse Hill-Sachs = posterior · coracoid fracture = rare · GT fracture = less common than Hill-Sachs

"Clunk" in 22-y basketballerBankart + Hill-Sachs

Combined anterior & posterior labral tears

Pan-labral tear270–360° labral tear (anterior + inferior + posterior); anterior and/or posterior instability

Exampositive Jerk + Kim (posterior) + apprehension + relocation (anterior) → 270° tear → anterior + posterior labral repair (arthroscopic)

✗ Wrong options (images)bony Bankart / anterior Bankart (anterior repair only) · subscapularis tear (cuff repair) · Kim lesion (posterior only)

270° repair15% failure (Mazzocca)

Militaryhigh incidence of posterior and combined front-to-back tears → unrecognised pan-labral tear = cause of recurrence

HAGL lesion

HAGLhumeral avulsion of the (inferior) glenohumeral ligament, anterior band IGHL, without subscapularis tear; term coined by Wolf (1995)

RHAGLreverse HAGL = posterior band IGHL → posterior instability

Frequency7–9% of unstable shoulders (Wolf 9.3%: Bankart 73.5%, capsular laxity 17.2%) · Taylor 1/67 · Rhee 2% — rare

Patientslightly older than Bankart (Orthobullets) · older + more violent trauma (OB) · female collegiate athletes · hyper-abduction + ER

MRIbest on coronal sequences: J-shaped IGHL, contrast extravasating down humeral neck; bony HAGL variant; "floating" AIGHL = HAGL + capsulolabral detachment

Associationsalways with other lesions (Bankart, LHB tear, cuff tear); more severe anterior pain

Significance"other end of the IGHL" → missed HAGL = cause of failed Bankart repair → higher recurrence if unrepaired

Treatmentopen repair = classic / gold standard · arthroscopic possible but technically hard (70° scope, accessory portals)
✗ Wrong options: arthroscopic contraindicated classically

2Mechanism

Hill-Sachs lesion

Hill-Sachscompression/impaction fracture of posterosuperior (posterolateral) humeral head against anteroinferior glenoid rim; chondral impaction injury

Frequency80–100% of traumatic dislocations · 25% of traumatic subluxations · 68% (Hintermann) · 73% on X-ray (Edwards)

Most common associated intra-articular finding with Bankart
✗ Wrong options: cuff tear · SLAP · posterior labral tear · Buford

Arthroscopyindentation on posterior head beside the bare area
✗ Wrong options: bare area = normal cartilage-free zone

Significanceclinically irrelevant unless it engages; end-range (ABER) instability, not mid-range (TO)

Glenoid bone loss (TO)from anteroinferior rim fracture or erosion by humeral head; 6.8% loss per dislocation (average)

Reverse Hill-Sachsanteromedial head; posterior dislocation; lesser tuberosity fracture = posterior dislocation

3Presentation

Historytraumatic event; ask formal reduction vs spontaneous; instability feeling; pain from subluxation/excess translation

Apprehensionsupine, 90° abduction + 90° ER → apprehension; positive in mid-range abduction = glenoid bone loss

Relocationposterior force on humeral head → ↓ apprehension

Load and shiftgrades 0–III (table below); sulcus sign with arm at side

Diagnostic criteria – hyperlaxity

Criterion Threshold
Beighton score >4
Hyper-ER at side >85°
Hyperabduction (Gagey) >105°
Load–shift >2+ in ≥2 planes

ISIS hyperlaxityanterior (ER >85°) or inferior (Gagey) laxity = 1 point

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Modality / view Use
Trauma series: true AP (Grashey) + scapular Y + axillary Required; Grashey = beam ~45° off AP, end-on GH joint; Y = humeral head over Y intersection (scapular spine + coracoid)
Axillary Best for detecting dislocation; bone loss visible here = already significant; Velpeau if can't abduct
West Point Glenoid bone loss / bony Bankart
Stryker notch Hill-Sachs (supine, hand on head, 10° cephalic); poor for Bankart
AP in ER Hill-Sachs (ISIS item)
Bernageau profile Glenoid profile, "cliff sign"; less accurate than 3D imaging
CT ± 3D Bony injury, % glenoid bone loss; 3D CT = gold standard
CT arthrogram MRI contraindicated (pacemaker, cochlear implant); poorer soft tissue
MRI Best for labral tear; validated for bone loss
MR arthrogram Study of choice for soft tissue: sens 86–91%, spec 86–96% (MRI 44–100% / 66–95%)

MRI positioning – ABER view

ABERabduction + ER → humerus in coronal plane, glenoid in axial plane

Showsanteroinferior labrum, anterior band IGHL, articular surface of supraspinatus, posterosuperior labral peel-back (sens 73%, spec 100%)

Glenoid bone loss – assessment & critical thresholds

Method Fact
3D CT en face Gold standard; highest interrater reliability; predictive error similar to MRI (Rerko)
Best-fit circle (TO) Circle fitted to posterior + inferior glenoid ≈ original glenoid; or contralateral glenoid reference
Bare-spot method Bare spot = glenoid centre (Burkhart); GBL = (B − A) / 2B (A = bare spot→anterior edge, B = →posterior edge)
MRI Tends to overestimate GBL (✗ Wrong options: underestimates); less bone–soft tissue contrast; cuts must be en face
MR arthrogram Not a substitute for CT (poorer bony definition)
X-ray (Bernageau, West Point) Significantly less accurate

Worked example (OB)bare spot 9 mm anterior, 12 mm posterior → (12 − 9)/24 = 12.5% + non-engaging HS → Bankart alone

Worked example (OB)6.9 mm lost of 28.3 mm → 24.4% = critical → coracoid transfer

Inverted pearglenoid morphology with ↑ bone loss (>25%, TO/OB); 89% failure after arthroscopic repair

Glenoid shapenormally pear-shaped (narrow superior); anteroinferior loss → inverted pear

Threshold Meaning Source
>20–25% Critical; soft tissue alone fails (>2/3 failure) → bony procedure Orthobullets, most OB
>25–30% Osseous augmentation needed OB (bone loss explanations)
20–30% "Glenoid bone deficiency" → Latarjet; >60% recurrence with Bankart alone OB
15–25% Biomechanically unstable OB
21% of glenoid length Instability + ↓ ER after Bankart (Itoi) OB
17.3% Critical value (Shin: 43.9% vs 3.7% recurrence) OB
>13.5% Subcritical – critical may be this low; open Bankart ↑ recurrence Orthobullets, OB
<15% Soft-tissue stabilisation alone works OB, TO

5Management

First-time traumatic anterior dislocation
  • Reduce under sedation / IA lidocaine→traction-countertraction (commonest)
    • fails 5–10%→blocks: biceps tendon, capsule, fracture fragments
  • Low-risk→sling ≤1 wk + PT (cuff + periscapular)
  • Age >40 + persistent weakness→MRI shoulder (cuff tear)
  • In-season athlete, no bone loss → rehab, RTP in-season→surgery end of season
  • Young (<20–25) contact / military + Bankart on MRI→early arthroscopic Bankart
Recurrent instability – glenoid side (3D CT)
  • GBL <13.5–15% + on-track→arthroscopic Bankart (≥3–4 anchors)
  • GBL <15% + off-track→Bankart + remplissage
  • Subcritical 13.5–25% → contact athlete / high ISIS→Latarjet
    • non-contact, off-track→Bankart + remplissage
  • GBL >20–25% / inverted pear→Latarjet (coracoid transfer)
  • Failed Latarjet / massive loss→ICBG (Eden-Hybinette) or distal tibia allograft
Recurrent instability – humeral side (Hill-Sachs)
  • On-track / non-engaging (<20%)→nothing extra
  • Off-track / engaging 20–40% (>25%)→remplissage
  • >40%→humeral head allograft / ICBG; hemiarthroplasty if >40–45% + arthritis

✗ Wrong options: dorsal scapular · lateral pectoral · MC · axillary

Persistent pain/weakness ≥2 wk after dislocation (>40 y) → MRI shoulder
✗ Wrong options: EMG · C-spine MRI · steroid injection – harms later repair · PT first · CT glenoid

Test for commonest pathologydrop arm test (supraspinatus)
✗ Wrong options: O'Brien – SLAP · apprehension – young/bone loss · bear hug – subscap · Spurling – C-spine

MR arthrogrammost sensitive (and specific) for full- + partial-thickness cuff tears; MRI ≈ US

Treatmentsurgical repair → better pain + satisfaction; full-thickness tears don't heal nonop; GT fracture with dislocation >50 y (↑ recurrence)

Terrible triad of the shoulder

Shoulder terrible triad (TO)anterior dislocation + rotator cuff tear + brachial plexus (mostly axillary) nerve injury; cuff usually complete tear

EXCEPT (TO)proximal humeral fracture

Late complications – chondrolysis, osteonecrosis & dislocation arthropathy

Osteonecrosis (skeletally immature)rare; after fracture-dislocation or stabilisation → observation (revascularises)
✗ Wrong options: arthroplasty · grafting · capsular release

Chondrolysisprogressive pain + stiffness ~1 y after Bankart with heat (RF) probe → joint space loss
✗ Wrong options: frozen shoulder · subscap failure

Dislocation arthropathyage at first dislocation (>25 y, Hovelius) + high-energy primary dislocation → severe OA; "goat's beard" inferior osteophyte; ↓ ER
✗ Wrong options: current age · dominance · diabetes · sex

After Bristow-Latarjetmild arthropathy 35%, severe 14%; first dislocation >23 y = risk
